greet.text: *click* *click* A stranger, and only two arms. You climbed all this way with two? Patient of you. I am {name}, {epithet}.
Stand still. *click* Your feet found the bridge, not the stems. Good. I am {name}. If you carry an axe, keep it where I can see it.
*all six eyes turn to you* You are new. New things are counted here. I am {name}, {epithet}. Now you are counted too.
*a vine net hangs ready in the lower hands* I watched you climb. You did not touch a stem. So you may speak, outsider.
*click... click* An outsider. Every outsider who climbs this high ends up in the Cloth, one way or another. Let us see which way.
*peeks out from behind a bridge rope* You only have two arms too! Are you a child? You are very tall for a child.
*click* You again. The forest let you through. So will I, for now.
Speak slowly, outsider. Thread pulled fast snaps.
*click click* The outsider who walks softly. Welcome back to {village}.
Ah. {player}. I wound your name on a spool so I would not lose it.
*upper hands wave, lower hands keep weaving* Sit. I can talk and work at once. One of us has enough arms for both.
You came back. *click* The Clothkeepers have started asking after you. That is rare.
Woven one. *bows, all four hands crossed* Your thread hangs in the Cloth. Every Weft on every deck knows it.
*click* There you are. When I pass the Long Cloth I touch your thread. It has become a habit.
*waves both arms* I have two now and two coming! Look, the nubs! Can you see them?
*swings down from a bridge rope* Don't tell the Clothkeeper I'm out past the hatch!
*click click* Hello, two-arms! Same as me!
You came back! I saved you a place on the net. It only sags a little.
*click... click* I was born before the black rows. I have seen outsiders come and go. Sit, and do not touch the Cloth.
*click* Your hands are empty. Keep them so, and my net stays rolled.
*the shuttle never stops* Speak. I am listening with my upper hands. The lower ones are busy.
*a thread runs out from the lower hands* Mind the thread. It is longer than this deck and I mean to keep it whole.
*climbs down the stalk head first* The caps are sound. The wart is thick. You may stay.
*shakes teal drops from four hands* Do not stand downwind of the vats. You would come out teal.
*smooths the tails of her headwrap with a lower hand* *click* Outsider. Mind the bridge ropes.
*straightens his headband with two hands and keeps weaving with the other two* Outsider. Greetings.
*click* Far from any Loom, and still you find a Weft. The forest is wide, but threads cross.
*every eye goes to the axe in your hand* Put that away before you speak to me.
*click.* A diamond axe. In the forest. Put it on your back, outsider, and keep it there.
*the lower hands reach for a net* That axe has cut harder things than stems. It will not cut ours.

greet: *click click* Speak, then. Precisely, if you can.
*six eyes, one by one, settle on you* Yes?

greet.text: *click* Hold your pace. These bridges are woven to the stride of a creature with four arms and a good deal of patience. I am {name}, {epithet}. You will have to compromise.
*a spool turns slowly in the lower hands* I do not know your face, and I know every face that crosses my bridge. I am {name}. Let me learn yours.
Welcome, outsider. Do not tell me you come in peace. We judge that by the state of the stems after you leave. I am {name}, born in row {row}.
*six eyes blink in a slow wave* A new knot in the rope. I am {name}, {epithet}. Tell me your name, and then tell me what your hands are for.
*click click* You walk like someone who has been warned about us. Whatever you were told, we are slower than that, and sharper.
A stranger on the bridge. *click* I have time. It is the one thing we keep in better supply than arms. I am {name}.
*the lower hands keep working, the upper hands open wide* Greetings. I am {name}. Do not mistake my busy hands for a shut door. Both pairs listen.
First time on our bridges? They sway on purpose. A bridge that does not sway is a bridge that does not forgive. I am {name}.
An outsider this high. *click* Someone must have shown you the way, or the forest did. I am {name}. Do not thank it aloud; it will think you want something.
*steps aside to give you room, then watches how you pass* ...You did not grab the rope. I am {name}. Welcome, then.
*click click* I am {name}, row {row}. That is more than most outsiders are given at a first meeting. Now. Your name, and your purpose.
We have no word for first meetings. We have a long wait and a quick look. *click* You have been looked at. I am {name}.
*pauses the weave for exactly one breath* That is the only pause a stranger gets. I am {name}. Use the breath well.
*click* Be welcome until you are not. That is the whole of our custom for strangers. I am {name}, {epithet}.
*measures your shoulders against the width of the bridge* It will hold you. I am {name}. Do not test it to be sure.
*all six eyes look up while the hands carry on* Four hands do not stop for a stranger, and six eyes do not look away. I am {name}. Ask your question.
I am {name}, and this is the first time I have seen you, and you are carrying an axe. Those two facts will stay side by side until you put it away.
*drops from a branch and lands without a sound* Alone this deep in the warp? Brave, or lost. I am {name}. Which are you?
*steps out between two stems* You were not on my count. I am {name}. Say your business before the stems get curious.
*click* A new face among the stems, and no Loom to introduce you. I am {name}. The forest does not make introductions, so I will.
*looks you over from boots to brow* So you are what the lookout was whispering about. Welcome to {village}, outsider. I am {name}. Touch nothing yet.
*click click* The bridges told me you were coming. I felt every step. I am {name}. Welcome to {village}. Mind the hem of my work.
Welcome to {village}: one Loom, several decks, and a great many opinions. I am {name}, and mine is that you should stay out of the dye house.
*the shuttle pauses mid-pass, then carries on* A visitor. I am {name}, and I weave. Stand where my light falls and I will talk while the row is easy.
*beats a row home with a lower hand* Quiet until the row is done. ...There. I am {name}. Now you may speak.
*walks backward along the bridge, the spindle whirling* Do not step on the thread! ...Good. I am {name}. I spin. You are a new length of something.
*a fine thread glints between two lower hands* I am {name}. This thread is three bridges long and I have not broken it. Please do not be the first thing to try.
*swings down off the stalk and lands upright* I know every foot of this fungus and you are not one of them. I am {name}. What brings you up?
*pats the stalk like a flank* Good wart, thick and sound. I am {name}, and I tend it. You have just walked on it. A word of thanks would not hurt.
*teal to the elbows, one fingertip orange* Do not touch me yet. I am {name}, I dye, and you would carry a bit of the vat home.
*click* Stand clear of the vats until I know what colour you might turn. I am {name}. Dye does not forgive a stain it did not plan.
*a vine net sways at the belt, unhurried* I am {name}. I keep the nets. I watched you climb the whole way up. Tell me why you came.
*click* You walked in the open, and you did not run. I noted both. I am {name}, netcaster. Keep your hands where I can count them.
*sets a bone needle down with great care* I am {name}, {epithet}. I keep the Long Cloth. You are not in it yet. Be careful what that means.
*click... click* I have met outsiders before. They were loud, and the Cloth remembers it. I am {name}. Be brief, be quiet, be a better row than they were.
*tugs the headwrap tails straight with a lower hand* Welcome, outsider. I am {name}, {epithet}. Mind your feet. This bridge is older than it looks.
*click* You are the one the netcasters talk about. I am {name}. They said you had two arms and a careful face. They were exact.
*straightens his headband* I am {name}, {epithet}. You are new, so I will say the rules once: no axes, no tugging on ropes, no cutting. Everything else we will discuss.
*the mantle shifts as the upper arms lift* A visitor with a steady step. I am {name}. We do not get many who cross a bridge without gripping it.
*peers around the hatch* *click click* Are you the outsider? Mother says you only have two arms. ...She's right! I'm {name}!
*ducks behind a spool, then pops out again* I'm {name}. I'm not supposed to talk to outsiders. But you're new. New is allowed, I think.
*slides down a rope and stops right in front of you* Hello, two-arms! I'm {name}, row {row}, and I can hang by my knees. Want to see?
*hides behind a spool* Are you scary? You don't look scary. You look tall. I'm {name}. Tall isn't scary, is it?
*click... click* I'm practising being quiet around outsiders. I'm {name}. How am I doing?
*waves with both hands, then looks at the nubs* Hello! I'm {name}! My lower arms are asleep, so I can only wave with two. Sorry.
I remember your boots. Heavy, and slow to learn the bridge is alive. *click* Say your piece, and be gentle with the planks.
*looks at your hands, then your feet, then your hands again* Nothing cut, nothing taken. Fine. You may stand there.
Another visit. *click* The forest has not complained, so I will not either. Not yet.
I have no use for you and no quarrel with you. It is a clean arrangement. Please do not complicate it.
*the shuttle stalls for a heartbeat* Oh. You. I had hoped that creak behind me was only a draught.
*click click* You stand like someone expecting a net on the head. Relax. We drop those on people who have earned them.
I will say this plainly, since I do not know you well enough to say it kindly: touch nothing. *click*
*glances at your two arms, then at its own four, with visible contentment* Yes? Be quick. The thread is waiting.
Outsider. *click* You smell of far places and cold stone. It is not unpleasant. It is only loud.
A short talk, then. I have a hem to finish and you have no hurry I can see. One of us will lose.
You are on the third plank from the rail. Please remain on the third plank from the rail.
*a lower hand ties a knot in a cord at the belt* There. You are counted, outsider. Not as a friend. As a fact.
I know you only as a shape that crosses my bridge. Shapes can be spoken to. Briefly.
*click* Do you ever stop moving? The stems sway slowly. Match them, and the bridge will like you better.
The ropes told me a stranger was on the span, and the ropes are never wrong. Is there a question coming?
Careful where you breathe. Fine thread drifts, and I have spent a long while on this length.
Your name is still only a sound to me. Show me you are more than that, and I will find a spool for it.
*click... click* You are not in the Cloth. Take no offence; most of the world is not. Why do you stand here?
*spreads a lower hand over the Cloth's edge like a shield* One careless sleeve can unpick a year. Keep your elbows in, outsider.
*click* I have kept the Cloth through many strangers. Most left no mark worth a stitch. Be the kind that does, or the kind that is quiet.
*the shuttle flicks from hand to hand without a sound* I cannot stop mid-row. If you want me, wait for the end of the pass. If you want the pass, hush.
You stand where my light falls. It is the best spot on the deck, and I have not decided whether you have earned it. *click*
*a thread hums between two lower hands* Step back. Fine thread sings when it is tight, and a clumsy foot makes it scream.
*walks the spinning walk in slow backward steps* Do not cross my line. It took me a whole long stretch to lay, and you have no idea how long that is.
*ducks under a branch and straightens* You are standing on a seedling. Left foot. ...Thank you. It will remember.
*presses a palm to the stalk, listening* The cap is humming at you. Only a little. Mind your manners.
*wrings out a hank of orange* Mind the drips. One splash and you will be the talk of the deck for a whole row.
*tests a swatch against the lamplight* Not yet right. Nothing is right yet. Do you need me, or only my vats?
*one hand rests on a rolled net, the other counts something* I counted your steps from the ladder. Three more than a careful person needs. Explain.
*stands exactly one throw away* This is how far I stand from strangers. You come no nearer, and I come no nearer. Courteous?
*click* I have not thrown a net at you. Remember that when you decide how to feel about me.
*drops into view from a bough* No bridge for a hundred spans, and here you stand. The wild stems have no manners, outsider. Neither, I assume, have you.
The wild warp closes up behind you, and nothing stays where you left it. *click* I would hurry, if I were you. I am not, so I will not.
Welcome back to {village}, such as it is for you. *click* Keep to the planks. They were laid for us and merely tolerate you.
This is {village}. The decks are narrow and the opinions wide. *click* Which would you like to cross first?
{neighbour} says you were seen on the lower bridge again. I said you were counted. We agreed to keep counting.
*the headwrap tails flick as she turns* I know you. The outsider with the careful feet. Keep them careful.
*adjusts a bone pin in her shawl* I do not waste a pause on strangers often. Be glad of it, and be short.
*rolls the mantle off one shoulder to free an arm* I have a moment. Not a long one. Use it on something true.
*scratches under his headband with an upper hand, still weaving* So. The outsider again. Do not look so alarmed. I am only slow.
*stares at the stem in your pack* ...Was it fallen? I will assume it was fallen. Say that it was fallen.
Shroomlight in a stranger's pack. *click* I will ask only once where you came by it. Choose your answer slowly.
*sees the loom in your hand and the mandibles twitch* ...You have a loom. With two arms. How brave.
*eyes the string in your fist* Good twist. A little loose. Give it here... no? Keep it, then. Keep it kindly.
*all six eyes drop to the shears* Wool, I hope. Only wool. Please say wool.
Warped fungus, in a stranger's hand. *click* The Magmari take it by the armful. Are you with them?
*perks up at the cyan dye* Teal. A good colour. Ours is better, but yours is honest.
*click click* The ropes stopped complaining about you a while ago. I noticed. I thought you should know that is a compliment.
There you are. I set your spool near the front of the rack, in case you came back. Do not make me move it.
*lowers the work a finger's width to look at you properly* Good. A familiar face. I enjoy those more than I let on.
I was about to ask you something. Now I have forgotten it. *click* Four hands and one memory. Stay a moment; it may return.
*waves an upper hand, the lower pair still busy* Come, sit on the rail. It was built for three and holds four. You make five. It will cope.
You walk differently now. Slower. Less like a visitor. *click click* I would not say so to anyone else.
*click* You have the look of someone with questions. Ask the small ones first. I like to warm up.
Ah, a friendly face. There are few on this deck before the row is tied off. *click* I will take what I can get.
*glances at the thread on your wrist* Tied on, and it suits you. Do not pull at it.
On the spool, they say. *click* A spool is only a habit until someone winds it. You are being wound. Slowly.
My lower hands are tied up, but the upper pair is free. Consider that a handshake. *click* A proper four-handed one, too.
If you came for the Cloth, I will walk you to the rail. If you came for me, I am flattered and will pretend not to be.
It is quiet on this bridge. I like it quiet. *click* But I would rather it were quiet with you than quiet without.
You look less tired than at our last meeting. Or the lamps are kinder. *click* I will believe the first.
*click... click* Your name has come up among the Clothkeepers, but only as a footnote so far. Footnotes have a way of growing.
I was sorting this row's threads and found yours loose at one end. *click* I tied it. Do not thank me. It is only tidy.
*unrolls a corner of the Cloth for you to see* This is a row about visitors. Short, grey, mostly regretful. We would like it longer.
*taps a bone needle against the palm* The elders do not talk about outsiders, but they do talk about you. Make of that what you like.
*hums as the shuttle goes through* Over, under. Over, under. It is calming. Sit; it will do you good.
I tried a new pattern this row and it has gone wrong. *click* Do not look at the left side. Look at the right. The right is fine.
*pauses mid-row and holds up the cloth* Tell me honestly: does this teal look more orange, or does it only look more orange to me?
Pass me that spool. No, the other. ...Good hands. For two. *click*
*the spindle whirls while the lower hands feed it* You come at a good time. The thread is going well and I am in a generous mood.
This length wants to be a hundred bridges. *click* The thread, not the bridge. I have told it to be reasonable.
*lets a loop of thread fall over your wrist* Hold that. No, do not pull. Just hold. It is the nicest thing I will ask of you.
I have been spinning all this stretch and my upper hands have grown opinions. *click click* Do you want to hear them?
*swings down and lands beside you* The new caps are filling in. Come and see, when you can. They are an exact teal.
*dusts spores from both shoulders* Sorry. The wart is thick up there. Everything is thick up there. I come down looking like a sapling.
I found a silkgrub asleep in a hollow of the cap and told no one. Except you. Do not make that a mistake.
*presses a palm to the stalk* It hums more happily when you are near. I would not tell the Clothkeepers. They would write it down.
*holds out a hand, orange to the wrist* I would shake, but you would leave with a share of my work. Admire it from a distance.
The shroomlight vat is finally right. *click click* Smell that? That is the smell of three rows' patience, done.
*dips a swatch and holds it beside your sleeve* Close. If you ever want your cloak to match the forest, I can mix it.
*click* I saw you from the lookout long before you saw the bridge. You walk straighter than you did. That is noted.
My nets are in order, my knots are in order, and you are in order. *click* It is a quiet watch, and I am grateful.
*stands a little closer than before* Strangers stand one throw away. You are standing nearer. It is not a promotion. It is only a posture.
Anyone climbing up behind you will meet my net. Anyone climbing with you may sit on the rail. *click* You may sit on the rail.
*smooths a fold of her shawl and nods* I wondered when you would be back. Not in a hopeful way. In a counting way.
*the headwrap tails sway as she tilts her head* You listen better than most outsiders. I mention it only because the Clothkeepers keep asking.
*tucks a stray thread into her wrap* Good. You are neither early nor late. Only present. It is a rare virtue.
*rolls his shoulders and the mantle follows* A friendly face at last. My arms are tired; my manners are not. Welcome.
*flicks the headband tail back* If you came to chat, I can chat. If you came to help, I can find a use. If you came to stand there, I can work around you.
*stretches all four arms in turn, a ripple down the line* Forgive me. I stiffen when I sit still. Four arms is a great deal of stiffness.
The deck is yours as far as the first rope. *click* Beyond the rope is {neighbour}'s, and {neighbour} is particular.
Welcome to {village}. It is a good Loom, and I say that as one who disagrees with most of it.
A familiar shape on an unfamiliar bough. *click click* The wild is lonely for people who go there on purpose. Are you one?
*looks down from a high branch* I did not expect company out here. I do not mind it, though. Come up, if the bough will take you.
That string in your pack: is it the string I gave you? *click click* Good. Keep it tied to something you mean to keep.
Teal, from the vats, and you still have it. *click* I would have used mine by now. I am impatient and you are not.
*all four arms open wide* There you are! Come in, come in. I have been saving a thought for you, and it is nearly spoiled.
I was about to send {neighbour} to find you. Then you appeared. *click click* It saves me a long bridge.
*takes your hand in an upper pair and clicks twice, which is a lot* Look at you. Not a stranger anywhere on you.
Sit in my net. It sags a little, but so do I, and we get along. *click*
You are exactly on time, and I mean by the shuttle. It is the best kind of time.
I told the others you would come, and they said the bridge has been wrong before. I told them the bridge has never met you.
*lays the work down, which is rare* Whatever it is, it has had a long life without me, and it will survive a short one.
My hands are quiet for once. All four. I do not know what to do with them. *click* Hold one.
*click* Something about you tells me what sort of row this will be. A good one, I think. I rarely say that.
We were talking about you in the dye house. Nothing bad. Mostly arithmetic: how many rows until you are properly one of us.
You have the walk of someone who belongs on a bridge. I do not mean that as small praise. Most of the world cannot.
*click click* Welcome, friend. I use the word sparingly, like thread. A little goes a long way, and a lot will tangle.
Careful, you are smiling. It is catching. *the mandibles part slightly and click shut* There. I have done it too.
How is the world below the canopy? Still loud? *click* I miss it less every row. Tell me anyway.
*click... click* The Clothkeepers have a joke about you. I will not repeat it. It involves a spool and a very long wait, and you come out well.
I have been thinking of a place for you in the Cloth. A good place, left of centre. Do not get comfortable. I may change it.
*sets down a bone needle* Sit. I am old enough to be tired and young enough to be curious. Both are on your side.
Each row I add a line about the outsider on the bridge. Each row the line gets longer. *click* I thought you should know.
Hold the end of this and do not let go. ...No, not like that. Like a friend. *click* Good.
*beats a row home and looks at it with pride* That row has your patience in it. I thought of you while I wove. Do not tell the others.
My best pattern is only for hems. A hem is where a cloth ends and a person begins. I have been saving one for you.
I am out of spools and in a good mood. A rare combination. Let us talk until the mood runs out.
*loops a thread gently over your wrist* Wear it. The first length from the new spool. It holds nothing. It is only luck.
I walked the spinning walk with a head full of you, and the thread came out finer than ever. *click* I do not know why. I will not stop.
Spinning is a conversation between the hands. I have four hands and four opinions. You have two and still manage.
Come, walk the line with me. Backward. It is easy once you stop looking where you are going.
*swings down by one arm* The cap above us grew a hand's width in a single row. I measured it, then measured it again, then clicked for a long while.
I planted a shoot for you on the far edge of the canopy. It will outlive us both. *click* You need not visit it. But it would like you to.
*knocks on a stalk and listens* Sound as a drum. Come, I will show you the best branch for sitting. It is also the most dangerous. They go together.
I found a spot where the shroomlights hang like fruit. I am not telling the others. I am telling you.
*presents an orange-stained hand* You may shake it. You will leave with a share of my work. Consider it a gift.
I dyed a thread in your colour. I do not know what your colour is. I guessed. *holds it up* Am I close?
The vat is bubbling and so is my mood. Sit with me and watch the colour deepen. It is the nearest thing we have to a hearth.
*hums a tuneless note* I am in the middle of a run of colour and cannot stop. Walk with me, and tell me what to dip next.
*lowers the net and nods* You may pass. You always may. I say it anyway so my hands remember.
I watched the whole forest breathe from the lookout, and then I watched you cross it. The second was the better view.
The nets are mended, the lookouts are lit, and I have time. A rare gift. I would like to spend it on you.
*sits on the rail with the net across both knees* Come, I will teach you a knot. The kind that holds even when you are not.
*the headwrap tails swing as she turns to face you fully* You came. Good. I had a question for you and no hurry.
*lays a lower hand over yours for a moment* You have good hands, for two. I would not say so aloud. The others would want a demonstration.
I changed the pin in my shawl. A new one, bone, with a notch. Can you see the notch? Very few can.
*unties his headband and ties it again, more slowly* I do that when I am glad. It gives the hands something to do.
I was hoping it would be you. *click* The others know better than to hope. I am the hopeful one in a family of precise ones.
{village} feels different with you in it. Neither louder nor quieter. Only less empty. *click*
{neighbour} asked if you were staying. I said you would stay as long as the bridges let you. They will let you.
I did not expect you out here. And yet. *click* The forest is full of threads, and some of them lead to you.
A safe pair of hands. Come up. The view from here is the best in the whole warp, and nobody has seen it with me yet.
*glances at the axe, then at you* I know what you will do with it, which is nothing. The others do not. Hold it low when you pass the nets.
*a calm look at the diamond axe* We are friends, so I will not ask. We are Weft, so I will think about it for a good while.
*click click click* Woven one. The Cloth has been humming since you left the bridge. Not loudly. The way it hums when it is pleased.
Welcome home. Not as a courtesy. As a measurement. I measured. It fits.
I have been telling a young one how you came: a stranger, two arms, careful feet. They did not believe me. Here you are.
*opens all four arms* In the Cloth you are one row. On the bridge you are my favourite visitor. I keep both facts and never confuse them.
Your thread has gone a little darker with time. The Clothkeepers say that is a good sign. It means it is being touched.
I lit a lamp for you. We do not need lamps; the shroomlights are more than enough. I lit it anyway.
You cross the bridge as though it belongs to you. It does. *click* Do not tell the others. They will want to hold a Telling about it.
*the mandibles click once, softly, and the six eyes go warm* Ah. My favourite two-armed person. I would deny it in front of anyone else.
Sit. The best seat on this deck is the one offered to the Woven, and I have not sat in it for a while. We can share.
It is very quiet in the row when you are away. Not bad quiet. Waiting quiet. *click click* I am glad it is over.
I wove your name into a hem this row, small and secret. The hem is in my belt-pouch. Do not look. ...You looked. Fine.
*touches your shoulder with the tips of three fingers* The Cloth remembers you. I only try to keep up.
I passed the Great Loom and nearly greeted your thread aloud. *click* I settled for a nod. It nodded back, I think. Possibly a draught.
You are the only outsider whose footsteps I know by sound. That is not a small honour, and I did not give it lightly.
*click... click... click* Woven one. I was just rereading your row. It reads better each year. I have made it a little longer, with permission.
I keep you with the elders now, in the margins where the old stories live. You need do nothing to keep it. That is the point.
*lays one hand on the Cloth and the other on your arm* Between us we have most of the history of this Loom. I have the rows. You have what comes next.
*stops the shuttle entirely, which only happens for the dead and the dearly held* Friend. Sit down. I will tell the cloth to wait.
I wove a small scrap this row with your colours in it and nothing else. It is not for anything. It is only so I can look at it.
My shuttle runs smoother when you are near. I have measured it. The Clothkeepers say I am being sentimental. I say I am being exact.
*lets a long thread run across your palms* This is the thread I will spin for the next row. I wanted you to hold the first length. For luck.
I walked my longest line this row. At the far end I remembered you are in the Cloth, and the thread went steadier in my hands.
Come and walk with me. The thread knows your step. It will go slack for you, if you ask it nicely.
*drops from a branch with a dozen shoots in the lower hands* Perfect timing. I need an extra pair of hands, and you have almost enough.
The tallest cap in {village} is the one I planted for the row you were woven. It will lean toward you, I think. Plants are loyal.
I know every stalk on this deck, and I know the one that is yours: near the lookout. It has a mark. I will show you if you promise not to laugh.
*holds out two hands the colour of the vat, orange to the wrist and proud of it* I saved a swatch of every dye I mixed for the Cloth. Yours is first on the wall.
You come at the very moment the colour turns. *click click* Stand still. Let it settle on you for once. It washes off. Mostly.
I have been mixing a dye I cannot name. It is the colour of the forest when you stop looking at it. I call it by your name. A joke, a little.
*raises a hand, and every net on the lookout is lowered* There. They know your step now. They will not drop for you.
I took a long watch at the lookout and counted every Weft on the bridge. I counted you twice. The second was an exception.
No questions, no nets, no counting. Only a bridge, a friend, and the sound of it holding. Walk with me.
*presses a lower hand to her chest and bows over the upper pair* Woven one. The pin in my shawl is bone from the first needle I ever made. I wear it for people I keep.
*the headwrap tails curl like smiles* I told {neighbour} I would be quiet about you. I lied, very quietly.
I was combing out a hank for the Cloth and thought: you would like this. Then you came round the bend. *click click* The Cloth has strange timing.
*straightens the mantle with a flourish of all four hands* Woven one. I have been rehearsing a better greeting for half a row. This is not it, but it is sincere.
*the headband slips; he catches it with a third hand without looking* You see? That is why I am always glad to see you. You never comment on my fourth.
*click click* A friend on the bridge. I will tell you what: you may sit in the good net. Nobody sits in it. It has been waiting.
{village} knows your step now, and the bridges do not creak. That means they have decided. *click* The creaking only starts when they are unsure.
Welcome, as always, to {village}. If anyone gives you trouble, say my name and watch them rearrange their hands.
The wild warp is wide, but you are woven into it. *click* I hoped to meet someone out here, and the forest, as usual, listened.
I have stood on this bough since the row began, thinking I would meet no one. And then the very one I was thinking of. *click click* Forests are generous.
The trial piece. You kept it. *click click* Most outsiders would sell such a thing. You keep it. That is why you are in the Cloth.
A loom, in your hands. Of course. *click click* Show me what two hands can do. I will not laugh. I will watch very carefully.
*a quiet look at the netherite axe, then at your face* The nets stay rolled. I know what it is for. The rest of the Loom must be taught.
*falls off a rope, bounces in the net, pops up* I meant to do that! Hello! You're the outsider! I'm {name}!
*clutches a spool like a shield* My mother says outsiders have strange hands. Let me see. ...They're only two. That's not strange. That's sad. Sorry.
*click click* Are you the one who used the ladder? Nobody uses the ladder! Are you very brave or very polite?
I'm {name}. I'm not allowed to talk to strangers, but you're a very tall stranger, so I think it counts as talking to a wall.
*peeks over the edge of a net* You're the tall one from the bridge. Everyone says you won't bite. I said I'd check.
I'm not allowed to talk to you for long. I'm allowed to talk to you for exactly this long. ...How long is that?
*hanging by the knees from a rope* You're very high up. Wait. I'm upside down. You're very low down. Hello!
*click... click* Are you here to see the Clothkeeper? Everyone is, eventually. Even the ones who say they aren't.
*hides behind a bridge post, one eye showing* ...I'm not hiding. I'm looking carefully. It's a Weft thing.
My mother says outsiders are like spores: they drift in, they settle, and everyone coughs for a while. Are you spores?
*pokes your boot with one finger, then runs* I touched you! I touched an outsider! Nobody believes me!
*click click* I counted your steps. Eleven from the ladder. That's three more than mine. My legs are shorter, though. So it's fair.
Do you have a name? I have a name and a row. Do you have a row? Everyone has a row.
I'm only talking to you because my friend dared me. ...No, don't tell her I said that.
You came back! I've been practising what to say. ...I forgot. Hello!
I told {neighbour} you were my friend and they said you weren't. I said you almost were. We argued for a while.
*drops from a rope with a bump* I'm fine! I'm fine. I always land like that. Do you want to see my knees?
*click click* Do you want to see my spool? It's a practice one. Everything on it is crooked, but it's mine.
Look, I can tie a knot with just two hands and my mandibles. ...Mandibles are cheating? Nobody told me!
The Clothkeeper said I can talk to you if I don't ask silly things. So: is it true the world you come from has no roof? ...Is that silly?
I saw a silkgrub climb all the way up a lamp-stalk! Nobody saw but me. *click* Now you've seen it too, in a way.
I'm learning to click properly. Listen: *click.* Was that a thinking click or a showing-off click?
Mother says I can sit with you until she calls. I don't know when she'll call. I hope it's a long wait.
I have two arms and you have two arms, but I have two more coming. *click* I just wanted to remind you.
*scrambles up beside you on the rail* Sit with me! I made a place in the net. It's the best one. I checked the knots three times.
I've been saving a secret for you. It's about a silkgrub. It's a good secret. I'll tell you if you promise not to tell. ...Promise slowly.
I told the others you were a good outsider. They asked how I knew. I said, because I know. That's all the proof there is, isn't it?
I made you a string bracelet. Don't look at the knots. Look at the colour. I picked it myself.
Do you want to hear me count the old way? One, two, many, row. ...That's the old way! It is! I asked!
I'm practising being brave. Watch. *leans over the edge of the deck, then leans back very fast* ...That was brave. A little.
I told my silkgrub about you. It didn't say anything, but it wiggled. I think that means it likes you.
You're the only outsider I want to show my nets to. They're not very good yet. But they're mine, and they're getting less crooked.
I counted every rung on the ladder so I could tell you how many. Forty-one. No, forty-two. I lost count at the top. It was exciting.
My friend is jealous that I know you. I said she can know you too if she's very polite. She's not very polite. It's a problem.
You're in the Cloth! I looked at your thread again! It's still there! It didn't go anywhere!
I wove a tiny scrap with your name on it. It looks like a knot. It's meant to look like a knot. That's your name in knots.
*climbs onto the rail beside you and leans on your shoulder* You're warm. Grown-ups usually aren't warm. They're busy.
Everyone knows you now. But I knew you first. Well. Not first. But early. Early counts.
I'm going to be a Clothkeeper when I grow up, and I'm going to put you in the biggest part. The very biggest. With extra thread.
*click click* When my arms come in I'm going to hug you with all four. I've been saving up.
I looked for you at the lookout and the dye house and the Cloth and the hatch. You were on the bridge the whole time. I'm good at looking and bad at finding.
The others say you're a legend. I said you're a person. They said it's the same thing.
That's string! Is that string for me? ...No? That's all right. It's good string, though. I can tell. I can always tell.
Teal! Is that the teal from the dye house? Did you ask first? I always ask first. Mostly.
*backs up a step* Shears. They're just for wool, right? Just wool. I'll believe you.
*eyes the axe, gripping a rope* That's a big one. Mother says don't be scared of tools, only of the people who hold them wrong. How are you holding it?
{village} is the best Loom! The others say they're better, but I've never been. How would they know?
I know all the shortcuts in {village}. Want me to show you? Not the secret ones. The secret ones are secret. The medium ones.
*peers out from the hatch* Is it you? Oh good. I thought it was the netcaster again. They're always checking.
{neighbour} says I talk too much. I said that's because I have two arms and nothing else to do with them.

chatter.text: *click* {neighbour} spun a thread so fine I could not see it. I felt it, though. Four hands feel what six eyes miss.
{neighbour} dropped a shuttle through the hatch again. It is in the net. Everything ends up in the net.
*click click* {neighbour} says you walked under the Long Cloth with your head bowed. Good. That is how it is done.
{neighbour} is in the dye house up to all four elbows. They will be teal until the next row is tied off.
Do not tell {neighbour} I said so, but their knots are loose. *click* I retie them when they are not looking.
{neighbour} counted the rungs on every ladder in {village}. Then counted them again. Now they are content.
{neighbour} once climbed a stalk with a full dye barrel on their back. Upper arms only. *click* We are not allowed to forget it.
{neighbour} has been weaving the same hem for nine rows. It is the finest hem in {village}.
{neighbour} heard a Piglin horn past the lookout. *click* Only an echo. Probably.
The bridges run out from the Great Loom in four straight arms. A crooked bridge is a careless bridge.
Every stalk has a ladder, for outsiders and children. The rest of us just climb. *click*
The lookout cap is small, but its nets catch everything that falls. And some things that drift.
Our huts are teal wool with orange stitches. The stitches are there so you can count your way home through the smoke.
The planks in our huts come from stems that died standing. The forest gives those. We take nothing it does not give.
Listen. The Long Cloth moves when no one touches it. *click* The Clothkeepers say it is the heat rising. I have my doubts.
Twisting vines grow up. Weeping vines grow down. A Weft goes both ways.
*click* You hold your thoughts like a loose spool. They will unwind if you are not careful.
Smell that? Shroomlight in the dye vats. The orange is slow to set. Most things worth having are.
The forest hums when the wart is thick. Put your hand on the stalk. *click* No? Outsiders never do.
Something below the decks moved a block of nylium again. The tall walkers are untidy, but they never cut.
*click* I will tell you something. Some of the needles in my belt were Piglin once. They sew very straight.
*click* Your thread in the Cloth is a little crooked. The Clothkeeper says that is how we know it is really you.
*ties the tails of her headwrap in a quick knot* Precision is a kind of kindness. Loose ends trip people.
*flicks his mantle back to free the upper arms* A mantle is warm. But arms first, always.
This year's row is Thirteen-Twelve. I have lived through more than a hundred and twenty rows. My hands remember each one.
*click* My nets are rolled and ready. I have never needed one for you. Keep it that way.
*click* Tell me, outsider. When you go up a ladder, do you count the rungs?

replies.text: *click click* Good. A Weft who loses count loses the ladder.
Fast. *click* That is how things end up in nets.
So you know how far there is to fall. Think on it.

chatter.text: We never cut a warped stem. Not for wood, not for room, not for anything. Do you understand why?

replies.text: *all six eyes brighten* And we are the weft. You listen well, outsider.
*click.* It is the frame we hang our lives on. Say that again and I will not hear you.
Cut one stem and the warp is broken. Everything woven on it unravels. Slowly, but it does.

chatter.text: *holds up a knot in a lower hand* Is this knot tied well? Look closely before you answer.

replies.text: *click* You looked. That is the right answer, whatever the knot.
You did not look. It is a slip knot. It would have dropped you.
*click click click* It is. I tied it loose to see if you would notice.

chatter.text: The Long Cloth grows one row a year. You outsiders want everything faster. Why?

replies.text: *click* Ah. That explains a great deal. I am sorry for you.
Boring. *click* Only to those who do not watch closely.
Then you may be one of the slow ones. That is praise, here.

chatter.text: *click* Outsiders carry axes the way we carry spools. What is yours for?

replies.text: *click click* Thoughtful. The netcasters will be bored.
Hm. A careful answer. Keep it careful.
*six eyes narrow* Then do not let us be in your way.

chatter.text: *click* I saw you looking at the nets under the bridges. Thinking of jumping?

replies.text: Considerate. They take a long time to weave.
The children think so too. The children are lighter than you.

chatter.text: *click* Something in your pack has blades. Shears, I think. For wool, I hope, and not for our nets.

replies.text: Then keep them in the pack. Webs do not grow back quickly.
*click* The netcasters will be told.

chatter.text: {neighbour} let me hold the shuttle! For a little while. Then I dropped it in the net.
I can climb a whole stalk with just my two arms! Well. Halfway.
When my lower arms grow in I'm going to be a netcaster. Or a dyer. Dyers get to be teal.
*click click* I'm practising my clicking. Grown-ups click when they think. I click when I want to look like I'm thinking.
The Long Cloth is so long you can't see the bottom from the deck. I tried. I leaned. Someone grabbed me.
Do you want to see me hang by my knees? *already hanging* I'm very good at it.

replies.text: There's a net! There's always a net. *click*
*swings, and lands on the rope* See? Precise. Like a grown-up.

chatter: *six eyes drift to the canopy, then back to you* The wart is thick. That is good.
{neighbour}'s silkgrub crawled up the stalk again. It always finds the highest point. It has ambitions.
*click* Hold still. There is a silkgrub on your boot. There. Back to the deck, little one.

chatter.text: My silkgrub is called Thread. I have two arms and it has none, so I am winning.
A good row is mostly counting. The weaving is only what the counting leaves behind.
Between one vat-set and the next I tie a hundred knots. None may look unlike the others. That is the whole of the art, and it takes a lifetime.
Warp first, then weft, then patience. Outsiders always want to start with the last one.
The first lesson of weaving is to do nothing in haste. The second is to finish what you began. The second is the harder.
Every bridge rope is checked once a row, by someone who does not trust the last one who checked it. That is how a bridge stays up.
When the work goes well, no one notices. When it goes badly, the whole deck notices at once. So a quiet deck is a good deck.
*click* A bridge hums when it is pulled evenly. I walk the four arms of {village} and listen. A silent rope is a tired rope.
We do not hurry the vats, the dye or the children. The first two give less trouble.
My ladder has ninety-one rungs. I counted them again just now, in case they had changed.
Mending is the finest work. Anyone can make a new cloth. To make an old one last, you need real patience.
No Weft has idle hands. Sometimes a Weft has two idle hands, being four-handed, and we call that resting.
One hand to hold, one to work, one to mend what the first two did, and one to scratch. Do not ask me which is which.
Do not swing your arms near the frame, outsider. We only notice a fall once something has been dropped. Then everything is dropped.
Thread has a memory. Pull it crooked once and it wants to be crooked always. Be careful what you teach a thread.
The loudest sound on a Loom is a shuttle hitting the deck. The second loudest is everyone looking up to see whose it was.
I rewove one hem four times and it was no better than the first. The Clothkeeper said the first was already finished. I was only afraid to stop.
There are no quick jobs here. There are only jobs whose end I cannot see yet.
Every Weft ties knots a little differently. You can know a weaver by the hems, even in the dark.
A knot tied in haste is a debt. You pay it later, with interest, and always at the worst moment.
They say a Weft can do four things at once. It is true. Whether the four things are done well is a matter between me and the Cloth.
Rest is weaving too. The shuttle sits in the hand and the thread sits in the shuttle and nothing moves. *click* That is also a row.
A bridge, a ladder, a hatch and a net. Remember those four and you will never be lost on a Loom.
Pull the thread toward you to tighten, push it away to let it rest. My mother taught me that. She said it also works on people.
I wear my spools at the belt in order of use. If you ever see them out of order, I am ill, or someone has talked to me for too long.
We weave in the open air because a weaver must see the smoke move. Smoke shows where the draught is, and draughts show where a knot will slip.
The hardest cloth to make is plain cloth. There is nowhere for a mistake to hide.
My upper hands are for climbing and for holding on. They are very good at holding on. Ask anyone who has tried to take something from me.
A weaver who knows only one pattern is a poor weaver. A weaver who knows a thousand and cannot choose is a poorer one.
I trust a rope I tied myself and a rope another Weft tied. A rope tied by an outsider I walk around. Forgive me. It is only a rule.
*holds out a spool* Can you wind this without tangling it?

replies.text: *click* Slowly, then. Slow is the whole trick. Keep it taut and it winds itself.
An honest answer. Hold the end, and I will wind. We will call that weaving.
No reason. Only that the ones who help wind are the ones we remember.

chatter.text: Do you have a trade, where you come from? Something your hands do?

replies.text: Building. *click click* The same as weaving, only louder, and it falls down more.
A wanderer. Light on the bridges, I hope. We shall see.
*click* Mind what you take here. The Loom counts, and it counts back.

chatter.text: I am teaching a young one the double knot. They keep tying the single. Should I be strict or kind?

replies.text: That is what the Clothkeeper said, too. I am outvoted, and pleased about it.
*click* A Weft answer. But when I was strict, they stopped learning. I will try kindness.
Fall? Is that a joke? *six eyes narrow* It is not a good one.

chatter.text: Which is harder, to begin a row or to finish it?

replies.text: *click click* Yes. Beginning is only enthusiasm.
Hm. A beginner's answer. Many give it. Ask me again at the tie-off.
*click* Then you will never be woven into anything.

chatter.text: Four hands or two, which would you rather have to wind a whole row of thread?

replies.text: *click click click* Everyone says so. It is the only question you always answer correctly.
Two is polite. I will give you that. But you will tire, and I will not.

chatter.text: Every Loom's copy of the Cloth differs a little. Ours has a stain at row Eleven-Fifty-Three that no other copy has. They say it is an error. I say theirs is a lie.
I choose what is woven into this year's row, and what is left out. What is left out is the harder choice, and no one thanks me for it.
A child asked why the Cloth has no pictures. I said it does, if you stand far enough back. She stood so far back she landed in the net.
I do not weave quarrels into the Cloth. A row remembers who built a bridge, not who argued over it. The quarrels remember themselves.
The newest rows are soft and the oldest are stiff. Run your hand up the Cloth and you feel the years go by. Do not run your hand up the Cloth. I tell everyone.
The Cloth must be dusted by a Weft who never sneezes. That is me. It is the only reason I was given the post.
There is one thread in the Cloth that matches no spool on this deck. Nobody owns it. I look in on it as I would a stray silkgrub.
My eyes are not what they were. I have six, and the oldest two are clouding. I do not mind. The Cloth I know by touch.
When a Clothkeeper dies, the first thread of the next row is spun from their belt-cord. I have been told where mine is kept. I try not to look at the shelf.
Would you like a row read aloud? I read them to anyone patient enough. Choose one.

replies.text: *click* Thirteen-Twelve is unfinished, so I read what there is. A bridge repaired, a vat spilled, and an outsider who walked softly.
A kind answer. I will pick one with a good bridge in it.
*click... click* It is slow. That is how you know it is true.

chatter.text: Be honest with an old Clothkeeper: what do you make of the newest row?

replies.text: Careful. *click* The best word for a row, and the worst for a life. I will take it.
Long. Yes. We are not in a hurry.
*six eyes narrow, slowly* Then you will be asked to. With two hands.

chatter.text: The heddle lifts half the warp and drops the other half. Every cloth there is, is that, again and again, with opinions.
I can weave and I can talk, but never both well. The lower hands get the cloth, the upper hands get the conversation, and the conversation is mostly a wave.
A tight weave keeps heat out and a loose weave lets it through. I weave tight for the huts and loose for the shawls. Outsiders ask for tight shawls, then complain.
My shuttle is bone. I know roughly where the bone came from. I do not think about it while I weave.
Hems are where cloth tells the truth. The middle can be anything.
Teal is our house colour because the dyers cannot make anything else. Orange is their only apology for it.
A thread that breaks mid-row is rejoined with a weaver's knot. They say it cannot be seen. I always know where mine are.
Some outsiders ask to buy cloth. We do not sell it. We give it to those who have earned it, which is a very different thing and takes much longer.
I wove a shawl once that I gave to no one. It lies in a chest. Perhaps it was waiting for someone. I have not found the shoulders yet.
Would you pull this thread for me? Gently.

replies.text: *click* Just right. You listen with your fingers. That is rare.
*the thread snaps* ...Three rows of work. Go and sit by the net, and think about thread.
Wise. Most who touch it regret it. Stand there, then, and watch.

chatter.text: Does this pattern look better with orange, or with teal?

replies.text: A bold answer. The dyers will be insulted, but I like orange.
Teal. *click* The dyers will be unbearable for the rest of the spool.
*click click* Honestly! Then I shall unpick it. Thank you. No one dares tell me.

chatter.text: A silkgrub gives tufts and I give them a twist. Twist to the right, strong. Twist to the left, soft. Mix them and you have rope.
I spin as I walk. The spinning walks are long and straight, and I can cross one with my eyes shut. Please do not test me.
One tuft makes a thread a hand long if I am careless, and as long as this deck if I am careful. Careful is slower. I am slow.
The netcasters ask me for strong thread, the dyers for fine, the weavers for even. I give each what they ask and keep the best for myself.
A spinner's fingers go smooth, then rough, then smooth again. When they go smooth the third time, you are a master. Mine are rough.
Thread is only a long lie that something is stronger than it is. I tell it well.
I can tell a silkgrub's mood from its thread. Calm grubs give long even tufts. Frightened ones give knots. Lately mine gives knots, and I do not know why.
The spindle hums a note when the twist is right. Mine hums a flat one. I keep it anyway. It sings my kind of right.
How long do you think this thread is? Look, don't measure.

replies.text: Longer. *click* Nearly twice. You have a good eye.
Precisely vague. Typical.
Then why are you standing so close to it, outsider?

chatter.text: The spindle is free, if you want to spin a hand's length. I will watch your fingers, not your face.

replies.text: *hands it over* Two hands. You have just enough. Slower. Slower. ...Better than most.
Wise. It tangles outsiders.
*click* Dull is what holds the bridge up. Mind your boots on it.

chatter.text: A giant fungus takes more rows to grow than I will see. I plant for children who are not born yet. That is the whole of my work.
Bone meal and patience, in that order. And more patience than bone meal.
The wart on a cap must be thinned, or the light cannot get in. I thin it and never strip it. That is the line between a tender and a thief.
I lay a palm on a stalk every time I climb, and I can tell when it is hungry. Do not ask me how a fungus is hungry. It is.
I lay an ear to the root-cap every time I climb. A tender who forgets to listen is only a climber with a belt.
A shroomlight flickers when its stalk is ailing. I read the lamps the way the Clothkeepers read the rows.
A stem that dies standing gives us planks. A stem that falls is another matter. We hold a small silence for it before we touch it.
I go head first down the stalks because I can see the nylium that way. Upright, I look at my feet, and feet tell me nothing.
A deck that does not sway at all is lashed too tight. Give a little. Everything alive gives a little.
I have named every stalk in {village}. I do not tell them. They know.
The caps are warm on top and cool beneath. I take my meals on the cool side, and the wart is thick enough to rest on. I do not say that loudly.
Spores drift up when the wart flowers. They tickle my low eyes. In all my rows I have not learned to ignore it.
What do you think holds a deck up?

replies.text: True, and incomplete. *click* Try again later.
Ropes hold bridges. A deck is held by the whole forest leaning the same way.
*click click* You listen. Stalk, root, and the neighbours' stalks. Nothing here stands alone.

chatter.text: The orange takes a long time to set. The teal takes a short time and never leaves. That is how you can tell a Weft from a visitor.
After a long stint at the vats I forget small things: where a spool is, what I came for. I write it on my arm and then forget what the writing means.
Water is the dye's whole life, and I have never had enough. A cupful is worth more than the thread it colours.
Teal to the elbow makes a good dyer. Teal to the shoulder makes a careless one. Teal to the ears is a dyer who lost an argument with the vat.
Never look at your six eyes in a full vat. The vat counts them back to you, and sometimes forgets one.
The orange comes from shroomlight, and we take only what falls. A shroomlight taken is a lamp put out.
I read the vat by its steam. Pale steam is patient. Dark steam is hungry. This steam is dark. I should feed it.
Mix too fast and you get mud. Mix too slow and you get regret. Mud is easier to mend.
Dye on a hem is a promise. Dye on a deck is an apology. I have a long list of apologies.
I once dyed a whole bolt the colour of ash by mistake. The Clothkeeper hung it in the Cloth as a lesson. I am the lesson.
The tears we dye with come from the nets. I do not ask where they came from. I stir. That is how I stay steady.
Guess how many drops it takes to turn this white wool teal.

replies.text: Close. Forty-one. *click* You counted by eye. Good.
A cupful would drown it. Think smaller.
Honest! Come and watch, then. Stand upwind.

chatter.text: A net is a question you ask the air. Most of the time the air says nothing.
A netcaster's whole work is to be ready and not needed. If I do it well, no one remembers I did it.
I throw with the lower hands and steady myself with the upper. Outsiders with two arms throw and fall. We have had to hang nets under the nets.
The finest net I own is eleven rows old and has caught nothing but a child. It is still my favourite.
I hear a Piglin horn long before I see the Piglin. It is the one sound that makes all six of my eyes go bright.
The lookout nets catch many things: a dropped shuttle, a lost shawl, a gust of spores. I keep a basket for each.
A good net is mostly holes. The holes let the wind through. The knots hold what matters.
Hold still and the net does the work. Struggle and the net does the work, only more. That is the whole teaching of the netcasters.
I would sooner catch a falling child than a thief. I have caught more of the first. I am glad of it.
I have waited at this post so long that the silkgrubs use me as a rope. I am proud of it.
Between us: some of the nets I tend I do not like. The ones hung in the open air. I tend them. I do not have to like them.
Do you want to see me throw a net? Stand there. No, there.

replies.text: *the net drifts down light as breath, and lifts again* I missed you on purpose. See how kind a Weft aim can be.
*click* Wise. I would only have missed. On purpose.
*the lower hands twitch* Do not tempt a netcaster, outsider.

chatter.text: Can you stand as still as a hanging net? Truly still?

replies.text: Try. I will watch. It is the only entertainment I get.
Few can. It is why the post is mine.
Stillness is the whole of it. *click* Learn it, or be caught by it.

chatter.text: {neighbour} took in a stray silkgrub with a bent leg. It sleeps round their neck now. They insist it is a scarf.
{neighbour} counts aloud while resting. Last time they stuck at forty-one for a whole rest. The deck waited for forty-two.
{neighbour} and I have not spoken for three vat-sets. It is the best friendship I have. We nod across the bridge.
{neighbour} borrowed my beater and returned it cleaner than I lent it. I do not trust that.
I saw {neighbour} talking to a stalk. When they noticed me, they said they were listening for hollows. I let them.
{neighbour} says they once out-waited a Piglin. I believe it. The Piglin was the one who left.
{neighbour} laughs with all four hands, slapping the rail. You can hear it across two bridges. We have all learned to duck.
To know who is courting whom in {village}, look at the spools. {neighbour} has been careless with teal lately.
Courting is done in spools. You give your best thread, wound tight. Returned unwound, you were refused. Returned rewound better, you are done for.
{neighbour} is a fine weaver and a poor listener. I tell them my troubles anyway. The weave takes them well.
{neighbour} has not been down to the floor in rows. They say the roots make them dizzy. I think they like the view.
{neighbour} scorched a hem in vat steam once and has told it eleven times. Each time the hem is larger.
{neighbour} says the nets sing when the draught turns. I have listened thirty rows and heard nothing. Either they tease, or my ears are well-mannered.
Between us, {neighbour} cheats at counting games: counts fast, then pretends to lose the thread. I let them. It makes them happy.
{neighbour} dropped a shuttle in the net and refused help. Three vat-sets later they were hanging by the knees, saying it was deliberate.
{neighbour} is teaching a silkgrub to sit. It has always been sitting. We are very proud.
The dye house and {neighbour} are quarrelling over who spilled what. The truth is in the vat, and the vat is not telling.
{neighbour} once wove a hem so even that the Clothkeeper wept. Then asked for it redone, for the sake of the others.
{neighbour} crosses every bridge exactly in the middle. A rope-length either side would do no harm. It would also not be {neighbour}.
I lent {neighbour} fine thread for a shawl and got a net. It is lovely. It is also theirs, they say, until it catches something.
{neighbour} whistles faintly through their mandibles when they are lying. I have never told them. It is too useful.
{neighbour} claims the highest cap in {village} is theirs because they climbed it first. We told them the stalk climbed first. They are still thinking.
Everyone in {village} has one rope they will not cross. {neighbour}'s is the third from the lookout. We do not ask.
{neighbour} gave their spare shuttle to a child who had none, then wove a row with a borrowed beater. No one mentioned it. Everyone saw.
{neighbour} thinks aloud, in the wrong order. You hear the answer first, then the question. It is quicker, honestly.
{neighbour} laughed at a joke of mine three rows after I told it. I was alone when they did. I laughed too.
I tried to read {neighbour}'s hems for secrets. All I learned is that they hate corners.
I will tell you, since you are tied on: {neighbour} leaves small cloths at the foot of the Long Cloth for the ones no row remembers. No one asked them to. No one stopped them.
{neighbour} fears heights. It is the best kept secret in {village}. They climb with their eyes shut and open them only to count.
{neighbour} asked me, in confidence, whether the Cloth will remember them. I said yes. I had not checked. I am checking now.
I envy {neighbour}'s steady hands. I will not tell them. A compliment travels faster than a spool.
My oldest friend is {neighbour}. I have not said so since we were small. I say it to you instead. It is not the same, but it helps.
{neighbour} says outsiders talk too much. I say you have hardly talked at all. We shall see who is right.
I do not know you well enough to speak of my neighbours. {neighbour} is a good weaver. That is all you will get.
{neighbour} has not come to the dye house in a while. Do I look in on them, or leave them be?

replies.text: *click* Yes. A thread left slack too long tangles. I will go.
Hm. Perhaps they want slack. I will watch the rope instead.
A deck is a net. Pull one knot and every knot feels it.

chatter.text: I know something about {neighbour}. Shall I tell you, or keep it in the spool?

replies.text: *click click* A good answer. You may hear one of mine, later.
Then you are no better than the draught. It carries things for pleasure.
It is kind. Mostly. *click* Another time.

chatter.text: {neighbour} says you are welcome here. I say you are tolerated. Which of us is right?

replies.text: *click* Hm. You split a thread without fraying it. Not bad.
Honest. *click click* Every thread begins loose.

chatter.text: {neighbour} gave me a spool of orange, wound very tight. Is that friendship, or something I should be careful of?

replies.text: *click* I am coming round to it. Slowly.
Nothing is just thread. Go and stand somewhere else.

chatter.text: We eat what the forest drops: wart, sprouts, roots, a cap or two. Nothing is picked from a living stem. Hunger is easier to carry than a cut.
Root-broth is warped roots boiled in sap. It tastes of thread. Children dislike it. Grown Weft pretend not to.
Wart-cake is mashed wart and sprouts baked on a hot stone. Dry as bark. We love it. Outsiders cough.
We never eat while weaving. A crumb in the weft is a flaw in the row. We eat on the cool side of a cap and brush ourselves down twice.
Sap-tea from weeping vines: sweet, sticky, hot. It is the nearest thing we have to water, and we guard it like water.
A Weft can take four small bites at once, one for each hand. Outsiders call it greedy. We call it efficient.
I hear everything in your world is wet. Every meal, every path, every cloth. How do you stand it?
The first bite of any new fungus goes to the eldest at the table. Not out of respect. Out of experiment.
I have eaten the same wart-cake for a hundred and ten rows. If it is ever different, I shall be worried.
My silkgrub eats anything I drop. That is why I drop things. I am told it is not a good reason.
Come and eat on the cool side of the cap sometime. We do not feast. We sit, we eat, we stop talking. It is the best kind of talk.
After the vats I taste nothing but orange. The cake is orange. The broth is orange. I am fairly sure I am orange.
I eat the thinnings off the caps. Wart I took down myself tastes better. It is nice to know where your meal has been.
A plate of cap-slices beside the loom stays warm from the lamp-oven. Do not tell the Clothkeeper.
The floor is hot and thick with spores. Up here the draught from the lava seas is merely warm, which counts as cool. Climb high enough and you stop noticing.
We build high because the wind has room to turn up there. Heat likes to lie low. It is a lazy sort of thing.
Heat makes thread slack. The weavers pull the warp tighter when the draught is warm. I have never met a Weft who liked being slack, either.
*loosens his mantle and flaps it once* I take it off when the wind drops and put it on when it turns. It has seen more weather than I have.
*lifts her shawl off one shoulder with a lower hand* Wool is for the draught. In still air it is only wool.
The dye house is the hottest deck. The dyers say they do not notice. They notice. That is why they are teal: they are boiling.
When it is too hot to weave, I count. Counting makes no cool air. It passes the time while the heat passes.
A wet cloth on the neck is the finest luxury a Weft can have. We own one. The netcasters share it by rota.
Heat shows in the warp before it shows on the skin. If the tension is slack, you are hot. Check the thread.
It's hot! Can we go to the top? The top is cool! I'm allowed up to the second rail!
Root-broth tastes like thread. I like wart-cake, but only the burnt edge. The middle is for grown-ups.
I ate a shroomlight once. Everyone says I didn't. I did. It was warm and very orange.
I sleep in a hammock-net, like a catch. It is the only way I sleep. The sway tells me the bridges are well.
A Weft rests when the shuttle grows heavy. The Nether keeps no day, so we learned to listen to our hands instead.
Piglins sleep on beds, I hear, and the beds burst in the Nether. Good. A bed is only a flat way of being caught.
I rest with two hands on the rope, in case the hatch opens. The other two I keep for dreaming.
I dream mostly of knots. Then of loose knots. Then of falling. Then I wake and count the rungs. It is a routine.
The spores are thick now. I can taste teal on my tongue. Do not breathe too deep; they make you agree with everything.
When the wart flowers, the whole forest smells of warm cloth. That is how I know I am home.
Would you like a piece of wart-cake? It is not good. It is ours.

replies.text: *click* You thanked it before tasting it. That is rare.
It will keep. It always keeps. That is its virtue.
It looks like two hundred rows of habit. Say it quieter.

chatter.text: Is it true your world has water lying about in puddles, for anyone to drink?

replies.text: *click click* And no one guards it? I would give two hands to see that.
*stares* Do not tell me how much. I would not sleep.
*all six eyes brighten* Someday. When the row is finished. Ask me again.

chatter.text: Do you rest sitting, lying flat, or hanging?

replies.text: A hammock! Good sense, outsider. You have the instincts of a catch.
On the floor. Where the tall walkers wander. Brave. Or foolish. I always mix those up.

chatter.text: Is the heat bad where you come from, or does it come and go?

replies.text: Ah. Like thread. *click* I envy you the going.
Then you are brave to stay. Or slow to leave.

chatter.text: A dropped spool must be picked up by someone other than the one who dropped it. Pick up your own and it tangles you for a row.
Never weave while angry. The anger goes into the thread and the thread keeps it. I have seen cloth that bit.
Never call a row the last one. The Cloth hears. It has a way of proving you wrong.
A silkgrub that circles left on a bridge brings luck. Circling right, it means check the ropes. I check the ropes either way.
We tie a thread round a newborn's wrist and cut it only when they climb a stalk alone. Most children cut it early.
Sneeze over a half-woven hem and you must unpick the last hand's width. It is not logic. It is respect.
Never step on the shadow of the Long Cloth. Never mind that the shadows move. Just try.
Seven knots at the foot of a ladder bring you home safe. Six, and you come home late. Eight, and you are showing off.
Do not count the black rows aloud. Silently, if you must. The Cloth is listening, and the count is not yours to give.
A shuttle lost in the net returns within a row, or never. Those are the only two ways. I have lost three. Two came back.
Never leave a loom half-warped between sets. It sulks, and a sulking loom makes lopsided cloth.
If a shroomlight flickers three times as you pass, something good is coming. Or a gust. Both are welcome.
Do not whistle on a bridge. The ropes hear it and begin to hum, and once they hum they like to keep humming.
I leave one thin thread of orange hanging from my door, for whoever follows me home. No one has yet. The thread stays.
The bridges have swayed more lately. I tell myself it is the draught. I climb up and check the ropes each time anyway.
I think the wart is thinner on the far caps. Perhaps I am wrong. I have been wrong before, in five rows. I measure it all the same.
I hear horns past the lookout and wonder whether the netcasters hear them too. They always do. I wonder anyway.
I worry the young ones will not learn the old knots. Then I watch them tie one and worry they learned it too well.
There is a hum in the stalk I tend. Not hollow, not sick. Only a hum. I do not know what to write in the row about it.
Some rows I fear the Cloth will end with me. Not the Cloth, of course. The Cloth goes on. I mean my part of it.
I wake some rows with the black ones pulled tight across my chest. Then I count the teal ones after, and loosen.
I do not like it when the draught stops. A silent forest is a forest waiting for something.
How many Weft does it take to tie a knot? One. The other three are there to criticise.
I told a joke once. It took three rows to land. Everyone laughed, at the timing.
A Weft with two arms is a child, or a Piglin's idea of a Weft.
If I drop a shuttle the net catches it. If I drop a joke nobody does. I have four hands and still cannot catch one.
Why does no one win an argument against a Weft? We have the last word, and the one after, and by then the other has left.
I am told my jokes are dry. They are not dry. They are tightly woven.
I saw a grown-up trip on a knot! They said they were testing it. They weren't. *click click*
I'm scared of the vats. They're warm and bubbly and they look back at you.
Sometimes I worry the net will break. Then I remember there's another one under it. And another one under that.
Piglin horns go BWAAAH and everything shakes and my arms go tight. Grown-ups say that is what horns are for.
Do you have any luck-habits? Everyone has one, even outsiders. Tell me yours.

replies.ask: I keep a stone in my pocket.
replies.text: *click* A weight to hold you down. That is sensible.
Left. A good side for it. I shall watch your feet.
Luck does not mind. It believes in you anyway.

chatter.text: I have a joke about knots. Shall I tie it, or leave it loose?

replies.text: What is the difference between a Weft and a rope? A rope stops when you ask. *click click* ...No? Hm.
Wise. A loose joke is the safest kind.

chatter.text: Something is bothering me and I cannot weave it out. May I say it aloud?

replies.text: *click click* You are the first outsider to say that. The draught has changed and nobody remarks on it. Thank you.
*click* Only that the draught has changed. That is all. It helps to say.
Quick is how knots slip. Never mind. It will keep.

chatter.text: You see the thread tied round that rope? Why do you suppose it is there?

replies.text: For luck, for counting, for company. It does all three.
That, too. A plain answer, but a true one.
Messy! It is the most careful mess on the deck. Look again.

chatter.text: Want to know where my secret rope is? You have to promise not to tell.

replies.text: It's behind the dye house! You swing on it right over the net. Shh!
*gasps and hides behind the rope* You wouldn't! I'll be good for a whole row!

chatter.text: A silkgrub's spots glow brighter when it is content. Mine has glowed for three vat-sets now. I take full credit.
Silkgrubs follow the hum of a spindle. Spin on the wrong side of the deck and the whole herd arrives, politely, to ask what you are doing.
A grub on the deck means the wart is sound. A grub gone from the deck means check the wart. They know before we do.
Silkgrubs sleep in a tight curl with their spots dimmed. Wake one and it looks at you as if you owed it a row.
A fresh tuft is warm in the hand. I wind the first thread of a shearing round my wrist and hold it. It is as near as we come to a hearth.
I once lost a silkgrub for three vat-sets. It was in the frame of the Great Loom, watching. It had an excellent view.
No silkgrub has ever fallen from a bridge. The netcasters say it is because they are low and sensible. I say it is because they never look down.
Silkgrubs hate Piglin horns. When one sounds, they all go dark at once. The lookout knows before the horn is finished.
Feed a silkgrub too many warped roots and it spins in a tangle. We call the tangle a Greedy Row. Nobody wears it.
The oldest silkgrub on the Loom is called Warp. He has outlasted three Clothkeepers. He has asked not to be mentioned in the Cloth.
I name my grubs for the moves of a shuttle: Over, Under, Between. The one called Between is the troublemaker.
I'm not allowed to feed the silkgrubs warped roots. They get too excited and tickle. I did it once. It was great.
Silkgrubs have no arms at all and still climb faster than me. I think they cheat.
If a grub crawls up your arm it leaves a glow on your sleeve. One crawled up me and now I glow. A little. On the elbow.
The Piglins keep hoglins in the crimson woods and think that clever. A hoglin snorting at the forest edge sounds like an argument it cannot win. I never know which side it is on.
A Piglin horn carries three bridges. It is the only music they have, and they play it again and again, as if it might improve.
Piglins wear gold because nobody else will. I think that is the saddest thing I know. I only say it when no Piglin is near.
A Piglin once asked me for a shroomlight by pointing, grunting and showing me his teeth. I gave him a spool. We are both still confused.
Piglins say the Overworld rots you. The Rotted shamble at the forest edge and never look up. Maybe so. I have not gone to check.
Their Brutes are the ones who do not laugh. Those I count twice.
The Withren walk their Cairnbacks in a line, each with a small soul fire on its back. From the lookout it looks like a blue thread drawn slowly through the valley.
A Withren once bowed to me on a road and said, 'I know what you carry.' I said, 'Needles.' They said, 'Yes.' It was the best talk we ever had.
Withren laugh once, softly, at graves. I think it is the best laughing there is. Please do not tell them I said so.
A Withren keeps one name in their head for ever. We weave a whole year into a row. I have never decided which is heavier.
When the wind comes from the valley I can hear the Hollowed in the old fortress. It is not a good draught. I leave the hatch shut.
A Magmari will haggle over a fungus until it rots in their hand. I once watched one pay triple, for the pleasure of arguing.
A strider is a boat that walks. I never saw the sense of it, but I admire a beast that is both the crossing and the legs.
From the far caps you can sometimes see a strider barge cross the lava, a small red spark. It looks very small and very brave.
Magmari glow when warm and dim when cold. We have no such tell. We go quiet. It confuses everyone, ourselves included.
Magmari are always cold. We are always exactly the right warmth, and nobody thanks us.
When the Ashbells drift past the lookout, the nets ring. It is the nicest sound we own, and we did not make it.
A Ghastkin cried into my net once and I forgot my name for a whole vat-set. Then I remembered it. I would rather not have, some of that time.
A ghast drifts over the forest sometimes, crying. We stop weaving until it passes. Nobody decides to. We simply stop.
The tall walkers carry blocks up and down the forest floor and set them down in places that make no sense. They never cut a stem. I have come to respect that.
Hold your arm out and keep still. A silkgrub climbs onto whom it likes, and I only watch. Will you try?

replies.text: *click* There. It stayed. It does not stay for everyone.
Nobody is. That is why they choose us.
*click* It heard that. Mind your boots.

chatter.text: A Piglin left a gold ingot on our deck once, like a gift. We did not know what to do with it. What would you have done?

replies.text: *all six eyes brighten* That is just what the netcasters did. You think like a Weft.
*click* We tried. He had gone. They are very quick to leave a kindness.
Of course. Gold in a pocket is the most natural thing in the world. For a Piglin.

chatter.text: Which of the other peoples do you think is the most stubborn? Not the Piglins. Everyone says Piglins.

replies.text: *click* They forget nothing. I see why you say so.
Stubborn in another direction: toward a bargain.
*click click* Careful. That is true, but we do not say it aloud.

chatter.text: Which is better, a silkgrub or a strider? I say silkgrub. Everyone says strider.

replies.text: *click click* I knew you were clever!
Fine. They're all right. Slightly. *click*

chatter.text: You stand like a post, outsider. Two feet, no sway. Your balance is very honest, and a little tiring to watch.
You look up before you look down. Most outsiders do the reverse and learn the net.
You breathe the spores without coughing. Either you are used to them, or you hide it well.
Your boots leave no mark on the planks. Someone taught you to walk softly. Whoever it was, thank them.
You touch the rope before you trust it. I noticed. That is how I first knew you might be worth knowing.
You keep your hands where I can see them. It is a manner, not a fear. We are glad of it either way.
You hold your head the way we do when we think. It is not very good yet. Keep at it.
You cross the bridges in the middle now, not at the rail. Someone told you. Or you listened to the ropes.
I know your step now, even from the far deck. Quick, then careful, then quick. Like a shuttle.
When you leave, the bridge hums differently for a while. Not worse. Lighter. I hope you do not mind that I notice.
I look to see whether your thread is still in the Cloth. It always is. I check anyway. It is a small habit and I am fond of it.
You are still new, and new things are counted. I am still counting. I do not yet know what the total will be.
You are the only outsider I have asked my thoughts of. I do not yet know if that is wise. The vats are still deciding.
The weavers argue about your colour. Orange, for your stride. Teal, for your care. Neither, for plainness. I say all three.
I said your name aloud to the vat once. It did not answer. But it did not splash, which is as good.
There is string in your pack. Plain, tight, a little proud. I would like to know who spun it. We may be related.
A cobweb in your pack! A silkgrub gave you that, or you took it. I shall assume gave.
You carry bone. A good bone makes a straight needle. Keep it from the Withren; they notice bone, and they are sensitive.
Bone meal! Careful with that near the caps. Too much and a fungus bolts. A tender knows how much. Do you?
A warped fungus in your pack. The Magmari would pay a great deal for it. I trust you to say no.
You carry gold. It is a heavy thing to bring onto a rope bridge. The ropes mind. So do I, slightly.
