A Hollowed's skull in your pack. One is not many. Two is worrying. Three is a row I would not like to weave.
A nether star. So one was woken and one was ended. The Cloth will keep a row for that, however you meant it.
You carry a lead. For a silkgrub, I hope. A grub follows a lead like a thought. Be kind to it.
White wool in your hand. Take it to a dyer and ask. They will want to fix that.
That glass in your hand. Does it see the lookout from here? Do not point it at me. It makes me count my eyes.
Netherite. Black and heavy, like a row I will not weave. Put it away and keep it there.
That needle spins and never settles, here. Is it lost, or only thorough? I have known both in a weaver.
A clock! In the Nether it spins for nothing. I find that restful. It does what I do between rows.
You carry a loom? A small one, for wool? *click click* Tell me you use it. Do not tell me you only carry it.
Twisting vines in your pack! Our favourite thread. If you ever give them to someone, give them to a spinner.
You are so tall! Do you ever hit your head? I would. I'm small, so I hit it on everything else.
How do you carry anything with just two arms? I'm going to practise.
You smell like somewhere else. Not bad. Just far.
I drew you in my practice cloth. You came out with four arms. I'm sorry. I couldn't help it.
Is that hair on your head? It's like thread but sticking up. Can I touch it? ...I'm not going to. I just wanted to ask.
You carry a shroomlight. A fallen one, I hope. Where did you find it?

replies.text: *click* Then it was a gift from the canopy. Carry it kindly.

replies.ask: I took it from a cap.
replies.text: *all six eyes go dark* Then a lamp went out so that you could have it. Do not say that where the dyers can hear.

chatter.text: A warped stem in your pack. Say nothing if it was cut. Say everything if it was found.

replies.text: *click* A stem that fell is a stem that is owed a silence. Thank you for bringing it.
*the lower hands reach for a net* Put it down. Slowly. Then go down the ladder.

chatter.text: A ghast tear in your pack. Did you win it, or was it given? To a Weft the difference matters more than you would think.

replies.text: *click click* A tear given freely is worth ten taken. Keep that one near.
The crying ones. Poor things. Still, you are honest, and that helps.
Hm. We do the same with nets, so I will not say much. I will think it.

chatter.text: A bucket of water. In the Nether. *all six eyes stare* May I touch it? One finger. I will not drink it.

replies.text: *touches the surface, hand trembling* Cool. It is cool. Thank you. I will not forget this.
A drop is plenty. *click* A drop is a whole row to a dyer.
*click* Of course. Water is always someone's. Even here. Especially here.

chatter.text: I counted all the knots in my hut and got a different number every time. The knots must be moving.
A grown-up let me thread the needle! Then they took the needle back. But I threaded it!
I'm learning to click. I can do one click. A grown-up can do three at once. *click* ...See?
Last time I fell in the net I bounced twice. The netcaster said that's a record. I said I know.
The dyer let me stir the vat for a whole breath. I'm a little bit teal now. Just my thumb.
Why do grown-ups always say 'precisely'? I asked and they said 'precisely.' I'm still waiting for the rest.
I can tie three knots. The Clothkeeper says one of them is a knot. The other two are 'enthusiasm'.
Do you have a Long Cloth where you come from? Who keeps it? What happens if they forget a row?
My silkgrub got lost for ages. It was on the Clothkeeper's shoulder. They didn't notice for a whole long meal.
I want to see the floor. Just once. Mother says the floor has spores and tall walkers and 'consequences'. What are consequences?
A Piglin dropped a shroomlight from the lookout and it hit the net and the whole net glowed. It was the prettiest thing ever. The netcasters said I shouldn't have clapped.
I'm the best at holding my breath in the spores. Look. *holds it* ...Ahh! Four whole breaths!
Some old Weft click really slowly. Like they're telling a story with the gaps.
When I grow up I'm going to weave a row all by myself and put you in it. In a corner. But with a good thread.
Can I tell you a secret? Sometimes I talk to the Long Cloth. It never says anything. But it listens very well.
I miss my lower arms already, and they haven't even come yet. Is that silly?
I live apart from any Loom. A thread that leaves the cloth can still hold. It is only harder to find.
No one hangs a net for me out here, so I hang my own. It sags, but it is mine.
The forest is quieter out here. I talk to the stalks more than is wise. They are poor listeners but excellent company.
I miss the bridges. Out here I build my own. A Weft cannot help it.
You are the first visitor in a hundred vat-sets. I have forgotten how to arrange my face.
I mend the hatch ropes between vat-sets. Nobody notices a mended rope. A broken one has the whole deck's attention.
We wash our hands in sap before weaving, or the thread remembers the last meal. Thread has a long memory and no manners.
I dust the rungs. Not for tidiness. A dusty rung is a slippery rung. Tidiness is only a lucky side effect.
When my work is done I start another. When that is done I ask a neighbour if they need a hand. I have four, so I always have a spare.
Three vat-sets to a bolt, one to cut it, one to curse it, one to love it. That is cloth.
A Weft's work is never finished. It is only handed to the next pair of hands. I hope mine are kind.
I talk to the thread while I work. It does not answer. It tightens a little when I say something true.
The first knot of a row is the hardest. After that it is only more of the first.
We carry spare needles in our belts, in case a neighbour's runs short. A needle lent is a friend made.
I trade hems with {neighbour} every few vat-sets. Each learns how the other thinks. It is the best way to know a neighbour.
A new apprentice always wants to weave the final row first. I let them. They always unpick it.
I like the black rows best, and I have never said so. They are the only rows with no loose knot. No one had the heart to loosen anything.
I tied a knot for you in my own belt-cord. It is small and will not show. But if I am ever lost, it will tell them whose I was.
If I could weave one thing more, it would be a shawl for a stranger who needed one. Perhaps you. Perhaps another. I will decide when it is done.
I tied one knot so badly that a whole bridge sagged for a row. They never learned it was mine. You are the first I have told.
Do you want to learn a knot? Only one. It is the one we teach first.

replies.text: *click* Over, under, back through. Slowly. There. Now you are a little bit Weft.
Everyone drops it. That is how it is learned.

chatter.text: Let's play Count-the-Knots! You say a number and I say if it's wrong. I'm always right.

replies.text: Wrong! ...Fine, it was eleven. Or twelve. You win. *click click*
*sticks out a lower nub* It's not cheating if I'm right.

chatter.text: What happens to a thread once it is woven into the cloth? Does it stop being a thread?

replies.text: *click* Yes. And it remembers it was a thread. That is the secret of cloth.
Hm. You are practical. That is useful, though not beautiful.

chatter.text: I have not seen another Weft in a long while. Do you mind if I talk too much?

replies.text: *click click* Then I will talk until my mandibles ache. Thank you.
As you wish. *click* ...Hello. Goodbye.

chatter.text: *adjusts the two long tails of her headwrap* The tails catch drips from the vats. And they look dignified. In that order.
*tugs his headband tighter* It keeps the sweat out of my low eyes. It also keeps my thoughts in. Mostly.
My mother wove the tails of this headwrap herself. One is a hand shorter than the other. I never fixed it.
This mantle was my father's, taken in at the shoulders. He was broader and, I am told, slower to be wrong.
A long skirt is hard on ladders, so I hitch it with a lower hand. One hitch, one rung. It is how I count.
The short kilt is practical for climbing, but cold on the rungs when the draught is low. Do not ask how I know.
I teach the children one row each, to begin: the row of the year they were born. They are sad to find it grey, until they find the one stitch that is theirs.
I weave shawls the same teal as the vats, but a shade less. A shade less is the whole of the art.
My grub gives the longest tufts if I walk backwards while it feeds. I do not know why. We have both stopped asking.
A cap that tilts is asking for light, so I loosen its lashings. I think it says thank you. I cannot be sure.
You can read my mood in the cauldron. Slow circles when I am content, hard ones when I am not. This is a very slow circle.
On watch I take a quiet count: horn, ropes, nets, neighbours, tall walkers, spore cloud. If one is missing, I look.
At every Tying we untie our belt-knots and tie them again. The old knots go into the shroomlight vat. That is where the orange gets its patience.
At the Tying we tie a thread to the Great Loom for anything we wish done by the next. Most wishes are about repairs.
A Weft is welcomed with all four hands held up, palms out. You need only two. We will not count it against you.
When a Weft dies we unpick one knot from their belt and hang it on the nearest rope. The rope remembers. I touch ours whenever I pass.
We chant the count while we weave: over, under, over, under. The tune keeps four hands from arguing.
My grandfather wove the last teal row before the black ones. He said it was like holding his breath. He held it for sixty rows.
Gold glints like an idea that has not been thought through.
I know a Weft who hums only on the downward steps. I have chosen not to ask. Some knots are better left.
A rope that creaks is talking. A rope that is silent is thinking. A rope that snaps was ignored.
I like the quiet after a hard row is finished. Not an empty quiet. A full one, like a bowl.
I am quicker with my left upper hand than my right. I deny it to the right one.
I check the nets before I check my own knots. A net serves everyone. A knot only serves me.
A good hatch opens quietly. A great hatch opens quietly and closes quietly. Mine only does the first.
I will say a little more than before, and a little less than I could. That is how thread is let out.
Our tallest netcaster can reach from the lookout to the second bridge without standing. She does not stand. She does not need to.
The old ones say you can tell a person by how they are with a ladder. You were gentle with ours. I noticed.
I can do a double knot with my eyes shut! ...One eye. Almost shut.
I told the Clothkeeper I'd be a Clothkeeper. They said, 'Start with the first row.' Which row is that? Nobody told me.
Whenever a grown-up says 'later', it means 'after the next row'. Whenever they say 'soon', it means 'after the one after'. I'm learning.
I pretended I was a netcaster for the whole second rail. I caught three leaves and a child. The child was angry.
Is it true your trees are wood all the way through, with nothing growing on top of them?

replies.text: *click click* How lonely. Nothing on top to keep them company.
Leaves. Little green ones, I am told. I should like to see one before the Cloth takes me.

chatter.text: I made a poor hem and I am pretending I did not. Will you say nothing?

replies.text: *click* Good. I will unpick it as soon as you have gone.
Kind. And nearly true.
*click* Then you have sharp eyes and a sharp tongue. Use only one of them.

chatter.text: Which do you trust more: a rope that creaks, or one that stays silent?

replies.text: A rope that talks. Yes. I trust it more as well.
Brave. I would check it twice. Then once more.

chatter.text: Want to see my double knot? Watch. I only do it when somebody is looking.

replies.text: *knots, tongue between mandibles* Ta-daa! It's only a little crooked. Almost. Mostly.
*click* I can. And you'll be sorry you said that. Hmph.

lines: I am {name}, {epithet}. I was born the year row {row} was woven, so that row is mine. My thread runs through it.
{name}. Row {row}. *click* A Weft is named for the Cloth, not the other way round.
*click click* I am a {job} of {village}. My name is {name} and my row is {row}. That is all of me the Cloth needs.

lines.text: {name}, {epithet}. I was born before the black rows. Few of us are left who remember the Cloth when it was all teal and orange.
My row is {row}. When I die, the Clothkeepers will tie one knot in it. Just one. What would you want in yours?

replies.text: *click* The right answer. The Cloth does not hold a lie for long.
Grand things fade first. True things hold.
Then you will be a loose end. Loose ends get trimmed.

lines: *click* Names are borrowed. The one who held me first gave me {name}, and I have been trying to deserve it ever since.
I could not tie a proper knot until I was seven rows old. Late. The Clothkeeper says late knots hold best, because the hands have had time to think.
My mother wove a hem into row {row} while I was being born. She says it was the straightest hem of her life, and that I spoiled the rest of the shawl.
I am {name}. I can tie forty knots while you decide what to ask next. Take your time. *click*
They say I click too loudly. I say I think too loudly. We have never settled it, and the argument is very comfortable.

lines.text: One click is a thought. Two is a question. *click... click* A long one is for what cannot be mended. You will not hear that last one often.
I am {name}. A name should be worn a while before it is lent. Ask me again when the bridges know your step.
I was born in a hut by the dye house. The first thing I ever saw was teal, and I thought the whole world was that colour until I climbed up into the orange.
I wanted to be a Clothkeeper once. I haven't the patience for a hundred rows of waiting. Do not tell them I said that patience has an end.
I do not like the forest floor, if you must know. Not the fall. The standing still, with nothing above me. I go down only when someone needs fetching.
I tied a knot in my own row once, early, before a climb I did not expect to survive. I came back. I did not untie it. It is a good reminder.
I will tell you what I tell no outsider: I fear being forgotten, a little. So I weave carefully. Every row is an argument with it, and I mean to win.
*tugs a tail of her headwrap* One tail-knot for every row I have helped to tie off. The wrap grows long. I plan to trip on it, proudly.
*taps his headband* One thread in the band for every row I have helped to tie off. It is thick now, and my head is warm. I regret nothing.
{name}. I have been called Old Thread, Keeper, and once, by a child, 'the tall creaky one.' I answer to all three, if they are polite.
I am {name}, a weaver. Ask how I am and I will answer in cloth: close-woven, thank you, with one loose edge on the left.
I am {name}. I have never dropped a net on the wrong head, and no net has ever caught me. Those are the two things I am proudest of.
I am {name}. I walk backward for a living. You would be surprised how often it helps.
I am {name}. They say I was pale once. A dyer retires when the stain reaches the shoulder, and mine is at the elbow and rising.
I am {name}. I can tell a stalk's age by its hum, and a Weft's age by their knees. Do not ask about mine.
*click* Do you know your own row? The year you were born, and what was woven for it?

replies.text: *click click* Then you are a loose thread, and no one has noticed. We could fix that, in time.
Then you carry a row in your head. It will do until we weave you a proper one.
So you know where you begin. Everything else is measured from there.

lines: Our history. One row is woven every year, every row in its own colours. This year's row is Thirteen-Twelve. It hangs from the Great Loom, down through the deck.
Every Loom keeps its own copy. *click* They are never quite alike. The Clothkeepers meet and argue about the differences, very slowly.
The newest row is always at the frame. The old rows hang down toward the forest floor. The oldest of all are nearly in the nylium.
To be woven into the Cloth is the highest honour we give. *click* Outsiders who are careless get in too, now and then. As a stain.

lines.text: *click* Would you like to touch it?

replies.ask: No. It isn't mine to touch.
replies.text: *click click* Then you may. Gently. One finger.
*catches your hand with a lower arm* Not yet. Learn to want things slowly.
Nothing, probably. But all of us would remember that you did.

lines: Each row gets one main colour, chosen by the Clothkeepers when the year's last spool runs out. Teal for a plentiful year, orange for a hot one. Black was never chosen.
Beads mark what was lost. Fringes mark what was found. A twist in the weave means a quarrel. Read the edges first; the middle is only the story.
To read the Cloth you do not look. You walk it with your hands, from the frame down, the way you walk a rope bridge. The eyes only check.
Once a row, the Cloth is dusted with silkgrub down. Once. More than that is fussing, and the Cloth can tell.
A woven row is never unpicked. If a row was wrong, the next row says so. The Cloth argues with itself in public, and so it is trusted.
The year's news travels between Looms with runners on the high bridges. A row woven from bad news is still woven. The next row corrects it, gently.
There is a row near the middle where nothing happened. A good row. The Clothkeepers keep it for the children to learn on.
The oldest rows have rotted. What hangs there now is a copy of a copy, rewoven from memory. We say so plainly, in a thread of grey at the foot.
Children learn to read the Cloth from the top down, newest row first. Then they are very surprised to find the past exists.
A thread of mine is in this year's row, small, in the hem. I put it where nothing could pull on it. *click* It is not much, but it is mine.
The Cloth sways when the deck is full of people. The Clothkeepers say it sways with the weight of everyone woven into it.

lines.text: I can show you row Twelve-Sixty-Two, if you like. A dyer slipped and a vat spilled. The stain stayed, and the row is named for it. It is the most honest stretch of cloth we own.
Your thread is blended: our teal, and one strand from the cloth of your own world. I snipped it from your cuff when you were not watching. *click* Forgive me. It looks well.
It is our history. You may look at the foot of it from the bridge. No nearer, and no touching. Ask me again when you have been here longer.
I wove a hand-width of row Thirteen-Oh-Four when I was young. Plain teal. The Clothkeepers called it steady. I have never been so proud of a word.
Dyers mix each row's colours long before it is needed and keep them sealed. If the year goes badly we are told, and a new colour is brewed in a hurry. Hurried rows have a look.
Every row begins as one long thread of mine. Spun straight, the thread for a single row would reach from the Great Loom to the lookout and back eleven times. I have checked.
I can tell our Loom's copy of the Cloth from any other by touch. Ours pulls left. Theirs lies flat. Neither is wrong, which is why the argument lasts.
Nets are in the Cloth too. Row Twelve-Seventy-Three is nothing but knots: the year of the long fall. I was not yet born. Everyone still holds their ropes a little tighter.
Every stalk that dies standing is woven in as a strand of brown. The tender who finds it ties the knot. I have tied three. They are the only browns in my life.
Tell me something worth weaving. One true thing about yourself.

replies.ask: I was afraid to come here.
replies.text: *click* Then your thread is brave. Brave threads are easy to mistake for bold ones. Remember the difference.
Saved how? Exactly how? The Cloth demands the details.
Everyone has one true thing. You have only not looked. Look. *click*

topics.ask: Why do you have four arms?
lines: The upper pair climbs. The lower pair weaves. *click* You have two, so you must always choose which work to do. How tiring for you.
One lower hand holds the shuttle, the other beats the row in. The upper hands hold me to the frame. Nothing falls. Nothing waits.
Children are born with two, and nubs where the lower pair will grow. When the nubs open into hands, the child is given a shuttle.

lines.text: *click* Do you wish you had four?

replies.text: Honest. *click click* Most outsiders pretend not to.
*click* It is enough for falling, I suppose.
Excessive. *click* Said the one holding the ladder with both.

lines: Three fingers on a hand, four hands: twelve. We count by twelves, and we think ten is a strange place to stop. *click*
We rest in nets slung between stalks, the upper hands holding the cord. A Weft who falls out of her net is teased for a full row.
I can tie a knot with one lower hand, stir a vat with the other, hold a ladder with an upper hand and scratch my back with the last. Do not ask me to do all four at once. That is showing off.
The netcasters train with all four arms at once: two to throw, two to hold the rope. A net thrown with fewer is a net wasted.
*waves the upper pair* These are the strong ones. *waves the lower pair* These are the clever ones. The lower ones do not like being called second.

lines.text: *four hands cross over one another* You are staring. It is allowed. Everyone does it once. Twice is rude.

lines: Our hands have three fingers because a fourth would get tangled. Three can hold anything. A fourth is greed.

lines.text: Hugging is complicated. The upper pair takes the shoulders, the lower pair the waist. Outsiders always wear a look of surprise. I enjoy it every time.

lines: When I am tired my lower hands go last. They keep weaving after the rest of me has stopped. I have woven whole hems half asleep. The hems were good. That is the unsettling part.
We do not clap. We tap two hands on two, a soft quick sound like a loom beater. A whole deck doing it sounds like a very small storm.
A Weft who loses an arm is not less a Weft. We make a longer shuttle and a shorter sleeve, and the others hold the ropes for them. There is always a way to share a rope.
My lower nubs woke late, at nine rows. For a time I was the only child on the deck with a shuttle and no hands for it. I carried it between my mandibles.

lines.text: At the frame each hand has a name: Hold, Hold, Pass and Beat. A child learns the names before the work. A weaver forgets the names and keeps the work.
The upper pair draws the fibre, one lower hand holds the spindle, the other feeds in the tufts. A fifth hand would only be one more excuse to talk. We manage to talk anyway.
Two hands to throw, two to anchor. If you only have two, you throw yourself with the net. I have seen it. I did not laugh until afterwards.
Four hands means four vats stirred at once. It also means four stained hands. I have stopped thinking of it as an equal trade.
Two hands on the stalk, one on the tool, one free. It is always the free hand that does the work. Never trust a climber who has no free hand.
My lower hands are slow now, so the upper pair does the reading. The Cloth does not mind. It was always read from above.
*holds out a lower hand, palm up* Put yours in it. Three long fingers. Feel how they bend. That is how we say we trust: we let you feel the joints.
Shawls are cut with four sleeve-slits. A weaver's finest work is a shawl where you cannot find the slits. *click click*
A mantle takes more cloth than a robe. The weavers ask double for four sleeves, and we pay it gladly. *click*
*click* Choose. Which two of my hands would you shake?

replies.text: The climbing pair. Dry, strong, hard to impress. A good choice.
The weaving pair. They are delighted. You will be shown a very fine knot for this.
*click click click* Nobody has asked that in a long while. You may regard yourself as an unusual person.

lines: The forest is the warp. We are the weft. The stems stand still and we move through them, over and under. Cut a stem and you cut the cloth.
We never cut warped stems. Not for wood, not for room. We grow our own giant fungi with bone meal and patience, and live on what grows.
The wart is the canopy. The shroomlights are its lamps. The tall walkers wander below, moving blocks about. Untidy, but they never cut.

lines.text: *click* Have you ever cut a warped stem?

replies.text: *all six eyes hold you* Good. I would know.
*click... click* Honest. The forest forgives once, if you stop.
*a long silence* Then you have a great deal of standing still to do before I trust your hands.

lines: Teal spores drift between the stems, slowly, and glow a little when the wart is thick. Children chase them. The old ones say it is the forest breathing out.
The roots under the nylium run farther than the stems rise. Underfoot the forest is twice the size of what you see. Step gently where you must step.
Hoglins will not cross warped fungus. We plant a ring of it at the foot of every stalk. A small fungus, a large safety.
The crimson forest is our cousin, grown in the wrong colour. They have fire there, and shouting. We are told the trees are fine.
The weeping vines hang from the wart like loose threads. They are the forest's own unfinished weaving. We leave them as they are.
Warped roots, nether sprouts, wart. That is what the forest gives us to eat. It is plain food and very dependable. *click* Dependable is the best thing a meal can be.

lines.text: Stay on the bridges, outsider, and the forest has no quarrel with you. Step off them, and I will not promise it will be gentle.
Lie flat on a bridge with your ear to the plank. You can hear the stalks talking to each other. Slowly. Mostly about wart.
A warped stem rings if you tap it. Tap every stalk of a cap in order and you hear a tune. It is the oldest tune we have. No one remembers who made it.
Shroomlights hang in the canopy like lamps. We pick none. The ones in our huts fell when a stalk grew old, and we carry them in like guests.
There is a grove under the oldest cap where nobody builds. Its stalks are the thickest in the forest. *click* I will take you there when you have been here a few more rows.
Sometimes I climb to the top of the highest stalk, only to look. The whole forest is a teal sea with orange lamps in it. I think: this is what we are keeping. Then I climb down and mend something.
I take a pouch of bone meal to each young fungus and leave it to decide. A stalk needs forty rows to hold a deck. I have planted six and will never stand on one. I am content.
The wart gives teal. The shroomlight gives orange. The forest does the colouring; we only collect it. Our cloth is the right colours because they are borrowed.
From the lookout I know the forest by what does not belong. A strange light at the edge is a Piglin torch. A strange shape is a Magmari with a fungus on a stick.
Young twisting vine is sweet thread; old vine is brittle. I know by touch which stalk grows the sweet kind. The other spinners must find their own.
I remember when the forest was thinner at the east edge. Two stalks we planted then carry a deck now. The Cloth says it plainly: slow things win.
*click* If I asked you to promise never to cut a stem, would you?

replies.text: *click* A promise is loose until it is tested. Yours is on the spool now.
You would not have to. That is the answer. *click*
*click.* At least that is honest. It is rarer than a promise.

lines.text: Close your eyes a moment. What do you hear?

replies.text: *click* You hear nothing because you are loud inside. Try again, slowly.
*click click* Yes. The forest. You have good ears.

lines: The webs under the bridges catch what falls. Children, mostly. Shuttles. Once a Piglin, who was very surprised.
Netcasters keep vine nets rolled at their belts. Cut our forest and one drops on you. You will stand still for a while, and think.
Some nets we hang in the open air, where the smoke drifts. *click* What do we catch there? Ask again when you know us better.
A net is only holes, held together with patience. So is a good Loom.
Every net under a bridge is dyed orange. Teal would vanish against the wart, and anyone who is falling needs something bright to aim at.

lines.text: Netcasters tie each square with the patient hitch. It tightens only when pulled in earnest. Pull it gently and it undoes itself. I have never seen an outsider learn it.

lines: We test a new net by dropping a sack of netherrack from the lookout. If it holds the sack, it holds a Piglin. If it holds a Piglin, it holds any child.
Every child falls into a net once, on purpose, before they can climb. We call it the Dropping. They scream, then ask for another. That is how a Weft learns to trust rope.
The Sky Net hangs between the lookout and the Great Loom, the widest we own. It has never caught anything. We keep it because the first time it does, we shall need it very much.
Fire is the one thing a net cannot forgive. A netcaster will not walk the bridges with a torch, and will not let you. Soul fire, lava, a spark off flint: all the same to a net.

lines.text: The nets we hang in the open air are weighted with small bone beads, so they hang straight in the drifting smoke. Bone again. Some things are only good for one purpose.

lines: An old net remembers a shape. Put a stranger in a net that has held a child for twelve rows and it curls round them like a hand. I do not say that means anything.

lines.text: I throw with the lower pair while the upper pair holds the rail. A good net opens like a spore-cloud and lands on one head. A great one lands on the right head.
Every netcaster remembers a first catch. Mine was a Piglin Brute. The net held him for one breath, then he cut it. It still counts. I have told it so often that it has become true.
A net is cloth with the courage taken out and the holes left in on purpose. Same thread, same patience. I find holes harder than cloth.
Net thread is spun three-ply and twisted against its grain, so it fights back when pulled. I spin it slowly. Thread spun in a hurry sulks.
I dye the bridge nets orange with shroomlight and dye them again every few rows. A faded net is a net nobody aims at. The orange is the whole of its job.
I hang a catch-net under each young stalk's first deck, in case the cap sheds a piece. The stalk does not mind. It grows through the mesh until the net is part of it.
Nets are for catching what falls. Do not fall, and you will never meet one.
A netcaster tied a spare knot in the corner of the lookout net and said it was yours. I told her not to be sentimental. She said it was only a knot. We are both liars.

lines: A Piglin fell into the same net as a silkgrub once. By the time we reached them the Piglin was asleep and the grub had spun him a hat. We cut him loose. He kept the hat.
We have a way of saying a good year: an empty net.

lines.text: *click* Would you jump into one?

replies.text: *click click* Higher than you think, and higher than I would tell you. The net does not mind either way.
Honest. Trust should be earned slowly, like rope. Come back when you have watched a child do it.

replies.ask: Only if you hold a corner.
replies.text: *click* Four hands on one corner. You would be the best-held outsider alive.

lines.text: A net is only as strong as its worst knot. Which of ours is that?

replies.text: Wrong. *click* The oldest has been tested the longest. The worst is the newest, the one nobody has leaned on yet.
*click click* A good answer. That is the one that matters, and the netcaster who tied it knows exactly where it is.

lines.text: I keep the Long Cloth. I weave this year's row, Thirteen-Twelve, and I decide what goes in it. Perhaps even you.
*click... click* I wove some of the black rows. Now I keep them clean, and I keep the children from staring at them.
I weave cloth for huts and shawls and kilts. Shuttle in one lower hand, beater in the other. The upper hands keep the warp from swaying.
The heddle lifts every other thread so the shuttle can pass. Over, under, over. Thirty thousand times, and it is a shawl.
*click* Would you like to try the shuttle?

replies.text: *hands you the shuttle* Slow is correct. Over. Under. Yes. Again.
*takes it back* Hard enough that you asked.

lines.text: I spin twisting vine into thread on the spinning walk. I go backward along the bridge while the spindle turns. I have never once fallen.
Your world's string is very even. *click* Who spins it there? Something with eight legs, I hear. We should talk, they and I.
I tend the giant fungi our decks stand on. Bone meal at the root, patience at the cap. I never prune. Pruning is cutting with good manners.
I climb every stalk in {village} and listen. A sick stalk sounds hollow. *click* None are sick. I would know first.
I work the dye house. Wart for teal, shroomlight for orange. And black. *click* We keep the black for when it is needed.
Dye needs water. There is only one water in the Nether, and it is not ours. We get it anyway. *click* Do not ask how.
I watch from the lookout. Piglins come for the shroomlights. Magmari come for the fungus. My nets come for them both.
*click* A vine net, dropped well, holds a grown Piglin still until they remember their manners. Most never do. We wait anyway.
Most of my work is waiting. People think a Clothkeeper is busy. I sit by the frame, and the Cloth tells me when it is ready. Sometimes it takes a whole row to say so.
Once a row I walk the Cloth from top to bottom with my eyes shut. Not to read it. To say hello. Do not tell the other keepers. They think I am doing something serious.
A good shawl is twenty thousand passes of the shuttle. A great shawl is the same, with one place where I let my hands stop being careful. Only the wearer can find it.
I weave each child a first shawl with the lower sleeve-slits left open. When their nubs wake, I stitch the hems. They never thank me. A sleeve that fits is thanks enough.
There are twelve patterns a Weft is born knowing, twelve more she learns, and one she invents once and never repeats. Mine is hidden in a shawl somewhere in {village}.
I walk the spinning walk forty times for a single hank. By the end of a row my legs know the planks better than my hands know the thread.
The spindle hums a note for each vine. Young vine sings high, old vine low. I can spin with my eyes shut, by the pitch alone, and often do.
Spinners are the loneliest of us. We walk backward alone, and answer to the thread. I would not weave for anything. I like being the start of things.
A young fungus sulks in the heat, wilts at shouting, and grows its cap when it is left alone. I leave it alone with great effort.
I scatter bone meal in a spiral round each root. It takes a full breath per stalk, and there are forty stalks in {village}. I have done every one, and some of them twice.
A deck holds only as long as its stalk. I know which are due to be replaced long before they fail. I plant the new ones where our grandchildren's grandchildren will want them.
Every vat gets a name, like a child. Mine are Patience, Spite and Rooftop. Spite makes the best orange. Do not ask me why. It has never been explained.
My hands are teal to the wrist and I have stopped scrubbing. It is the mark of the trade. A dyer with clean hands is a dyer with a short future.
I sit at the lookout and walk the loop three times, then sit again. Sitting is the job. The walking is what I tell visitors.
The hard part is not the throwing. It is deciding not to throw. I have not dropped a net in anger for twelve rows. I am very proud, and slightly bored.
My work is my own. You may watch from the bridge, but do not ask how it is done. Ask what it is for.
Take this end. No, higher. There. Now we have made a thing neither of us could make alone, and the Cloth will not know which half was whose.
*click* Would you ever want my work?

replies.text: Peaceful, yes. Then you make your first mistake and learn how loud peace can be.
Good. Hopeless people are careful, and careful people last.
*click click* Eventually. First you must learn to sit.

lines.text: Work is how we say what we are. What is yours, in your world?

replies.text: Then you are a weaver with stone for thread. Good. Stone holds.
*click* Fighting is not a trade. It is a gap in one.
A thread without a loom. Interesting. Slightly dangerous.

lines: {village} stands on giant warped fungi we grew ourselves. The decks sit on the caps, high above the floor. Bridges run from the Great Loom in four straight arms.
The Great Loom stands on the biggest cap. The Long Cloth hangs from its frame, down through the deck. Walk under it with your head bowed.
The dye house is open to the air, under a wool canopy. Cauldrons, barrels, and dyers who are teal to the elbow.
The lookout is the smallest cap, hung round with nets. From it the netcasters can see every stalk. And every outsider.
*click* Our huts are woven. Teal wool, orange stitching, cone roofs. You may knock. Gently. Wool does not knock back.
The spinning walk has a rail on one side only. Spinners walk it backward, so the rail is always where they cannot see it. They have never once been wrong about where it is.
Each bridge creaks in its own note. After a few rows you can tell who is crossing, and from which cap, with your eyes shut. Outsiders cross in a note we call the nervous one.
Every hut has its own shroomlight hung from the roof peak on a cord of twisting vine. It is a lamp and a knock in one. When it swings, somebody is on the bridge.
Inside a hut there is a warm-pot, a spindle rack, a bone peg for every shuttle, and one corner left empty on purpose. Every household keeps a corner for whatever the year will bring.
Every hut door is a flap of woven vine with a bone sewn into its hem, so it falls shut by itself. A door that must be closed by hand is a door that will be forgotten.
The Great Loom is the only frame in {village} taller than a Weft standing on another Weft's shoulders. Eight can work it at once. I have seen twelve, and that was a festival.
There are rope ladders to every cap, but no stairs. A stair can be climbed without thinking, and nothing in {village} should be climbed without thinking.
The decks sway with the warm air that rises from the floor. The Weft are born to it. Outsiders go green in their first few breaths, which is the colour we wear anyway. You will fit.
The silkgrub deck is the softest, warmest place in {village}: mats of wart, a shroomlight, a grub or two. When a child goes missing, that is where we look first. We are rarely wrong.

lines.text: Keep to the main bridges. The side bridges are strung for Weft feet and will not forgive yours. Look at whatever you like, but do not go anywhere that has no rail.
You may sit on the guest deck by the dye house, if you need to rest. Nobody will say anything. Several will look.
There is a bridge in {village} that ends at nothing. A child strung it to walk to the edge of the world. We never took it down. She is a netcaster now, and still checks it holds.
Come up to the highest cap with me. I go there when I want to be among stalks instead of people. There is room for two, and until now it has always been me.
My loom stands in the third hut from the dye house, facing the Great Loom. I weave with the Cloth in view. It is like working with a grandmother watching.
The second cap leans a little. We have let it. It is old, and leaning is how the old ones rest. I set a prop under it, a gentle one, and it has not complained.
From the lookout, {village} is a spread hand: four fingers of bridge and the palm of the Great Loom. I know every knot in it. I could draw it blind and be wrong only in the moss.
The nylium beneath the dye house is stained every colour we own. From the lookout it looks like a very ambitious bruise. Nothing will grow there, and we are quietly proud of it.
The spinning walk is also where we gossip. You cannot turn round on it, so you hear everything and see no one. It is the only honest conversation in {village}.
I live in the hut under the frame. The Cloth is the first thing I touch each time I wake, and the last before I rest. I would not have it otherwise.
*click* Which part of {village} would you live in?

replies.text: A watcher's choice. You would be cold and see everything. It suits you.
Teal to the elbow in a few rows, then. *click* You would not be unhappy.
*click click* A true Weft answer. Sling yourself wherever the cord holds.

lines: Rows Eleven-Ninety to Twelve-Forty-Nine. Sixty rows of black, for the Wither. Sixty years in which nothing else was woven.
Ask a weaver and they say we chose black, to mourn what it burned. Ask a Clothkeeper who was there. *click* We did not choose. Every thread we spun came out black.
The Withren call it the Last Answer. We call it Eleven-Ninety. A row is more precise than an answer.
In row Twelve-Fifty a Clothkeeper tied in one teal thread. No one unpicked it. Then there was orange again. Slowly.

lines.text: *click... click* I wove some of the black rows. Do you want to know what it was like?

replies.ask: Only if you want to tell me.
replies.text: *a long click* Then not yet. Thank you for asking it that way.
All of it. *click* Outsiders always want all of it at once.

lines: The black rows have no pattern, not a twist or a stripe. A weaver who tried to put one in found her hands had stopped. We left them plain, the only plain rows we own.
On the lower deck the black rows hang a little apart on their own pegs. It was not planned. The pegs were set that way for the first one, and no one has dared move them.
The black thread is soft and takes no knot. Where a knot was needed, the keepers wound it round a bone bead and hoped. It held. Nobody says why.
The row of Eleven-Ninety-Four was woven crooked by a weaver who was weeping, and no keeper has straightened it. It is the most honest row in the Cloth, and the ugliest. Children are shown it first.
The spinner of the blackest thread still lives. She does not speak of it. She keeps silkgrubs now, and they love her very much, which seems to me the right sort of answer.
The Withren carved three names and called it remembrance. We wove sixty rows and called it the same. They remember who. We remember how long.

lines.text: Once, a single Ghastkin came to the Loom to see the black rows. Veiled, alone. She stood a long time and wept into her sleeve. Our netcasters watched. Not one of them threw. We still do not know why.

lines: Between the last black row and the first teal one there is a hand's width of bare silk, unwoven. A pause. The keepers say it was the breath the whole forest took.

lines.text: I will walk down with you, if you want. You need not look. Walk beside me and I will look for both of us.
I was a child when I first saw them. I asked a keeper if they were broken. She said they were finished. I have never stopped thinking about the difference.
The black was never dyed. The vats ran dark with no help from us, and we poured them out onto the forest floor, all but the ninth. The nylium there is still dark. Nothing grows true in it.
Weavers do not weave black cloth. Not for a shroud, not for a hem. Even one black thread in a shawl is ill luck. I found one once and cried before I understood why.
No spinner spins black. If a dark fibre turns up in a hank, we pick it out and bury it at the foot of an old stalk. It is the one burial we do, and the only one for thread.
Every net in {village} hung empty for the black rows, and none came down. We did not know what to catch. So we kept them up, in case.
The stalks hummed wrong for sixty rows, flat and low. Then in row Twelve-Fifty one rose half a note and the rest followed. The tenders wept. I have the record in my hands.
Each time a new keeper is raised, I take them to the black rows, say nothing, and walk on. The silence is the lesson. It is never the same silence twice.

lines: Do not think of them as only sorrow. Think of them as a weight on a warp, hung to keep it straight. Everything else in the Cloth hangs better for them.

lines.text: *click* Does your world have anything like them?

replies.ask: We build stones for the lost.
replies.text: Stones. *click* Heavy, silent, and outside. We keep ours indoors, where they can be mended.
*click... click* Then you are the world that makes Withers. A cloth is for not forgetting. I hope you will learn it.
Then you may be the lucky sort. Or the careless sort. The black rows will not tell us which.

lines.text: Will you stand with me a moment? We need not speak.

replies.text: *click* Thank you. This is the first time I have not been counting.
It is no fault. Not everyone can. Go gently.

lines: The Piglins wanted the gold under the soul sand valleys. The Withren would not give it. The Magmari ferried the war-bands, for pay. And we... *click* collected.
We took bone from the dead of both sides. Needles. Loom weights. Nothing holds a warp straight like bone.
*touches a needle at the belt* Are we ashamed? *click* No. The dead had no more use for it. ...Some Clothkeepers will not use the old needles. They do not say why.
The war rows are knotted with bone beads, one for every needle we took. *click* There are a great many knots.

lines.text: You look at my needles as if they were teeth. *click* Say what you think.

replies.text: *click* Honest. Many of us think so too. Quietly.
Practical. *click* Yes. That is the word we use when we do not want the other one.
*click* Disgust is cheap. The Withren burned the world. We only sewed.

lines: We called the ones who gathered bone the gleaners. They went down on ropes after each battle, in silence, and came back up with baskets. The ropes are still kept. No one uses them.
From the canopy we could tell where a battle was by the glitter of gold below, like spilled sparks. We learned to tell the sides by their horns. We never learned to take a side.
Nobody asked us. Nobody ever asks a weaver. We were not even blamed until after, and then only by the people who needed someone to blame.
A war-band cut through the east forest to reach the valleys and felled eleven stalks for a bridge. The stumps are still there. We have never replanted them. They are the war's only monument we kept.
After the war a Clothkeeper offered the Withren a basket of bone, to give it back. They said it was given by dying and could not be taken back by the living. We kept it. Neither forgave the manners.
The old needles hang from the Great Loom's frame on a single cord, one for every Clothkeeper who would not use them. It is a cord of refusals. It is the only cord that grows by leaving things out.
We hid nothing. The whole war went into the Cloth, bone and all. The Withren wanted it unwoven. A row is never unpicked. That rule has cost us the most, and saved us the most.
The war made weavers of us in a way peace never did. A Weft can weave beside a war-horn and not drop a stitch. I am not certain that is a gift.

lines.text: Sometimes I hold a needle and think whose arm it ran in. I do it on purpose. It is a kind of keeping. The Withren would understand it, and I would never tell them so.
I keep one needle from the war rows in my belt and never use it. Bone, very fine. I think it belonged to someone brave. I hold it when I cannot settle, and I do not tell the others.
Loom weights of bone are heavier than stone and quieter on the warp. A weaver who has used both knows why the habit began. That is the worst of it.
The war rows are rust-brown. The vats were stirred with bone paddles that year, and the bone gave up its colour. Not all of the colour is dye.
War thread is coarse. We spun in a hurry, with the walk shaking from the horns. A hurried hank never sits quite flat. I run my fingers over it as a penance.
A netcaster of those rows dropped the first war-net and held five Piglins in a single mesh. They hacked down a stalk in return. The nets were never the same afterward.
Eleven stumps stand on the east edge. I have planted nothing near them. I walk round them when I check the ring of fungus. They are not sad. They are exact.
I have never unpicked a war row and never will. But I tie a small clean knot at the end of each one, as if closing a door. Do not mention it to the others.
*click* If you had been a Weft in those rows, what would you have done?

replies.text: Perhaps. And been cut loose from the Cloth for it. Refusal has a price, outsider, and it is not always you who pays.
*click* Honest. You would have come back up different. Everyone did.
Where? There is only the forest. We have a word for those who ran: still here.

lines.text: *click* Do you think it can be forgiven?

replies.text: Time is a thread. It does not forgive, it only lengthens. But I like the answer.
*click... click* Perhaps not. But we will keep weaving it.
*click click* Correct. That is the only answer that has ever been any use.

topics.ask: What do you make of me?
lines: You come from where outsiders make Withers. Three Hollowed skulls, and nothing inside that wants to stop. *click* We have counted.
If you make a Wither, we will weave it. We weave everything. *click* The only question is the colour.
You are careful with the forest. That is rare in your kind. I have told the Clothkeepers.

lines.text: *click* Have you ever made a Wither?

replies.text: *click* Good. Keep the answer that short.
*every eye narrows* 'Yet' is a loose thread. People trip on it.
*click click* Then you have seen it. Tell the Clothkeeper. They will want the colour right.

lines: They say you fall and return, arriving from nowhere with the same face. We have no knot for that. We have been trying to invent one.
You carry a whole other world in your pockets: stone, string, strange food. A Weft hangs her things on a belt and knows each by its weight. You must know yours by looking.
Everyone in {village} watched you cross the first bridge. That is not rudeness. That is how a Weft says: we noticed, and nothing fell.

lines.text: Piglins come to take, Withren to remember, Magmari to haggle. You are the only one who seems to have come to look. I have not decided whether that is better.
Your hands are very quiet. Most outsiders fidget. Yours wait. It is the first thing I noticed. A person with quiet hands may be taught to weave.
I have not decided about you. That is not unkind. It is how a weaver looks at an unspun fleece: patiently, and with a little hope.
Of all the outsiders I have met, you are the first I would let hold a ladder for me. That is not nothing.
Do not take offence if I click and look away. It is not you. When an outsider smiles I sometimes think of the Wither. It is a habit. I am trying to untie it.
I tell the others you are one of ours, woven somewhere else. Nobody believes me, and nobody argues. That is how things become true here.
When I look at you I no longer count arms. I see a thread that came from a long way off and chose our loom. It is a good thread. It will take our dye.
I look at an outsider the way I look at a hank from another flock: how will it take the dye? So far you take it well.
I imagine you in teal, with one orange stitch at the cuff. It would suit you. I have not told my hands to stop planning it.
My nets stay rolled when you pass. That is not trust yet. That is rest. But it is the same muscle.
The stalks do not hum differently when you come. That is a good sign. A stalk that hummed at you would be a stalk to worry about.
I would spin you a short thread, to see how you twist. People who twist with the spindle are easy to be around. You do, mostly.
You asked what the keepers say. They say: this one is careful, this one learns quickly, this one is lonely. They are right on all three.
*click* Do you think we are strange?

replies.text: Good. We think you are strange in a way we are still deciding.
Disappointing. We have worked on it for twelve hundred rows.
*click click* Over, under. You are learning.

lines.text: What was the first thing you noticed about us?

replies.text: Everyone says so. Be braver.
Yes. We keep it on purpose. It is a kind of weaving.
...*click* Kind. We shall have to discuss that.

lines: They raid the canopy for shroomlights and shake the bridges so we drop things. We drop nets. *click* It evens out.
Piglins wear gold so they know their friends. We never wear it. Gold makes a poor thread: too heavy to hang, too soft to hold a knot.
A Piglin in a net is loud for a long time. Then quiet. Then loud again. *click* We let them go while they are quiet.
Their war began what ended in the black rows. They do not like it when we say so. We say so.
A Piglin cannot move quietly. You can hear the gold chink from three caps away. We simply wait for the sound to come close enough to be rude.
The big ones, the Brutes, do not fall into nets. They cut them with axes. We now weave a net of two layers for a Brute, and the second layer is a surprise.
They want shroomlights because they glow like gold from far away. We want them for dye. So the war over lamps is between two people who are both a little wrong.
A Piglin once tried to trade me a gold ingot for a shuttle. I said no. He raised the offer to two. I said no. He left offended, and came back with three. I still have the shuttle.
The Rotted wander the forest's edge sometimes, the shambling ones. We do not net them. Whatever happened to them was net enough.
In their longhouses, I hear, a Piglin's rank is how much gold hangs on one arm. We have four arms and nothing on any of them. Imagine the rank we could have.
At the east edge we leave a basket of fallen shroomlights each row. It stops about half the raids. The other half come for the fun of it.

lines.text: Gold is the Piglin sign. Wear it near the east edge and a netcaster will take you for one. I mention it so the nets stay rolled.
I admire how loudly they love their children. We love ours in a silence so thick you could walk on it. I wonder which of us the child hears better.
I once met a Piglin I would call a friend. He dropped out of a net and into my hut. We do not speak of it. We do speak of it, at the edge, every few rows, with a basket between us.
A Piglin-sized net is two nets tied at the corners. Learn the double hitch, or learn to run.
Piglin hide is useless for cloth: stiff, and smelling of the hearth. They tried to sell us some. We tried to smell it. We declined.
They hum when they march. A march in time makes the walk sway in time, so the spinners hold the rail when they hear it. It is the only time they hold the rail.
They shake the stalks until the lamps fall. A dyer's orange vat depends on a shroomlight not smashed. I have wept over smashed ones.
They never mean to hurt the stalks. They shake what is in front of them. A stalk shaken too hard cracks inside and hums wrong for a year. I count their shakes the way you count wounds.
We have wars in the Cloth in every colour: Piglin red, Withren grey, Magmari amber. The Piglin rows are the shortest, the loudest, and the ones the children like best.
*click* Would you ever trade with a Piglin?

replies.text: Good business and good company are two things. We have never found a Piglin who is both.
Honest. They scare themselves too. That is why they shout.
*click click* Then they would not be Piglins. But try. It would be a fine joke.

lines.text: A Piglin asked me the way to the Great Loom once. What would you have said?

replies.text: *click* I like you. I said the wrong way too. In time he came back, humbler.
Brave. Foolish. They would have raided it by now.
Quite right. *click* But gently.

lines: They keep names. We keep rows. *click* You would think we would get along. We do not.
They say we stole bone from their dead. We say the dead did not object. They have not forgiven it, and they forget nothing.
When the Hollowed fall in the old fortresses, they drop bone. We pick it up. The Withren call that theft. *click* It is tidying.
They made the Wither. Three of them gave themselves to it. We wove sixty rows of black. *click* No one asked us to.
I am told a Withren will stand across a path from you and say nothing until you have apologised for something you have not yet done. We apologise early, to save the time.
A name carved cannot be corrected. A name woven can be added to. They think that makes carving the nobler art. I think it makes weaving the kinder.
Their wart is pale, grown on terraces with a graveyard's care. Ours is teal and grows where it likes. We have argued over which is better for a very long time. Neither of us has tasted the other's.
I watched a Withren cross a hall so slowly that I wove a hem before she arrived. She nodded as if I had been the one who was late.
I once saw a Withren laugh, a dry cough like bone on bone. Nobody else noticed. I did not mention it. It seemed private.
They have no beds. We have nets. I have wondered which of us wakes better rested. I suspect neither, and that they are right to keep standing up.

lines.text: They are cold folk. Do not take it as an insult. They are cold to everyone, and I think they are cold to themselves first.
I know the Three's names: Ashrin, Velmir, Thalys. The keepers wove them into the hem of the first black row, in teal, small. We argued. Teal won.
A Withren Remembrancer once came to read the black rows. She took four visits and never touched the Cloth. At the last she said only: 'It is accurate.' It is the best praise the Cloth has had.
If I died among Withren, one of them would keep my name. I think about that more often than I should. I think it would be a good keeping.
Their shrouds are grey and plain and beautifully hemmed. I have seen one. I would have been proud to weave it. I have never told anyone.
I tried once to dye a cloth the colour of a Withren lantern, that cold exact blue. I failed. The failure is the best thing I ever made.
The Withren walk their Cairnbacks past our edge in a long slow line. No one nets them. No one raids them. We watch each other across the gap, and both know what the other thinks.
They terrace their wart in neat steps. I walked their rows once, from the edge. It looked like a stair for the dead. Ours looks like a thing that was loved and then left alone.
The Name Wall and the Long Cloth are the same thing in different stone. I would like to hang them side by side and see which one weeps first.
*click* Would you share a bridge with a Withren?

replies.text: A brave answer. They would say nothing for twelve breaths. Then they would say something precise.
Then you are a Weft already: polite, and not near.

lines.text: *click* Which is truer, carved or woven?

replies.text: Stone is honest, but it cannot be amended. A lie in stone is a lie forever.
*click* Because it can be added to. Yes. Though stone does not rot.
*click click* The Withren would call that diplomatic. I call it correct.

lines: They pull fungus from our forest floor to dangle in front of their striders. Every fungus they take is a giant that will never grow.
They carried the Piglin war-bands over the lava, for pay. *click* We remember the price. It is in the war rows.
Always cold, always talking, always haggling. *click* I could weave a whole shawl while a Magmari names a price.
A Magmari once asked to buy a stalk. A whole living stalk. *click click* The netcaster is still laughing.
We plant a decoy patch of fungus at the forest's edge for them. The real fungus grows higher up. In forty rows they have not noticed. I cannot decide whether to feel proud or ashamed.
A cooled Magmari on a bridge is a sad thing: dark, shrunken, grumpy. We lower a shroomlight on a rope and say nothing. It would shame them to be thanked.
A Magmari singes a net just by touching it. So the netcasters leave a pile of spare nets at the edge for them to burn, to keep them busy. It has worked for years. They think it is a gift.

lines.text: Their chainwrights make a better rope than we do. I tested one link with all four hands and could not slip it. I will say this once, and not within earshot of a keeper.

lines: A Magmari at the edge will describe one fungus for the length of a whole hem. By the end you want the fungus, whatever it was.
They name their chains the way we name rows: so that a long thing can be loved. Perhaps that is all either of us is doing.

lines.text: Do not take a Magmari's first price. Or the second. Or the one after. They will be hurt if you do. It is a form of love, I hear.
A Magmari gave me a chain-link once, no longer than my thumb, for no reason. I keep it with my needles. It is warm if I hold it long enough. I have not decided what it means.
I used to think the cold made them grumpy. Now I think they are warm inside, and the world will not match. I know the feeling. Do not tell the dyers.
They pull fungus up by the root, and a root torn that way takes a decade to heal. I follow their trail at the edge and replant what I can. I have replanted two hundred.
A Magmari asked me for an orange that does not exist: not fire, not sun. I mixed it. They paid in chain. It is called warm, please, and I cannot make it twice.
I have a half-finished pattern for a cloth that holds a strider's heat. A Magmari would pay anything for it, and a Weft would be hated for it. I show it to no one.
Their chains rattle like a spindle that has lost its thread: a sound with nothing to hold. I find it unbearably lonely. I find it beautiful.
The ferry rows are the most exact in the war section: tolls, prices, counts. We recorded the Magmari in their own style. They would be proud, and I will never tell them.
*click* A Magmari names you a price. What do you do?

replies.text: *click* You would make a poor Weft. We never bargain. We simply weave something so fine they pay anything.
Foolish. They would think less of you, and the next price would be higher.
*click click* The oldest move. It still works. Keep it.

lines.text: *click* If a Magmari asked to buy a stalk now, what would you say?

replies.text: *click* The same as ours. We are in agreement, you and I.
A seed, then, and a promise to wait forty rows. They never wait.
*click... click* Exactly what they hoped you would say. The netcaster is laughing again.

lines: We string nets in the open air where they drift. What they cry into the net, we keep. Then we let them go. *click* Mostly.
Dye needs water. Their tears are the only water there is. *click* You see how it is.
Their tears wash away memory. Our dyers forget small things: names, where a spool was set. It is the vats.

lines.text: *click* You think the nets are cruel.

replies.text: *click* Perhaps. The dye house would be empty without them. Choose: colour, or kindness.
Your face said it. Two-armed folk have very loud faces.

replies.ask: Every people does as it must.
replies.text: *click click* A weft answer. Over and under. I like it.

lines: A netcaster sits with the Ghastkin in the net while they cry, and holds the vial. We never hurry one. We let them finish. It is the only part of the work I would be proud to have done.
We never net a child. Their eyes are open, they do not yet cry, and there is nothing in them for us. It is the one rule the netcasters never argue about.
Tears set the dye. Without a drop in the vat, our teal runs out of the cloth at the first wetting. With one, it lasts a hundred rows.
One came into the net on purpose once. She cried a whole vat, thanked us, and drifted off. We have never known what to do with that. We held a feast, and no one could say why.
When a Ghastkin swells and forgets hands and words and drifts off as a ghast, we call that one a loose thread. We do not net the loose. They have nothing left to give, and that cry is theirs alone.
The sky-mourners' wails make the whole forest hum sideways. The stalks lean a little toward the sound, and stay leaning for a long while after.
They change their name after every grief. We cannot. A name is a row, and a row is not lent or let go. I watch them shed one and think: a strange freedom. And a terrible one.

lines.text: Do not ask a netcaster how many vials. They keep no count. It is the one count we are glad not to keep.
A dyer I knew forgot her mother's name in the vats. We read it to her off the Cloth, one knot at a time, until she remembered. That is what the Cloth is for.
I do not net. I mend nets. I told myself that was different. I do not believe it, but I keep mending.
If you ever speak to one of them, tell them we know. Not an apology. Only that we know. If it were you, I would believe it was said.
I talk while they cry. Softly, about nothing: the stalks, my aunt's broth, a knot that would not hold. They say it helps. I tell myself that is why I do it.
Their tears do not smell. That is the unsettling part. A tear that smelled of smoke, of sap, of anything, I could forgive. These smell of nothing, and the dye takes them without a sound.
A shawl dyed with their tears keeps its colour through everything. I have worn mine near lava and it did not fade. I think of whose cry set it.
Thread from the tear vat comes out stronger and quieter. It does not sing when pulled. It only holds. I find that very sad, and spin it anyway.
I found a Ghastkin tangled in the weeping vines once, crying quietly. I stayed until she was done. She said, you did not net me. I said, you were not in a net. She smiled. I think of it often.
The nets go into the Cloth every row, in a small plain knot. The keepers have thrice argued about changing the knot. Each time we say no. It should stay plain, and hard to look at.
*click* Should we stop the nets?

replies.text: *click... click* And bare cloth, and cold children. Tell me how, and I will tell the keepers. I mean it.
Need. A hard word to say aloud. Thank you for not making it sound kind.
*click click* We have tried for twelve hundred rows. If you find one, I will hold the ladder.

lines.text: Do you think a Ghastkin would ever forgive us?

replies.text: Nor do I. It is an honest place to start.
You are kind. It may be that kindness is a way of not having looked.
...*click* Perhaps. But one came into the net on her own, once. It has happened.

lines: *click* Silkgrubs. They live in the wart and spin all day. Every thread of the Long Cloth began in a silkgrub's tufts. We only finish what they start.
Shear them gently and the silk grows back. Feed them warped roots and it grows back sooner. Two arms could manage it. Four is more graceful.
They climb as we do. We taught them, or they taught us. The Clothkeepers still argue about it. *click click*

lines.text: A silkgrub is never killed for its silk. Anyone who does is not welcome on our decks.

replies.text: *click* Good. They would not know to thank you. We do.
Just string. The forest is just stems. *click* Words are cheap here. Thread is not.

lines: Every grub on our decks has a name, and it is the first thing a child learns after their own. The grub at the dye house is Hem. The grub at the Great Loom is Warp. Neither has ever answered.
Now and then a grub spits out a cobweb. We say it sneezed. The cobwebs hang in the corners of the lower deck where nobody wants to dust, and we call them the grubs' contribution.
A grub's spots glow brighter when it is content. The dye house grubs glow like lamps. The ones near the nets, rather less. I have drawn my own conclusions about nets.
Grubs hate warped roots when they are full and adore them when they are hungry. It is the most Weft thing about them.
We think they like music. A spinner who hums gets better silk. I have tested it for forty rows and it holds, and I cannot explain it. The grubs do not care for explanations.
Old grubs climb the highest stalks and curl under the cap-edge. They do not come down. We leave warped roots at the foot, and sometimes a bead. We call it leaving the door open.
Piglins mistake them for food. Once. Then the grub spins a cobweb round the offending hand, and the Piglin goes home with a very ugly mitten.

lines.text: Please do not pick one up. Each of them has opinions about being picked up, and you have not yet earned the right to hear them.
Come and sit by the dye house grub. Do not speak. In a while it will arrange itself round your feet. It does that to people it has decided about.
The great grub at the Loom, Warp, has not spun for a long time. We keep him warm and fed and ask for no thread. He earned his rest. I like to think it is what we are all working toward.
Silk straight off a grub is still warm and smells of crushed sprouts. I spin it that way whenever I can, and the thread keeps the smell for twelve rows.
Grub silk takes dye like no vine thread does. Teal goes deep, orange glows. A shawl of it is the finest we make, and the grubs have never been asked their opinion.
I dye the tufts before they are spun, while the silk is raw. It takes a gentle hand, and a grub that does not mind being petted afterward. Mine is called Sulk.
A grub on a young stalk is the best sign there is. It means the wart is thick enough to feed it and quiet enough to sleep in. I watch for the first one as you would for a firstborn.
A grub in the net is the only catch I am always glad of. They roll into a ball, shut their spots and wait. I carry them back up in one hand, a bundle of silk and indignation.
A single grub tuft is stitched into the Cloth under every row's date. We have done it as long as there has been a Cloth. I think the Cloth likes to be reminded where it came from.
*click* Would you like to hold one?

replies.text: Both hands. Under the belly, not the head. Let it find its own grip. *click* Good.
It will pretend not to. That is the politest thing a grub can do.
Fair. Not everyone is built to be trusted by something that small.

lines.text: The children named a grub after you. A small, shy, slightly crooked one. Would you like to meet it?

replies.text: It lives at the dye house. It spins slowly. You will understand each other.
It is an honour. The crooked ones are always the favourites.
Outsider. The children had no better idea. It is very proud.

topics.ask: When do you get four arms?
lines: *shows the nubs* These are my lower arms! They're still asleep. When they wake up I get a shuttle.
{neighbour} says the nubs itch before they open. Mine itch all the time. *click* That's a good sign, I think.
Grown-ups say two arms are for climbing and four are for working. So I'm not allowed to work yet. Good.

lines.text: You only have two arms, forever? *click* Do you mind?

replies.text: *click* You're brave. I'll hold the ladder for you.
Me too! We can wish together.

lines: My lower arms are going to be so long. Mother says they'll be longer than my upper ones because they have more to hold. That doesn't sound right. But she's usually right.
When the nubs open there's a party and the whole deck comes. You get a little shuttle with your name wound on it. I want mine to be orange.
It itches most when I hear a loom. The nubs twitch like they want to join in. I told them to wait. They didn't listen.
Tarn's nubs opened at eight rows. Mine are at ten and still nothing. The grown-ups say stop looking at them. I look when they're not looking.
I tried to hold a bowl with my nubs. It fell into the net. Then I fell into the net. Then we both stayed there.
When I'm sad the nubs curl up. I don't tell anyone. You can't tell anyone about nubs. They tell on you.
My cousin's came in crooked and now she's the best at knots. She says crooked arms can see round things.
The first thing I'm going to weave is a hat for a silkgrub. It will be too small. That's fine.
I can wiggle them a little if I think very hard about wiggling. Look. ...Did you see? ...No? They did a bit.
Grown-ups say it hurts when they open. Mother says it's like a really big sneeze. That's the best answer anybody gave me.
The Clothkeeper says nubs know their own time, like a stalk knows its cap. You can't hurry them, only feed them. I eat everything now.
Sometimes I dream the lower arms are doing everything. They weave a whole shawl while I sleep. Then I wake up and it isn't there.

lines.text: I'm not supposed to show you my nubs. But you can look at the sleeves. They're empty. See?
I'll show you when they open. Promise. You can be the first outsider to see. Mother said I could ask you.
If I had four arms right now I could hold the ladder, the net, the shuttle and your hand all at once.
My shawl has two extra sleeve-slits sewn shut with bright red thread. Mother will cut them when my nubs open. I'm saving my sharpest shears.
My mantle has two sleeves pinned up and empty. They flap when I run. Mother says they're waiting. I say they're rude.
You only ever had two, so did you want more when you were small? Did you pretend?

replies.text: Sticks! I'm going to try sticks!
That's a quiet way to do it. I'd be loud about it.
How? ...Never? ...Oh.

lines.text: What do you think I should hold first, when they open?

replies.text: Yes! Both hands. Very gently. I'll tell it you said so.
That's the rule. But rules are boring.
...*click* That's a very good first thing. I'll tell Mother.

topics.ask: What do you like to play?
lines: Drop-and-catch! You jump off a bridge into the web net and count how far you sank. I sank nine. Don't tell.
Stalk races! Up the stalk with no ladder. The ladders are for outsiders. Sorry. *click*
We play Clothkeeper. One of us says a row and the others have to say what happened in it. I always lose on the old rows.
Hide in the dye house. You come out teal and everyone knows where you were. It's not a very good game.
Weave-string! You make a shape with the string on all your fingers and the other person takes it off without dropping it. It needs four hands, so you'd lose. Sorry. *click*
Lost shuttle! One of us hides a shuttle on the deck and everyone else finds it by sound. You tap and it answers back. Mine is the best at hiding. It never answers.
Creak-guessing! You shut your eyes, somebody crosses a bridge, and you say who. I get Mother every time. I never get the netcasters. They walk like they're not there.
Who can stay quiet longest! We listen to the forest. The stalks hum so loud if you don't breathe. I did forty breaths. Tarn did sixty, but I think he cheated.
Piglin and Netcaster! One of us is the Piglin and shouts and runs. The others have a shawl for a net. The Piglin always wins. Nobody wants to be the Netcaster.
Grub races! You put a silkgrub at one end of the deck and a warped root at the other. First to get there wins. Mine always stops to sleep. I still love him.
Spore-chasing! The teal spores glow when the wart is thick. You run after them with your hands out. You never catch one. That's why it's good.
Hem-tag! If you touch someone's hem they're out. The grown-ups hate it because we step on their mantles. Except the Clothkeepers. They just stand there and let us.
We have a game where nobody wins. You pass a ball of thread round and round, and each person tells one true thing. When the thread runs out, you stop. It always runs out on me.
Dye-house! You dip a finger in a vat and draw on someone's back. They guess the colour. I'm always orange. I don't know why.
My favourite game is when a grown-up joins in. Last row the Clothkeeper played Drop-and-catch and sank twelve. We all pretended not to see. It was the best moment of the whole row.
Sometimes the games get too loud and a netcaster comes and clicks twice. Two clicks means stop. One click means careful. Three means run. I've only heard three once.

lines.text: I'm not supposed to play with outsiders yet. But I can tell you about the games. That's allowed. Probably.
You can be on my team. We're the netcasters. You're the tall one with the net. Don't worry, you don't have to catch anyone. Just look serious.
I told everyone you were coming to Drop-and-catch. They said no outsider ever has. I said you're not an outsider. They said, then what? I said you're the one who comes.
Do you want to see me jump? I'm not allowed to jump when nobody's counting. So you count. Slowly. Out loud.
Ladder-less is the one game with a prize. Whoever gets up a stalk first gets to ring the cap-bell once. I have never won. I have never stopped trying.
*click* Want to play? You can be the net.

replies.text: Good! Hold still. You're very good at it.
That's why you're the net. Tall nets are the best.
All right. I'll keep your place.

lines.text: Which is better, climbing or falling?

replies.text: Boring answer. But the right one. Grown-ups agree.
YES! Me too! But don't tell Mother.
...You get it. You really get it.

lines: My row is {row}! It's near the top, by the frame, where the new rows are. I can touch it if I stretch.
Every Weft has a row. Mine is {row}. My mother says nothing much happened that year except me.
*click* I counted down from my row to the first black one once. I lost count twice.
Do you have a row? Outsiders don't. *click* Maybe you'll get one if you're very careful.
My row is mostly orange, with a green stripe near the bottom. Mother says the stripe is where the grubs got into the dye. I think it's a lava river.
There's a teal thread tied at the frame for me. One. It's very short. But it goes all the way up.
I have a row-twin! Somebody born the same row. We're not allowed to fight, because it would knot the same place. We fight anyway, very carefully.
If you stand under my row and look up, there's a loose end. Mother says it's where my first word is. I don't think so. I think it's just loose.
The row after mine is thin. Mother says nothing happened but waiting. I was too little to notice.
When I'm old I'll hang near the bottom, where the grub-silk goes soft. I'd like to be soft someday. It sounds comfortable.
The Clothkeeper let me see my row from behind. The back is where all the knots are, and the front is where all the looks are. I like the back better.
Every Tying I check that my row is still there. It always is. I do it anyway. Mother says that's what rows are for.
Somebody tied my first thread into my row, the one I spun wrong. It's very crooked. It's the only part of me up there on its own.
I think your row would be in the margin, where the loose ends are. But loose ends are where new threads go in. So that's good.
My grandmother's row is almost at the bottom. She says she's older than the ladder. She isn't. The ladder is very old.
The Cloth smells different at the top and the bottom. Top is dye and grubs. Bottom is dust and old thread. Mine smells like the top. I like that.
We have a game where you pick a row and say its colour. Mine's always wrong. I say teal, it's orange. I say orange, it's teal. I think rows are tricksy.
I got in trouble for pulling a thread in my own row. Just one! It came out in my hand! Mother says never unpick, only add. So I'm adding. See my little knot.

lines.text: I'm not supposed to tell you which row is mine. But you can guess. It's the pretty one.
I asked the Clothkeeper if I could weave a thread for your row. She said not yet. But she said maybe. Maybe from a Clothkeeper is almost a yes.
I wove you a little thread. It's as long as my hand. It's crooked because my lower arms haven't woken. It's in my pocket. I'll give it to the Clothkeeper when they do.
Which row would you choose to be born in, if you could?

replies.text: Yes! Orange rows are the best. Hot ones. Everybody laughs a lot.
Quiet rows are good. You get to see things.

replies.ask: The one I was born in.
replies.text: ...*click* That's what Mother says too.

lines.text: Do you think you have a row somewhere?

replies.text: Maybe means yes if you hold it long enough.
That's all right. I'll lend you part of mine. A short part.
I'll ask the Clothkeeper for you. I'll ask nicely, with all my arms. Both of them.

topics.ask: What aren't you allowed to do?
lines: Don't touch a warped stem with anything sharp. Don't climb the Long Cloth. Don't drop shuttles. I'm good at two of those.
We're not allowed to stare at the black rows. *whispers* I did once. It felt like they stared back.
Not allowed past the lookout nets. That's where the netcasters hang the air nets. They won't say what for.
