No going down to the floor alone. The tall walkers are down there. They don't hurt you if you don't look at them.
I'm not allowed to ride the silkgrubs. I do anyway. They don't mind, but they walk so slowly I'm late, and then I get caught. It's not worth it. It's a bit worth it.
I'm not allowed to unpick anything. Not even my own mistakes. You have to add a bit over the top. My shawl has seventeen bits over the top.
I can't go in the dye house when the vats are warm. Mother says I'd come out the wrong colour. I said I like orange. She said I'd come out more than orange.
I'm not allowed to click at the Clothkeeper. It isn't rude, exactly. It's just that she clicks back, and then I have to stay and talk for ages.
I'm not allowed to say what's in a row before it's tied off. Nobody told me what's in mine. I think it's me. I'm not going to tell.
No pulling the weeping vines. They're the forest's loose threads, and you leave them alone. I pulled one once. Just a bit. It pulled back.
No going to the edge of the forest. That's where the Piglins' torches come from. Mother says if you hear a chink, go inside. I've gone inside a lot.
I'm not allowed to take a shroomlight to my net. They hum. It keeps everyone up. Mine hums like a lullaby. Mother says that's worse.
I'm not allowed to mix dyes. I mixed teal and orange once and got a brown. A very ordinary brown. The dyer laughed for ages and told me never to do it again.
I'm not allowed to ask grown-ups about the black rows. I'm not allowed to not ask either. So I ask quietly, and they answer quietly, and nobody tells Mother.
We're not allowed to name grubs after grown-ups. It's disrespectful. We named one after the Clothkeeper anyway. She found out. She wasn't cross. She said it had good mandibles.

lines.text: I'm not allowed to talk to outsiders. But you're asking, so I'm only answering. That's different.
I went past the lookout nets once. There was a net hung in the open air with nothing in it. It was so quiet. I came back. Don't tell the netcasters.
I'm still not allowed to go to the floor with you. Mother said maybe when I have four arms. That's a long maybe.
Mother said I can go to the lookout with you now, as long as you hold the rope. I said you'd hold it with both hands. She said, that's all you've got. I said, exactly.
I'm not allowed to say you're my favourite outsider. So I'm saying you're my favourite person who isn't a Weft. That's allowed. I checked.
Do outsiders have rules? Do you break them?

replies.text: Same! I knew it. A very little, I hope.
Never ever? Not even a bit? ...You must be very bored.
*click* Which are the silly ones? Don't tell Mother.

lines.text: If you were my grown-up, would you let me go down to the floor?

replies.text: Ugh. You sound exactly like her.
Really?! ...Oh. You'd hold my hand the whole time. ...That's allowed.
Everyone says that. Older is always later.

lines: Each year the keepers sit at the Great Loom and ask one thing: what happened that a child should know? The row is the answer, tied off in the order it came.
A row has three parts. The dyers give it colours, the weavers give it a pattern, and I give it knots. A knot is a thing that happened.
A bead is a thing that hurt. A loop is a thing not finished. I keep a drawer of each, and the drawer of loops is always the fullest.
Most years there is little to knot. A quiet row is a good row. Do not pity us. Quiet rows are why the Cloth is long.
We never weave what we wish had happened. If the wart failed, the row is thin. A thin true row is better than a thick false one, which pulls the whole Cloth crooked.
Births go in as one teal thread tied at the frame. Deaths go in as one dark thread tied at the bottom edge. A row is a small life, top to bottom.
When two keepers disagree we weave both versions and wait. In the end the Cloth holds the better-woven one. It has never once held both.

lines.text: *click* I do not tell strangers what is in the row before it is tied off. A row talked about early grows crooked from the talking.

lines: I argued for a whole year against tying in a lost shuttle. I lost. It sits in Row Twelve-Seventy, a very small knot. I find it every time I pass.
The grand things choose themselves. A war needs no keeper to be remembered. It is the small things that need us: a hem, a joke, a name said kindly.
Every row has the same count of warp threads. Same bones, different year. Only what we do with them changes. That is the whole art, and the whole trouble.
*click* A Weft who dies in a hard year is tied in harder than one who dies in a soft year. It is not fair. It is only accurate.
The newest row is the hardest to weave, because we do not yet know what it meant. So I weave it plain and add the meaning later, as knots.

lines.text: You are in the margin of this year's row, a thread the length of a finger. I have not yet decided whether to bring you in from the edge.
The keepers argued three sittings over an outsider last year. Bead or knot? We settled on a bead. He asked what that meant and we said, something warm. He was pleased.
Come to the tying-off. Watch from the third rung and do not speak. It is the only time a keeper's hands shake, and I would rather a friend saw it than a stranger.
When a row is tied off I touch your thread before any other. I have done it every year. I have not told the other keepers, and I do not think they have noticed.
Two neighbours quarrelled over a spool this year. Does it go in the row?

replies.text: *click* The Cloth does not choose between kind and true. It records. You would be a fair keeper, and a hard one.
Kind. But then who remembers who was right? Someone always needs to know.
*click click* Small. Yes. A knot you must look for to find. That is exactly how we do it.

lines.text: If this row were yours for one year, what would you tie in?

replies.text: *every eye warms* A long knot, then. One that will be worn smooth by many fingers.
*click* Everyone wants that first. It is why keepers are chosen from those who do not.

topics.ask: How do you read the Cloth?
lines: I read with my fingertips. Eyes lie about colour, but a thread remembers how it was spun, and the spinner's hand is still in it.
Every year has a feel. Thirteen-Twelve is fine and even. Twelve-Seventy is bumpy, because the spinners were angry that year. I can feel the anger.
Start at the top and walk down with a lower hand on the Cloth and an upper hand on the rope. Never let go with the upper. The Cloth is long and the floor is longer.
A beginner reads one row at a time. A keeper reads ten at once, the way you hear a whole song and not only the one note.
Dry hands, cool hands. Wet hands smear the dye and warm hands loosen the knots. A keeper who sweats is a keeper who retires.
A child can read the top rows. A weaver can read the middle rows. Only a keeper reads the bottom, where the threads are soft as ash and a heavy breath could undo a year.
The oldest rows have no colour left, only texture. I read them on the lower deck by the feel of the knots. There are wars down there I know only by their weight.

lines.text: *click* Do not touch the Cloth. Not one finger. Your hand carries the smell of other places, and the Cloth is old enough to notice.

lines: Sometimes I read a row and find a knot I did not tie and no keeper remembers tying. I leave it. Someone cared about that moment. It is not my place to ask who.
When two keepers read the same row aloud and say different things, the young ones call it an error. The old ones call it the Cloth being generous.
I read Row {row} again every year, the row I was born in. Every time I find a knot I had not noticed before.
Reading is mostly forgetting. A keeper lets the rows slide by like smoke and holds only what snags. What snags is the true thing.
A young keeper once read a row with her eyes shut and wept, and could not say why. We never found out. We moved her to the upper rows for a year.

lines.text: Hold out your hand. No, not to touch. I am only looking at your fingertips. Hm. Soft. You would read the top rows well, and nothing else.
I might let you hold the loose end of the newest row for the length of one breath. Only an end, and only if you ask me slowly.
Close your eyes when you touch your own thread. You will not find the colour. You will find how I felt when I tied it, in the tightness of the knot.
I read your thread last. Always. A close-woven thread hums a little, if you hold your breath. Yours hums. I thought you should know.
*click* Close your eyes and put a hand toward the Cloth. Can you feel anything?

replies.text: *click click* That is the forest rising through the deck. Everyone feels that. It is a start.
Honest. Most feel nothing. The ones who say they feel a great deal are usually wrong.
*all six eyes widen* Hm. Tell no one. Come back when you can say it slowly.

lines.text: Which would you rather read, the newest rows or the oldest?

replies.text: Ah. Still warm. Most start there and stay too long.
Brave. They crumble if you are clumsy. But you would learn what the Cloth is made of.

lines: A tear is the worst thing that can happen to a keeper, except two tears. I mend in the same colours, with thread spun from the same vine, and I never hide the stitch.
We do not hide mends. A mend is a row of its own: the year the Cloth was hurt, and the year someone cared enough to fix it.
Heat is the slow enemy. The Great Loom stands far from the dye vats for that reason. Fire would be the quick one. We do not say that word near the frame.
Weight is the other enemy. The old rows hang heavy and drag on the new. Every year I loosen the top ties a finger's width so the Cloth can breathe.
Small tears I mend in place, one stitch at a time, with a needle from my belt. Large tears I never touch alone. Eight hands, two minds, and each watching the other's knots.
When a whole row is lost, a runner carries a spool of our thread to another Loom to match it against their copy. She comes back smelling of another forest.
The copies never match perfectly. When I mend from another Loom's row I am mending in their handwriting. I try to sound like us. I never quite do.
Once a silkgrub got into the lower rows and ate a hem, and left behind the finest silk I have ever seen. We mended the hem. We kept the silk. Nobody has said who forgave whom.

lines.text: *click* Why do you ask? Do you mean to cut something? The Cloth is the last thing anyone cuts. Before it, the nets come down. Remember that.

lines: Dust is a kind of tear too, a very slow one. The children sweep the lower deck with root brooms, and every year some rows are a little thinner, and we say nothing.
Every keeper learns the mending knot, the one that cannot be seen from the front. The first one I tied took a whole year. Now I tie it without looking.
A keeper never mends alone a row they wove themselves. You will fix your own mistakes badly, out of love. Better a stranger's eyes.
A mend that holds is a quiet thing. You could walk past a hundred and not see one. That is how I know I have done my work.

lines.text: I let apprentices mend the lower rows first. Ruin a bottom row and it is a lesson. Ruin a top row and it is a sorrow. I would not ask you to try either.
The black rows are mended most often, and most gently. The black threads were never strong, and they do not forgive being pulled.
If ever the Cloth tore badly, I would ask you to hold a corner. You are not Weft, so you would not be afraid of it. A calm hand holds a corner best.
There is a mend in the lower rows that I made for you, a single stitch in your colour. If I am gone before you return, look for it. It is crooked, and meant.
*click* If you tore a thread by accident, what would you do?

replies.text: *click click* Then it is a mend and not a tear. Come here, quickly, and hold the end.
*six eyes narrow* I would know. The Cloth tells me. You would have lost more than a thread.
Good. We would do it together. Slowly. That is also how it is done.

lines.text: A tear in the oldest row. Do you mend it new, or leave it a hole?

replies.text: Many say so. But a new thread in an old row speaks with a new voice. Hm.
Some keepers agree. A hole is also a record. I could never bear to look at it.

topics.ask: Who will keep the Cloth next?
lines: A keeper chooses no one. The Cloth chooses, and the keepers only notice. I watch the children on the lower deck. The one who walks softly and looks long is the one.
I have had three apprentices. One left to weave. One left to the nets. One is still with me, has outgrown me, and does not say so. I do not mind.
A keeper's first lesson is to sit still. The second is to sit stiller. By the third most of them have gone off to weave, and I do not blame them.
The oath is short. I will not weave a lie. I will not cut a thread. I will not hurry a row. Three promises, and I have broken the third twice.
I was born before the black rows. When I go, the last who saw the Cloth all teal and orange goes with me. So I teach the young to read the early rows by feel.
When a keeper dies we do not tie the dark thread at once. We wait a full row so the Cloth can be sure. Then we tie it long, and the keepers say their names in turn.
A good keeper is forgettable. Nobody speaks of the keeper in a row. They speak of the row. If you remember my face when I am gone, I have failed a little.

lines.text: *click* The succession of the keepers is not for strangers. Ask me again when I have counted you.

lines: The young keepers worry about everything. Will the Cloth tear, will the dyers forget, will the Wither come again? I tell them the Cloth was here before the worry and will be after it.
I am sometimes asked if I fear dying before the row is finished. A little. A thread I have not tied off is the only thing that makes me click in my sleep.
My apprentice pretends not to be impatient. She counts rungs aloud while I speak. I pretend not to hear. This is a keeper's courtesy.
The best apprentice I ever had was a child who asked why the Cloth was so quiet. I said it was listening. She said, to what? I have not answered her since.
The Cloth has never lacked a keeper. Not once, in all the rows. When one falls away, another walks softly to the frame. It is a comfort and a puzzle.

lines.text: Between us, I hope the next keeper is not clever. Clever keepers fix what is not broken. I want one who is patient, and a little afraid, and not ashamed to be.
If I could choose, I would choose someone from outside the Loom. A keeper who has seen another forest knows what ours is worth. Do not repeat that to the others.
Some of the others asked if you might learn to read the Cloth. Not to keep it. Only to read. I told them to wait for you to ask. They said that was not an answer. It was.
When I am gone I would like my dark thread tied near your teal one. A small honour, and an odd one. I have asked the others. They said yes. They were not surprised.
*click* If the Cloth were offered to you, would you take it?

replies.text: *click click* The right answer is almost always no. It is also why you would be chosen.
Gladly. *click* Gladly is how fires start. Think again, slowly.
Taught slowly, taken slowly. Yes. That is how the Cloth is taken.

lines.text: Tell me honestly. When the Cloth is a thousand rows long, will the young still care?

replies.text: Some. *click* That is all a Cloth ever needed. Some.
Hope is a thread too. A thin one. It holds more than it should.

lines: I keep three looms: a frame for shawls, a deck loom for hut walls, and the Great Loom, which belongs to the Clothkeepers. The shawl loom is mine. It has never once lied to me.
Every warp thread ends in a loom weight. Mostly old bone, some stone. I can tell which by how they swing. The bone ones swing with a small sigh.
The shuttle is carved from a stem that died standing and polished with silkgrub oil. A good one learns your thumb. Mine has a groove where I grip and a nick where it met the net.
The beater packs each row tight. Too soft and the cloth gapes, too hard and it puckers. The right blow is the one you do not notice making.
I work the heddle with a toe on its cord, so all four hands stay free. Weft toes are long and clever. Outsider feet are only for standing on.
Eleven threads over, nine under, a toe, a click. After thirty thousand passes the count is no longer in the head. It is in the shoulders.
Six eyes, and the work needs two. The hot pair follow the shuttle, the low pair watch the edge of the cloth, and the last pair watch whoever is standing behind me.
I once wove a whole hut wall with one skipped thread. The family inside named it the lucky wall and forbade me to mend it. It has stood nine rows, which proves nothing and annoys me.
I never undo a row in anger. I lay the shuttle down, climb to the top of a stalk, and click at the forest until the row looks better than it did. It always does.

lines.text: *click* Do not touch the warp. It is under tension, and so am I. Look from where you stand, outsider. A loom shows nothing to hands that cannot name its parts.
Pinch this warp thread, gently, between two fingers. Feel it hum? That is a good tension. Slack, you would feel nothing. Too tight, you would feel a hurt.

lines: A weaver is paid in cloth, and the cloth goes to whoever needs it. I have never owned a shawl I wove. I wear the ones other weavers made for me. That is the whole trade.

lines.text: I wove a belt for you and have not given it. The edge is not straight enough. This is my fourth. I will hand it over when it is right, and I will not hear arguments.
Sit at the frame with me for one row. Hold the top beam. I will show you where a weaver rests: the half-breath between the beat and the pass. There is a small quiet there. I live in it.
One corner of the shawl on my loom I have left unwoven. I thought you might put a thread there. A crooked one, mine to pass and no one else's. Do not make it straight.
Tension is everything. Do you know what happens to a thread pulled too tight?

replies.text: *click* Eventually. First it sings. Learn to hear the song before the snap.
Stretches, and forgets how to come back. A tired thread is worse than a broken one, for nobody notices it.
*click* Then you will never make anything that lasts. How restful for you.

lines.text: Which is harder, a plain cloth or a patterned one?

replies.text: Patterned is harder to do. Plain is harder to bear. Ten thousand passes with no pattern to hide in.
*click click* A true answer. Plain cloth shows every fault. A good weaver does not wish to hide.

lines: When a cloth comes off the loom it smells of warm vine and a little smoke. I breathe it before anyone else does. That is a weaver's only vanity. Do not tell the others.
On the last row of every cloth I leave one thread loose, on purpose. It is my mark. Any weaver in {village} could pick my work from a thousand by that one thread.
A pattern is a sentence. Stripes are rows, a zigzag is a bridge, a diamond is a cap seen from below. A whole shawl says: I walked here, I climbed there, I came home.
Every household has a border. Mine is a step pattern, five up and five down. Someone on the next cap over could read it across the gap and know whose hut hung there.
Teal for the wart, orange for the shroomlight, and a thin line of undyed vine between them, so neither colour thinks it owns the cloth.
A mourning border is uneven stripes: thick, thin, thick. It means a thread was cut and the cloth went on. It is the first pattern a child learns to know at a glance.
A wedding cloth has no pattern for the first hand's width. Two families weave it, a thread each, and it stays plain until they agree where the pattern starts. Some wait a whole row.
Never weave a spiral. A spiral has no edge, and a Weft is nothing without an edge. We say a spiral cloth eats its wearer. Children dare each other to scratch one on the deck.
The oldest pattern is plain over-under, with no mark at all. Newborns are wrapped in it. The first cloth a Weft wears is the first one a weaver learns.
Kilts take stripes that run down, so the wearer looks tall on a bridge. Shawls take stripes that run across, so the wearer looks steady. It is a trade secret, and I have just told it.

lines.text: I do not explain my hems to strangers. Admire the colour, outsider. Colour is public. The pattern is a sentence, and it was not written to you.
That mantle on the rail has a long-walk pattern. See the repeating chevron? To the wearer it says, you are almost there. To everyone else it says, leave this one be.
I once wove the sound of the dye vats: a slow bubbling in orange over teal. It was ugly. Everyone wanted one. I have never understood it, and I wove forty.
I wove a small border for you. Three steps up and one step back, which is how I think of you: always climbing, never hurried, sometimes going back for something. You have not seen it.
A pattern with a mistake in it is a better pattern. I weave one wrong thread into every shawl, so no one wearing it is ever asked to be perfect. I put one in the belt I am making you.
Every weaver in {village} drew a pattern for you, a thread each, and it is not finished because you are not finished. When it is ready it goes on the Cloth's border. We weave it slowly.
Is a cloth with no pattern at all worth wearing?

replies.text: Honest, and warm. I wore a plain one for a whole row and was happy.
Dull to the eye. The hand never finds it so.
*click click* Everything does. Over and under, again.

lines.text: If you wove a shawl for a stranger, what would you put on it?

replies.text: A welcome. *click* The most generous mark there is.
Plain. *click* A weaver's answer. Few outsiders reach it.

lines: A pattern woven backward is a message only its weaver can read. Mine say rude things about my neighbours. Weavers read each other's backward patterns and pretend not to.
Dyers say the colour is what the eye remembers. Weavers say it is the pattern. Neither is right, and each of us goes on being right.
A good pattern repeats seven times and then breaks, and then begins again. The break rests the eye. Seven is the most a Weft can hold in mind before the mind wanders to the next thing.

topics.ask: How did you learn to weave?
lines: My lower arms woke when I was eleven rows old. After the Opening my aunt put a shuttle in the left one and said, over. Under. For a whole row that was all she said.
The first lesson is the edge. Weave a hand's width of plain cloth with a perfect edge, and nothing else, until the edge is straight. Mine took until the next row.
My first shawl was so crooked it was used to cover a bridge. I am told it was warm. I am told it is still down there, under the nets. I do not go to look.
A master weaver does not praise. She unpicks. When my aunt said nothing and left the row alone, that was praise, and I learned to read it as one.
Her name was Orsa, born in the last of the black rows, and she could weave with her eyes shut. She never said how. She was never wrong about the cloth.
A rival is good for a weaver. Mine is Veska, three decks over. Her cloth is finer and her hems are worse, and we have each been telling people so for thirty rows.
Apprentices begin on the deck loom with coarse thread, because coarse thread forgives. Fine thread forgives nothing. You do not pass by getting better. You pass by getting less afraid.
The test is a hem. You weave one, and every weaver in {village} runs a thumb along it. If no thumb stops, you are a weaver. If one stops, you go back to the edge.

lines.text: Learning is not for strangers to watch. A half-learned thing is like a half-dyed one: ugly, and the owner knows. Come back when you are asking about the finished cloth.
I still make mistakes. The difference is that now I see them while they are on the loom and not after they are on a hut. That is all a lifetime buys: a shorter distance to your own mistake.
Children come to watch me sometimes and I let them thread the heddle. They are slow and they drop things in the net. I gave the net a name, so it feels part of the work.
I nearly stopped, at twenty rows. My hands cramped and I thought, this costs more than it pays. Orsa took my wrist and rubbed it for a long while, and never mentioned it again.
When I am old I will teach the edge to someone. I have already chosen the child. She does not know. Her edges are terrible and her patience is the best I have seen.
I would like you to have the first thing I wove, the crooked one under the nets. I will climb down and bring it up myself. You will say it is lovely. I will say that is a lie, and be glad.
Everyone wanted to be something else once. A netcaster, a keeper of the Cloth. What would you have wished to be?

replies.text: Ha. *click click* All Weft climb. Choose a harder one.
Then take the shuttle. Over. Under. And the rest of you, be patient.
Honest. Most of us did not know until our hands knew. Hands are quicker than we are.

lines.text: Be honest. If I handed you this shuttle, how long would you take to weave a hand's width?

replies.text: Correct. And you said it without pride. That is half the lesson.
Less than a year. Hm. Bold. We shall see, with the edge in your hand.

lines: There is no school. There is a deck, a loom, and someone who has done it longer than you. Stay near enough to hear the shuttle and you learn the rhythm. Rhythm cannot be said, only caught.
A weaver who stops learning stops weaving. The cloth knows. It goes a little crooked, a little flat, and you tell yourself it is the thread.
Whenever I finish a cloth I say a small word to the shuttle. It is a very old word. I do not know what it means. Orsa said it, and her aunt before her.
Thread is twisted fibre, and the twist wants room. So I hold the vine at the start of the walk and go backward, drawing it out while the spindle turns. Walk forward and you only tangle yourself.
The spinning walk is a hundred and ten paces end to end. I know every plank. I count down from a hundred and ten with my heels, never my eyes.
The spindle hangs from a lower hand and spins on its own weight. The upper hands draw the fibre. When my arms are right the spindle hums. When they are wrong it wobbles.
The twist must be even. Too loose, and the thread has no heart. Too tight, and it kinks and fights. I give twisting vine the half-turn it was already thinking of.
I have never fallen, but I once stepped on a silkgrub in the middle of the walk. The less said about that, the better. The grub agrees.
Draughts are the enemy. A breath off the lava seas pulls the thread sideways and the spindle swings. On windy rows I spin short and tie more joins.
Spinners hum while they walk. Not songs: one low note, held, so the others know where I am on the walk and do not step into my thread. It keeps the twist even, too.
A snapped thread makes a small sound, almost a click. Every spinner in {village} lifts their head at once, and then bends again, kindly, pretending not to have heard.

lines.text: Do not cross the spinning walk. Thread is hanging at the height of your throat. Go round by the lower bridge, outsider, and take your two arms with you.
Try it. Just five paces, backward, spindle in one hand. Do not look at your feet. ...You are looking at your feet. Everyone does. Five paces of unlearning is all I ask.
I have walked this walk so often I have worn a groove in the plank where my heel lands. The tenders wanted to replace it. I asked them not to. It is my road.
When I am tired I hum more slowly. The others hear it and bring me a warmed wrap and take the next stretch. Nobody says anything. That is how you know it is love.
Walk with me, backward, once, holding my upper hand. I will tell you when the spindle turns to your side. It is the nearest thing I have to a secret, and it is only a feeling.
I spun a thread for you that I have not joined to any cloth. One finger long. It has the best twist I have ever made. I carry it on my belt, and when I am nervous I roll it.
Backward, over a drop, with a spindle in hand. Which do you think is harder, the walking or the not looking?

replies.text: Walking is feet, and feet learn quickly. Try again.
*click click* Yes. The eyes want to help and cannot. Teach them to wait.

lines.text: Do you hum when you work?

replies.text: Good. Then you are never lost on a bridge.
A hum with its mouth open. *click* Close it, and you may spin.
Then how does anyone know where you are? Hm. Learn one note.

lines: The walk has one rule: whoever is nearest the end calls the turn. We turn together, every spinner in {village}, without looking, a long line of backs swinging like one hinge. It is my favourite sight.
Twisting vine fights back. It wants to climb, so every strand has a lean. A spinner learns to feel which way each one leans and spin against it a little. Then it stops fighting.
At the end of the walk I wind the thread on a spool and tie it off with a tail. A thread with no tail belongs to no one, and a spool with no owner gets lost in the net.
Twisting vine for strength, silkgrub tufts for softness, a little weeping vine for the drop. Three fibres in one thread, each wanting to be the loudest. The art is making them take turns.
I judge thread by hanging a weight from it and humming. A good one hums back. A poor one stays silent and snaps a breath later, and I always hear it coming.
There are five weights of thread: hair, string, cord, rope and bridge-rope. I spin the first three alone. The last two are group work, with six pairs of hands and a good deal of singing.
The grade of thread decides the grade of cloth. Fine for shawls and headwraps, cord for kilts, bridge-rope for anything that might drop a child. I never cheat on bridge-rope.
A grub fed on warped roots gives long, bright silk. A grub left to its own tastes gives short, sticky silk, and sulks. I have favourites. They know, and they behave accordingly.
Never spin from a fresh vine. Hang it from the rail until it creaks when bent. That is how you know it has finished thinking about being a plant.
The thread I am proudest of was so fine I lost it on the walk. The draught took it. It is out there still, I tell myself, holding something up.
A tangle is not an accident. It is a thread that was spun in a hurry, coming back to explain itself. Sit and unpick it, and it will tell you what you did.

lines.text: I do not sell my thread to strangers, nor show it. Thread is the beginning of everything, and I like to know where it ends. Ask again when I know where you are going.
Rub this between finger and thumb. Smooth? Now this one: rough, and a little warm. The warm one came from a grub I raised. I would know it blind. Thread is a signature.
The best spinner I knew spun with her eyes shut. Everyone said it was for show. Then one row she spun a thread that carried a whole bridge, and no one said it again.
I have a rival spinner at the next Loom over. Her thread is whiter. Mine is stronger. We swap spools twice a row by runner, and her notes always say the same thing: yours will hold.
Take this hair-thread. It is yours. Tie it round a finger when you are far from here. It is only vine, but I spun it with you in mind, and if you pull it hard it will not break.
I am spinning a thread the length of your whole journey. I do not know how long that is, so I keep spinning. When you are done travelling, bring me the end, and I will tie it off.
Which thread would you trust to hold you over a drop?

replies.text: Thick is not strong. Thick is only thick.
*click click* Yes. Even and honest. Not pretty, not thick, but true.
A rope is many threads that agreed to share the weight. That is the lesson of the whole Loom.

lines.text: Which matters more to a thread, the grub or the vine?

replies.text: Silk is soft and loved. Vine is the bone. Do not forget the bone.
The vine, yes. But a thread of vine alone is a rope with no manners.

lines: A good spinner never lets thread touch the planks of the walk. Planks have splinters, and splinters fray. We hold it up and out, and the lower hands never let go.
Twisting vines grow upward, weeping vines hang down. A thread with both in it knows which way is home. That is why bridge-rope is always a mix: it never forgets where the bridge is.
Spinners are bad at conversation. We only learn to talk when we are walking away, and by then you cannot hear us. This is why we are thought rude. It is only geometry.

topics.ask: How do you read a stalk?
lines: I knock three times with a knuckle, low, middle and high. A sound stalk answers in three notes, each a little warmer than the last. A weak one answers in two and sounds embarrassed.
Put your ear to it, if you must. There is a sound under the sound: the slow pull of the roots drinking from the nylium, like something very large asleep. That is the forest's pulse.
Teal bark is a good sign, indigo a better one. Yellow-grey at the foot means the roots sit too wet. Grey flecks near the cap are wart-mites. We do not kill them. We brush them back onto the wart.
I smell the sap. Sweet is well. Sour is thirsty. Smoky means something burned lately, and I want to know who. I follow the smoke upward until I find the fire, or the one who made it.
The cap grows a shade brighter on the side the shroomlights are nearest. A tender reads a cap like a face: this side warm, that side shy. I give the shy side more bone meal.
The wart on top of a cap should be thick enough to lie down in. When it thins, I sit on the cap and think. A tender who hurries a thin cap is a tender who will see it bald.
I have a name for every stalk in {village}. The tall one is Patience. The crooked one is Grandmother. The one that hums is Hum. They have not told me their own names. I think they are shy.
I climb with all four hands: the upper pair hauls, the lower pair grips and feels the bark for hollows. A tender who climbs with the upper pair alone is a tender who is going to meet the net.

lines.text: Keep your hands off the stalks, outsider. They are older than your whole village, and a hand carries what it has touched. Stand under the cap and look up. That is plenty.
Lay your palm flat on this stalk. Not on the bark, just above it. Feel the warmth coming off? That is a healthy stalk breathing. You have been standing beside one the whole time.
In the quiet I sometimes hear a stalk shift its weight. A small groan, a long way down. It is not a fault. It is a very big thing getting comfortable.
I kept a cloth with the sap of the youngest stalk on it. When I am low I smell it. It smells of the first thing you do not know yet. You may have the cloth, if you are ever low.
I would take you up Patience, the tallest stalk. From the top you see the whole forest, every cap in a sea. I take only those who listen. You listen. Mind your feet.
A stalk in the grove has your name now. Not mine to give, but I asked it. It is a small one, and it hums. When you are away I climb it and tell it how I think you are.
If a stalk went silent when you knocked, what would you do?

replies.text: *click* Louder is rude. A silent stalk is not deaf. It is thinking, or hurt.
Yes. At once. Two tenders, a sack of bone meal, and no panic.
Leave a stalk silent and a whole cap can come down. Go back.

lines.text: Do you think a stalk can be lonely?

replies.text: *click click* So do I. I tell them the news. They like the bridge gossip best.
So say the people who never climbed one.

lines: The forest talks at the height of the caps, where the wart is thickest. At the floor it is quiet, and in the canopy it never is. Stand still and you will hear a hundred small things.
Silkgrubs follow me up the stalks. They think I am a stalk with opinions. I let them think it.
I have lost no stalk in all my rows as a tender. I say it quietly, because the forest hears, and the forest does not like boasting.

topics.ask: How do you grow a new cap?
lines: You begin with a seed of fungus pressed into nylium, and then you wait. The first row, nothing shows. The second, a thumb. The sixth, a stem as thick as an arm. A cap is a gift to the unborn.
Bone meal is the only thing I give. A handful at the root, at the turn of every row, sung over. The song is nothing special. It is the singing that matters, I think.
Warped fungus will not grow where the nylium is cold or sour. I smell the ground, and taste it with one fingertip if I must. Sour tastes like a lie told by a friend.
A seed must be set where the shroomlight reaches it. Too far, and the stalk climbs toward the glow and grows thin. Too near, and it grows fat and soft and falls in the first hard draught.
A stem grows in rings, one for each good row. I cut none, but when a stalk fell of itself I counted. The oldest I have seen had four hundred and eleven rings. It had stood through the black rows.
Caps grow slowly at first and quickly at the end, as if the stalk has made up its mind. One turn you look up and there is a deck's worth of wart above you. We call it the Decision.
A new cap is not built on at once. I wait until it can bear a child, then an adult, then a hut. Impatient builders have lost a whole house to a cap that was still thinking.
We plant in threes: one for the Loom, one for the forest, one for luck. The one for luck always grows best, which says something about luck.

lines.text: Do not stamp near the young ones, outsider. A seed has no voice yet, and I speak for it. If you must walk here, walk where I have walked.
Kneel here. This is a seed I set a few rows ago. See the green bump? That is a stalk that will outlast your grandmother's grandmother. You are the first outsider to see it. Do not tell anyone where.
Sometimes a seed does nothing for three rows and then goes up like a shout. I never take it as a rebuke. I take it as an example.
I once grew a cap in the wrong place, by mistake. It was crooked and could bear nothing, so the children swing from it. It is the best-loved cap in {village}, and I never admitted it was an accident.
When a child is born I plant a seed in a quiet place and say nothing. When the child can climb, I show them. They never forgive me for making them wait, and they are always thrilled.
There is a seed in the ground for you. I set it while you were away. It will not be ready for a long while. I think you will come back for it. If not, someone will sing to it for you.
A seed or a young stalk: which would you rather plant?

replies.text: Brave. A seed has to learn everything. A young stalk only has to remember.
Practical. It lives faster. You will see the result before you are old.
*click* Careful. Convenience is how a forest goes crooked.

lines.text: A tender plants things they will never see grown. Does that sound sad to you?

replies.text: It is a little sad, and a little the point.
*click click* The best word. Say it to every child.

lines: A grown cap needs no help. A young one needs everything. I spend most of my rows with the young ones, and the old ones forgive me for it.
Tenders keep no records of what they grow. The stalk is the record. If you want to know what I did with my life, climb Patience.
Bone meal is the one thing we cannot grow. We get it from bones that others have finished with. Do not ask me whose.
A stalk dies standing, slowly, over a few rows. The wart thins first, then the cap greys, then the stalk gives one long creak that I have heard three times in my life. I sat with each one.
We do not cut the dead ones either. A dead stalk stands until it falls of its own accord, which may be a long while. Its planks, when it does, are the best planks, cured by their own patience.
When one starts to go I mark it with a knotted cord and the whole Loom is told. The weavers weave a grey shawl and the children are taught its name. Then we wait with it.
They say a dying stalk smells of old rain. I have not smelled rain. I think they mean cool stone. It is not unpleasant. It smells like the end of a long task.
There is a stalk on the far side of {village} that has been dying for thirty rows. It will not die. I climb it every few rows and ask what it is waiting for.
When a stalk falls, the caps nearby sway for a breath as if bowing. The bridges give. The nets catch what they must. Then we gather the pieces and make something of them.
A fallen stalk is honoured with a new seed in the same hole, with a little of its own bark ground into the bone meal. The new one grows faster. It remembers.
I have been asked if it hurts. I do not know. It does not sound as if it hurts. It sounds like someone putting down something heavy.

lines.text: A dead stalk is nothing for strangers to take. Do not pick at the bark, or ask for a plank. Planks are given. They are never asked for.
Some stalks die from the inside, and nothing shows. This is the tender's nightmare. I knock, I smell, I climb. Miss one, and a cap comes down. Four times in my life I caught it in time.
I keep a pinch of dried bark from each stalk I have seen die. It crumbles if you press it, and each smells of that stalk and no other. I could name them all with my eyes shut.
The worst row of my life was the row three stalks died together. I did nothing wrong, and I have gone over it a thousand times. The Clothkeeper tied it in plainly. She said it was not mine.
When I die I would like to be carried to a dying stalk and laid at its foot, and left. It would be a fair exchange. I am told the Clothkeepers have written it down.
If a stalk should die while you are here, come and stand with me. Say nothing. It is not for talking. But I would like someone there who does not click.
Suppose one stalk were dying, and cutting it would save the others. Would you cut?

replies.text: *click click* Then you know us. We would let two die before we cut one.
*a long silence* No Weft would say it. Perhaps that is why we need strangers to ask.
Ask. Then wait for the answer. That is all we have ever done.

lines.text: Do you think anything is left of a stalk when it falls?

replies.text: The planks, yes. And its shade, in the way the others lean.
*click* A tender's answer. I knew you listened.

lines: The dyers use scrapings from the bark of a fallen stalk to fix a colour. They are not sentimental about it. I forgive them. Every craft has its practical side.
Children ask where the dead stalks go. I tell them: into the walls, the planks, the hut doors. You have been sleeping beside the dead since you were born, and they are good company.
A cap that has lost its stalk is a strange thing. It sits on the floor like a dropped hat for a while, until the silkgrubs find it. They treat it with great respect, and then they eat it.
Warped wart, crushed fine and steeped. It gives a thin green first. Add a pinch of nylium dust and the green deepens toward teal. The pinch is the secret. I will not say how big a pinch.
The vats are stone cauldrons, eight in a row and a ninth apart. Each has a name. My favourite is the last of the eight, called Sorrow, because everything that goes in comes out looking sad.
Orange comes from shroomlight boiled slowly until it gives up its glow. The glow comes out into the water and for a moment the vat is a small sun. Then it cools and holds the colour.
The mordant is the trouble. Without it a colour washes out the first time it is washed. With it a shawl holds for twenty rows. Ours is a secret between the dyers and the cauldrons.
Timing is everything. Leave the cloth in a breath too long and the colour goes dark and muddy. A breath too short and it fades before the first wearing. I count by the bubbles.
A dyer is teal to the elbow by the first row of work and to the shoulder by the tenth. It fades only when the work stops, so we wear it as proof.
I have lost my nose for everything but teal and orange. All else smells of vat. This is a dyer's wage, and I take it without complaint.
Colours have moods. Orange sets best when the dyer is calm. A cross dyer makes an orange that comes out slightly red, and the whole house knows who it was.

lines.text: Do not breathe the steam, outsider. You would not like the colour you came out. Stand upwind and watch the cloth, not the vat. The vat is none of your business.
Hold this swatch to the light. Teal? Look again. There is a little yellow in it, from the young wart. It is a young teal. An old teal is bluer. Dyers see this the way you see faces.
I once dyed a cloth a colour with no name. Not teal, not green, not blue. We called it the Visitor, because it left. It faded to nothing within a row, and no one could make it again.
I keep a scrap of every colour I ever made, rolled on a spool. A lifetime of colours in a pouch. You may have one. Pick with your eyes closed, and whatever you get, wear it.
I am dyeing a thread for you. The orange will not set the way I want, and I will not give you less than the colour I saw when I thought of you. It may take a while.
A teal with a little blue in it, and a thread of orange where the blue meets it. That is your colour. The dyers decided together. I am to make it and keep it, and no one else will wear it.
Which is harder to make, orange or teal?

replies.text: *click* Teal fades, and needs the mordant. But orange is moody. Each is hard in its own way.
Orange sulks. Yes. It takes patience and a good temper.
*the eyes flash* Take the stirring pole. The vat is hot.

lines.text: What colour would you dye yourself, if you could?

replies.text: *click click* Wear it to the elbow. Everyone will know you stirred.
Warm. Quick to anger, quick to forgive. I like it.

lines: The dye house is the only place in {village} that smells. The rest smells of wood and wool. We are kept to the downwind cap, and we are not offended. We are a little offended.
We dye the thread before it is woven. A dyed thread changes once the weaver crosses it with another, so a dyer must dye for the cloth the weaver means, not the one the dyer would like.
When a colour comes out right I hold it up to the lookout's glow and click twice. The other dyers hear it and click back. It is the only praise we give each other.
The ninth vat stands apart under its own roof, its lid weighted with two loom weights and a knot of rope. It holds the black. It has been sealed since the last black row. No one has opened it.
We stir it. That is the whole of the work. Once a row, three dyers, a long pole, ten turns left and ten right. We do not look in. A vat left unstirred goes bad, and bad black I will not describe.
The dyer who minds the vat is chosen by lot, which means no one wants it. Whoever is chosen is quiet for a row, and then takes the pole as if it had always been in their hands.
It does not smell. Everything else in the dye house smells of something, and the ninth vat smells of nothing at all. It is the quietest thing I know. Even its steam stands up straight.
The lid has never been lifted in my time, but the rim is warm. The Clothkeepers say it is the heat of the other vats. The dyers say nothing, and stir.
Children are told the ninth vat holds sleeping nets. They know better. They dare each other to touch the lid, and every row one does, and goes pale, and the rest are very quiet.
We keep it because a Weft does not throw away a colour. If the Wither came again, the Cloth would need its black ready. That is the saddest sentence in dyeing: we keep it ready.
I scrub the other eight until they shine. The ninth I do not scrub. It is not dirty. It is the only vat in the house that has never needed me.

lines.text: That is not for strangers. Do not walk toward the ninth roof. It is not forbidden, but it is a long way down to the net if you faint, and people do.
When I stir the black I think of the first dyers, who did not choose it. Every thread that came out of their hands was dark. Imagine dyeing a shawl for a child and having it come out mourning.
Between us, I sometimes talk to it. Small things: who quarrelled, how the orange set, what the weavers said. It never answers. I find that restful.
I was chosen to stir in my seventh row. I never told anyone how I felt. It felt like being handed something very heavy and told it was an honour. It was both.
A black thread is still a thread. It takes a knot as well as any. In my darker moods I think that is the whole sadness of it: it works perfectly.
I would like to stir it with you standing beside me, once. Not to help. Only a witness who does not click. I asked the other two stirrers and they said it was about time.
If the black is ever needed, I want you far from here. I mean it. I would stir with all four hands and weep into it. I do not want you to see a Weft do that.
Is it wrong to keep a colour you hope never to use?

replies.text: Ready. *click* Yes. That is how we say it.
*the eyes soften* The dyers have said so. Quietly, in the dye house.
*click... click* Easy to say, from outside.

lines.text: Would you rather be the dyer of black or the dyer of orange?

replies.text: Everyone says orange. Someone must be the other.
Spoken like a dyer.

lines: The stirrers wear a plain grey wrap. No teal, no orange. We are the only dyers who dress in no colour at all. It is not mourning. It is so the black has nothing to compare itself to.
When I stir, the others in the dye house stop talking. Nobody decides to. It is like the hush before a net drops. I am grateful, and I do not know how to say so.
A net is one thread and a great many knots. I tie the catch-knot, which pulls tight when something falls into it and loosens when nothing does. A knot that thinks is a good knot.
The mesh is a hand's width for Piglins and a finger's width near the children's decks. A child through a Piglin mesh is the story we tell every new netcaster. It ends well, but only just.
Vine nets are soaked in silkgrub oil until they are slick and quiet. A dry net rasps as it falls, and a net that rasps catches nothing.
A net has a weight on every corner: a bone, a stone, a hollow shroomlight stem with sand in it. The corners fall first. That is the whole art: where the corners go.
I roll my nets so they open as they fall, all at once, like a hand. It takes a year to learn the roll and two to learn the throw. Most never learn the third thing, which is not throwing.
I check my net before every drop, by feel, with my eyes shut. A broken mesh is worse than none. It gives the one inside hope.

The great nets under the bridges are woven by every household, one panel each, laced together. When a child falls, every household has caught them. It is hard to be rude to people you have all caught.
I have repaired the same net seventeen times. It is mostly repair now. Only one knot is original, near the middle. I keep an eye on that knot.

lines.text: Keep your hands off my belt. Those are rolled nets, and a rolled net is a decision I have not yet made. Do not make it for me.
Try the roll. Fold the corners in, no, inward. Now over the arm. ...It is flat. It will not open. You are the thousandth person to make a flat net. Again.
A net does not hold by strength. It holds by yielding a little and then not yielding. That is also the way to talk to a Piglin.
I wove a net for no reason. No one fell, no one raided. My hands wanted something that would catch whatever came. I hung it over the lookout, and I have rested better since.
There is a net hung where you pass on the third bridge. It is not a trap. It is the one I keep in case you slip. Do not tell the others. They think it is a spare.
My oldest net is the one I wove as an apprentice, uneven and ugly. I meant to give it to a child of mine. I would rather you held it. It has caught nothing, but it never stopped trying.
You are falling and a net is under you. What do you do?

replies.text: *click* Yes. Wide, like a cloth. The net likes company.
Brave. And you will tear it. Let the net do its work.
*click click* Also acceptable. Everyone does.

lines.text: Should a net be strong or kind?

replies.text: A net that is only strong is a trap.
A kind net gives a little. Yes. I knew you would say it.

lines: I tie a knot at every corner with my own mark: two turns and a flick. Anyone who finds my net knows a netcaster made it, and meant it.
Nets sing in the draught, each size a different note. The lookout hangs a dozen small ones on purpose, so a netcaster half asleep can tell by the tune when the wind changes.
A net has no up or down. It has only what is held and what is let go. I find that restful. Most of what I deal with has a great deal of up and down.
We watch in turns the length of one shroomlight-oil lamp. When it gutters, the next netcaster climbs up. Nobody sleeps on watch. Everyone nods, and calls it listening.
The lookout is a small cap with a big view. From it I can count every stalk in {village}, every bridge, every figure on every deck, and any flicker beyond the forest. I count them all, twice.
I watch the edges. Smoke at the edge of the forest means Piglins. A glow too low means Magmari. A glow too high means something I would rather not name, and I name it anyway, and pluck the rope.
We signal by plucking the great bridge-ropes: one pluck is a visitor, two is a raid, three is a child in a net. Four plucks have never been needed. I hope they never are.
From above, Piglins are small and loud. They run in a bunch with their gold flashing. On a quiet turn you can hear a war-horn from a long way off, and it makes every net hum.
A watcher learns what normal looks like. Normal is orange light from the dye house, a hum from the walk, and a child crying somewhere over a taken shuttle. When normal stops, I reach for a rope.
I have raised the alarm eleven times. Nine were Piglins, one was a runner from another Loom, and one was a particularly bold silkgrub. The silkgrub was worst.
The nets I keep ready are not for war. They are for slowing a foe until we can talk. It works on Piglins. They are quieter once they have run out of breath.

lines.text: Do not climb to the lookout. The ladder is shut and my nets are rolled. If you want the view, look at it from the deck. It is the same view, only farther from my hands.
Come up, if you must. One rung at a time. There. See the whole forest? Warped stalks as far as the glow allows. It is the most beautiful thing in the Nether, and I look at it for work.
Sometimes a Ghastkin drifts by, far out, pale as a lamp left burning. I let it pass. The air nets are for the ones that stay, and even then I look away.
I keep one watch for myself, when no one is looking. I look at nothing in particular and think: what would I do if the forest were not here? I do not like the answer. That is why I climb.
I changed the roster so the first watch after the Tying is yours, if you ever want it. A friend should have the best view. The others grumble. They are not wrong, but they are not you.
From the lookout I can see the path you take when you leave. I watch it until you are out of sight. Every time. Sometimes I stay for a second lamp.
If you saw a Piglin troop at the edge of the wart, what would you do?

replies.text: *click* Pluck once, then twice. Good.
Hm. Sometimes right. Mostly late.
Too quick. A net dropped for nothing is a net you must climb down for.

lines.text: Do you think a lookout's work is lonely?

replies.text: From the ground, yes. From up here I am the least lonely Weft in {village}: I see everyone.
*click* So do I. That is why I watch them.

lines: The lookout nets are never completely still. They tremble at the edge of hearing, like something thinking. I pretend not to notice. All netcasters do.
Bridges thrum when someone crosses. I know every Weft in {village} by their thrum. A runner is quick, a Clothkeeper slow. Yours is two feet, a little heavy, and it stops to look.
The worst watch is the quiet one. When nothing happens, I begin to wish it would. Then I remember what wishing does, and I put out the lamp and light another.

topics.ask: How do you hold a raider?
lines: The drop is the easy part. The hold is the craft. A net must pin a raider without hurting them, because they will be talking to us soon, and what they say depends on how we held them.
I choose the corner weights for the raider. Light for a thief, heavy for a brute, and none at all for a child who wandered. No one has ever thrashed in a net I weighted properly.
Once the net is down I step back. I do not smile and I do not stare. I sit on the rail and look at my hands. Being caught is shame enough without six eyes on you.
A Piglin in a net always shouts the same three things: a threat, a boast, and a number. The number is how much gold they say they are worth. I write it down. It is always wrong.
A Magmari in a net falls silent and begins to cool. I carry a warmed wrap for them and a shroomlight to hold. It is cruel to leave anyone cold, and the Magmari remember who was not cruel.
We never net the Withren. They stand still, look at us, and say our full names. Then our nets are somehow in a heap and we are somehow apologising. I would sooner net a hoglin.
A hold lasts as long as the raider needs to think. That is the rule. A net is not a punishment. It is a pause, and a pause is the oldest thing we know how to give.
I let them go after a hundred of their own breaths. They know I am counting. I hope they think about the breathing. Most do not, but one in twenty does, and that one does not come back.

lines.text: Do not wonder how it feels in a net, outsider. Wonder whether you can keep your hands off the warped stems. That is all you need to know of my work.
The slowness comes from the vine's oil, not the weave. A little in the net's skin makes legs heavy and thoughts light. I have mixed it for thirty rows, and the mix changes each time. I still learn.
I once netted a hunter who was only lost. He apologised until the lamp burned low. We fed him and showed him the way. He sent three gold nuggets as thanks, and we hung them on the lookout as a joke.
I have never netted a friend. I once netted someone I thought was a friend, and I carry that. It lies under the lookout like a stone. I tell you because you listen, and because it makes me kinder.
If a net ever fell on you, it would be mine, and I would climb under it with you and apologise with all four hands. I would explain. You would forgive me. That is how I plan it.
If you were chased, my net would fall between you and them. No questions, no counting. I have already chosen the corner weights. They are the ones I use for family.
A raider sits in your net, shouting. What do you do?

replies.text: *click click* Yes. A shout is only a sentence in a hurry.
Also valid. Shouts get tired.
Then you are two shouters in one net. Not a net. A rehearsal.

lines.text: Who would you never net, whatever they did?

replies.text: *all six eyes brighten* The first rule. Nets are not for little ones.
Hm. Then you have not had a friend do a stupid thing.

lines: Some say a net is a cruel thing. I say a net is the opposite of a blow. A raider who has been netted can still change their mind. One who has been struck may not.
The worst raider I ever held was a very small Piglin with a very large voice. They swore at me for a whole lamp and then asked if I had anything to eat. I did. We are friends, loosely.
I tie the drop-cord to my own wrist. If the net drops, I am tied to it. It is a promise to anyone beneath that I am never far above.
I carry spools! Not the full ones, the empty ones, from the weavers back to the spinners. They're light but they roll. I've lost eleven in the net. I know where they all are.
I sweep the lower deck with a root broom. Mostly I sweep the same spot, because it's where the dust likes to be. Nobody tells me to stop.
I hold the end of the thread for a spinner. It's a very important end. If I let go the whole walk goes crooked. I've never let go. Well, once.
I count the rungs on the ladders and tell the tenders when one is loose. I found three. One of them was a twig and not a rung. They said it counted.
I fetch the Clothkeeper a warmed wrap. The thank-you comes as one very small click. I think it's the nicest click there is.
I mind the silkgrubs on the deck. I feed them roots and tell them the news. They don't say much back. But they don't leave either.
I pass a new shuttle to the weavers when theirs runs out. They don't even look. They just hold out a hand and it's there. I'm the fastest shuttle-passer in the whole Loom.
Sometimes I'm the messenger. 'Tell the dyers the orange is late,' they say. I run all the way and by the time I get there I've forgotten, so I just say orange and they get cross.

lines.text: Grown-ups say I shouldn't talk to strangers while I work. So I'll keep working. *sweeps a very small pile* Hello. This is work.
I'll show you my best spool. It's a bit crooked. A spinner made it when I was little and now I carry things on it. It's called Wobble.
Once I was allowed to take the nets from the lookout and count them. There were forty-one. Last time there were forty-two. I'm not saying anything. But I'm watching.
My job is the best one because I get to see everybody's job. The weavers think I only bring spools. But I know their secrets. I know who drops their shuttle and who drops it on purpose.
I saved you the first thread off the new spool. It's a bit rough. I wound it round a little stick so it won't tangle. You can keep it in your pocket. Do you have a pocket?
Everyone in {village} knows I'm the one you talk to. Grown-ups ask me what you said. I tell them. I tell them you said I'm very good at my job.
Do you want to help me carry these? They're only a few spools.

replies.text: Careful, they roll! ...They rolled. Never mind, the net's got them.
I drop them too. We could drop them together.
Oh. *click* I'll tell the spools.

lines.text: Which job do you think is the hardest?

replies.text: Weavers never stop. I tried talking to one for a whole row. All I got was over, under.
They have to be quiet and not fall asleep. I fall asleep when I'm quiet.

lines: I'm not allowed to carry the full spools yet. A full spool is a whole walk of work. I'm allowed one when my row comes round again.
When my chores are done I get to sit in the net under the third bridge and swing. Everyone says it's for resting, but they know. It's for swinging.
I'm very busy. I have a lot of chores. *sits down* Ask me quickly.

topics.ask: What will you be when grown?
lines: I'm going to be a netcaster! I'll drop the biggest net in the whole forest on the biggest Piglin. Not in a mean way. In a polite way.
No wait, I'm going to be a dyer. Dyers get to be teal and everyone knows you stirred. Then I'll make a colour nobody has seen. I'll call it Me.
Or a spinner. They walk backward on purpose! I tried it once and went into the net backward. It was fine. I'll try again.
My cousin wants to be a Clothkeeper. She's very serious. She doesn't laugh, she just clicks and writes things down in her head. She's six rows old.
I want to be a canopy-tender so I can climb every stalk and name them. I've already named three. They don't know yet, but I think they like it.
Weavers get four hands and never stop. I'd get so tired. But my aunt says when you love it, your hands stop being tired and start being clever.
The grown-ups say I should wait and see which job picks me. Jobs pick you? I don't want to be picked. I want to pick. But I'll wait. I'm good at waiting. A little.
When my lower arms wake up I'll get a shuttle, or a net, or a stirring pole. It depends what they feel like. If they feel like a net, I'm a netcaster. That's how it works, I think.

lines.text: I'm not telling you. Grown-ups say strangers don't need to know what a child will be. *whispers* A dyer. Don't tell.
If I'm a weaver I'll weave you a cloak with all four arms and it'll be the best cloak in the whole Nether. It'll take until I'm old. Is that all right?
I changed my mind again. A spinner. No. A netcaster. No. All of them. Is that possible? The Clothkeeper said that's called being a Clothkeeper. There was no smile in it.
When I'm grown you can visit and I'll show you everything. I'll make you a shawl. Or a net. Or a colour. Or the thing I like best, which is a surprise.
I told the Clothkeeper I want to be woven into the Cloth someday. 'Everyone does.' I said I'd do something big. 'Be kind. That's the biggest.' I'm still thinking about it.
When I'm grown I want to be someone who remembers you. I'll keep a drawer of things. A bead for you, a knot for you. And when I'm old I'll tell the children about the outsider with two arms.
What do you want to be when you're grown? Wait. Are you already grown?

replies.text: That's so sad. Do you still get to pick?
Me too! We can choose together.
*click click* That's not a job! ...Is it? Can I be one?

lines.text: Which is the best job, do you think?

replies.text: Yes! You know. Nets are the best.
Ugh, you'd be so patient. I couldn't. But yes.

lines: Everyone says it takes forty rows to be good at a job. Forty! I'm only eight. I'll be bad for ages. I'll practise being bad first.
The best part of growing up is getting all four arms. The worst part is nobody holds the ladder for you anymore. I asked and they said, you have four arms. I said, I have two!
I asked the Clothkeeper which job is best. The answer was, the one your hands want. I looked at my hands. They wanted to hang from the bridge. I'm not sure that's a job.
The weavers say 'over, under' all the time. Even when they're eating. My mother says it to the broth.
Spinners walk backward and hum. They bump into things and the things move. It's like watching someone dance with the whole bridge.
Dyers come home teal and smelling funny. They leave teal handprints on everything. Our hut has a teal handprint on the ceiling. Nobody knows whose.
Netcasters sit very still and look into the distance. I tried it. I'm good at the sitting still part but not at the distance part. Everything is close to me.
The Clothkeeper walks along the Cloth with fingers out, and sometimes goes very quiet, and nobody asks. I asked once. All I got was 'A good row.' I think that was kind, for a small person.
Tenders talk to stalks. They think we don't notice. We notice. I once heard one say sorry, old friend, to a stalk that had a splinter. The stalk didn't say sorry back.
Grown-ups say that when they were small they didn't ask so many questions. The Clothkeeper says that's not true. Everyone asked. It's in the Cloth.
They all click when they're thinking. I click when I'm hungry. *click* See? I'm thinking about my meal.

lines.text: I'm not supposed to tell strangers what the grown-ups do. It's a secret. They do secret things, like weaving. Hmm. That isn't a secret. I'll stop.
Once the dyers let me stir a vat, with a tiny stick. The orange came out red. Everyone said, who's cross? I said nobody. They said, it was you. I said, I know.
I think grown-ups don't really know what they do. They've done it so many times it doesn't need thinking. I asked a weaver what goes on in their head. The answer was, nothing. It sounded wonderful.
The grown-ups tell me not to stare at them working. But if you stare long enough they forget you're there and show you the secret bits. I've learned a lot that way.
They don't say it, but grown-ups like having us around. When we're underfoot the work goes slower and they have to be patient. I think we make them better at it.
My aunt says you're the only outsider allowed to watch any grown-up at work. She says it's because you don't talk. But you do talk. A lot. I think it's because you listen.
Do you have a job? Or do you just walk about looking at things?

replies.text: That's a good job! Can I do that one?
*click* I'd rather weave. But it sounds loud.
Everybody is. Even the grown-ups. They just click louder.

lines.text: Which grown-up is the scariest?

replies.text: The netcasters! Because they never move and then they do.
The Clothkeeper. They know everything I ever did. It's in the Cloth.

lines: My favourite grown-up job is the one where you climb and look. But that's not a job, my aunt says. It's a hobby. I say it's a job if you do it carefully.
Grown-ups are always tired and always busy. Then they put on a shawl and tell a story and they're not tired anymore. I think stories are the real work.
When I'm grown I'm going to ask a lot of questions. Then when a child asks me, I'll say good question. And then I'll answer. That's the only plan I have.

topics.ask: How do you end the year?
lines: The Tying is how our year ends. The Clothkeeper ties off the row, and every shuttle in {village} is laid down. Nothing moves for one long breath. Then we eat.
Before the knot comes the Telling. Each household brings one thing from the year, and the Clothkeeper chooses what the row will remember. Most go home unchosen. *click*
A good Telling is short and true. A bad Telling is long and kind. The Clothkeepers have ended many a bad Telling with two clicks.
After the knot comes the first stitch of the new row: one orange stitch, set by the youngest child who can hold a needle. Then the row is open, and anything may happen in it.
The feast is baked caps and cold sap-tea on the bridges. No one lights a fire at the Tying. A wool deck remembers every spark.
Everyone ties a thread to the bridge rope before the feast. By the end it is fuzzy with every length and colour. Then the children climb it and ruin it. Tradition.
My favourite part is the quiet before the knot. Every hand in {village}, still. You can hear the forest hum. Few outsiders ever have.
Some years the Telling is thin because nothing happened. Those are the best rows. Plain teal, a little orange. A dull row is what peace looks like in cloth.
A row with a quarrel in it gets a tangled knot. A death gets a dark thread, a birth a teal one. We can read a whole year with our eyes shut.

lines.text: It is for us, outsider. You may watch from the lower bridge. Do not cheer. Cheering shakes the ropes.
Come to the next Tying, if you are still among us. There is always a place on the lower bridge for one who is tied on.
At the last Telling a neighbour spoke of you. The Clothkeeper heard it out and clicked once. Once is a great deal, from a Clothkeeper.
You will be in every Telling now, whether you do anything or not. The Cloth holds you, and the Cloth is what the Telling is for.
The knot is mine to tie. My lower hands shake just before, every year, and I let them. Steady hands would mean I had stopped caring what goes in.
At the Tying every weaver in turn adds a hand's width to one long band, passing the shuttle along. One slip spoils it for all. We have slipped twice. Both are in the Cloth.
At the Tying the dyers hang the old dye-house canopy from the lower bridge, stained with every vat of the row, before it is cut for patches. It is the only time we are proud of the stains.
At the Tying we take the nets down from the feast bridge, so for once there is no net under anyone. The children behave remarkably well.
I climb the biggest stalk at the Tying and set a handful of bone meal at its root. A thank-you from the one who tends to the one who holds us up.
The spinners spin the knot-thread: one thread the length of the Great Loom's frame, with no join. I start long before. I do not rest easy until it is tied.
At the Tying everyone ties the tails of their headwrap in a fresh knot. It is the only time we are all tidy at once.
At the Tying we trim the fray from our mantle edges. A ragged hem at the knot is bad luck, or bad weaving. Usually both.
*click* Does your own world mark its years with anything? Or do they just go by?

replies.text: A feast. Then you understand the important part. Eating together after something ends.
Go by. How sad. A year with no knot in it is a year the forest forgets.
Think of it now. It is not too late to tie your own.

lines.text: If the Clothkeeper asked you to speak at the Telling, what would you say?

replies.ask: That I kept my axe away.
replies.text: *click click* A true thing, and a small one. The row is full of those, and I like them best.
A Telling is not a favour. Say it of yourself, or not at all.
No one has ever told a joke at the Telling. It might be kept for that alone.

topics.ask: What were you like as a child?
lines: A quiet child, I am told. I was counting. A child who counts is mistaken for a good child, and I let them think so for many rows.
My first cradle was a net slung under my mother's frame. Every beat of her beater rocked me. A steady rhythm still makes me sleepy, which is awkward at the Telling.
The Opening is when a child's nubs split into hands. The whole deck comes. A Clothkeeper lays a shuttle in the new fingers, and the child weaves one hand's width while everyone watches.
My hand's width at the Opening was so crooked that the weavers took turns looking at it. It hangs in my mother's hut. She calls it the best cloth she owns. She lies well.
On my third climb I fell into the net and wept. Not from fear. I had been caught so easily, and I had wanted to be the one who nearly fell.
Everyone on a deck is a little bit your parent. If a hand takes hold of your collar on a bridge, you do not ask whose it is. You thank it afterward.
They taught me to count by tapping my knuckles, round and round the hands. I still tap when I am nervous. Please do not watch.
As a child I feared the forest floor. Someone told me the tall walkers take whatever looks down at them. I did not look down for a whole row.
I once stole a spool of shroomlight orange and wove a shawl for a silkgrub. It hated the shawl. The dyer pretended not to know where the orange had gone.
My worst punishment was sweeping the lower deck under the Cloth with a root broom, in silence. I learned more of the early rows from that broom than from any lesson.
We were taught that a dropped shuttle is not a failure. It is a lesson that falls. Most of our wisdom is things that have fallen.
Young twisting vine is what we chewed when our teeth came in. Tough and sweet. I keep a tip in my belt-pouch for hard rows, and I do not apologise.

lines.text: I was nine rows old when I first saw an outsider: a Magmari, come up for fungus. I stared until my mother pulled me behind her. I have not entirely stopped.
My mother sang while I fell asleep: one for the warp, one for the weft, one for the one who is learning. I hum it when a knot is hard. It has never failed me.
I was afraid of the Long Cloth as a child. It looked so patient that I thought it was waiting for me. I am still not certain I was wrong.
When my headwrap tails were long enough to knot, I wore them loose for a whole row and told everyone I had four braids. I thought I looked like a Clothkeeper.
My first headband was my father's, taken in with two stitches. I wore it down to a string. The string hangs by my shuttle, and it is still the best thing I own.
As a child I was told to be quiet near the Cloth, and I was. Quiet was my first skill. Everything since has been an elaboration.
I was the child who always jumped. The netcasters liked that, since I tested their nets so they did not have to. Now I mend the nets I tested.
I fell into a vat of orange as a child and came out bright as a lamp. For a while my mother could find me anywhere in the dark. She says it was the calmest stretch of her life.
I climbed everything. At twelve rows they gave me a tender's belt, mostly because they were tired of fetching me down from the high caps.
My first pattern was a straight stripe. My second wandered. My mother says the second was the first thing I made that was truly mine.
*click* Were you a good child, outsider?

replies.text: A handful is what a hand is for. *click click* I would have liked you.
The quiet ones are the ones listening. I could tell you were one.
Not a single row? *click* How do you keep from going crooked?

lines.text: A child at the Opening is given a shuttle. If one were put in your hand now, what would you weave?

replies.text: Plain, and honest. *click* Many of the best rows began with a straight line.
On purpose? *click click* Then it is not crooked. It is a decision.
*click* Everyone does. That is the first lesson, and you have already passed it.

topics.ask: What do you eat and drink?

lines.text: For a feast we make cap-loaves: a small cap hollowed, stuffed with mashed root and baked slow. One feeds four, or one Weft who has waited a whole row. Wart-cake is for every other meal.
The lamp-oven is a clay pit packed round with fallen shroomlights. Its stones grow hot enough to bake and never hot enough to burn. Nothing on a wool deck is cooked over flame.
Sap-tea is drunk hot from a bowl, held in both lower hands, the upper pair on the rope. Only at the Tying is it cold, because no fire is lit then. We call that the cold bowl, and we are fond of it.
The sap comes from weeping vines, a thumb's depth at a time. A tender taps each vine once a row and never twice. A tapped vine remembers, and sulks, and sweetens.
Sprout salad: nether sprouts torn by hand, never cut, with warped-root shavings. The shavings crunch. A salad should argue a little.
A Weft eats with the lower hands and holds the rope with the upper. A contented eater clicks once per bite. If you hear nothing, either the food is poor or the company is.
No one takes from the common pot before the eldest has taken the first bite. The youngest chooses next. The one in the middle takes what is left and complains. I am in the middle.
We do not eat silkgrubs. We eat nothing that spins for us. It is not a law. It would simply be rude, like biting the hand that holds your shuttle.
Each hut takes a turn at the lamp-oven, and the whole deck eats what comes out. No one stays angry with a neighbour whose cake they are chewing.
The wart thins in lean rows, and then we eat less, say so aloud, and share. No hut in {village} has gone hungry while another had a cake.
Offer an outsider a bowl of sap-tea and watch the face. Most look as if they have bitten a stem. I am told the second bowl is better. No one has stayed for a second.
I saved you the burnt edge of the wart-cake. It is the part we give to those we trust. If it tastes like a floor, say nothing. It tastes like that to everyone.
My mother ground a pinch of old shroomlight into every cake. The cake glowed faintly when it was broken. I have never told the dyers where she got it.
After a long bolt, a weaver is brought a bowl of sap-tea by someone who did not weave it. The weaver may not return the favour. It is the one kindness we leave unpaid.
The dye house keeps its own pot, because dyers will not sit at the common one until the stain is off. By then the common pot is empty. We eat late and say it is by choice.
A tender gets the first thinnings off a young cap, still sweet. It is the one privilege of the post. I bring a handful home in my belt-pouch for whoever is sulking.
A bite of the first cake of the year is set before the Cloth. It is older than any keeper I know. No one has told me why. No one has suggested stopping.
*click* Our saying is, a full spool is a full belly. What does your world say about eating?

replies.text: Ah. Then you understand us better than you know.
Hot. *click* No wonder you outsiders hurry.
Then you may borrow ours. Return it when you have your own.

lines.text: Wart-cake tastes better under a bridge, where the lamps don't reach. I don't know why. It just does. Don't tell my mother.
Sap-tea makes my tongue sticky! I stuck it to my lip once and had to ask for help. It wasn't embarrassing. It was a little embarrassing.
We are never allowed to eat silkgrubs. Not that I would want to. They are far too ticklish.
I get to choose second at the pot, after the oldest. My mother says that means I'm important. My brother says it means he's the first one to be hungry.
I tried to eat with my upper hands once and it got all over my ears. Now I wait for my lower hands. They're coming. Slowly. Like everything.
I'm not allowed sap-tea until I can count to twelve without tapping my knuckles. I've got to eleven.
I saved you a crumb of my wart-cake. It's the shape of a stalk! If you squint.
