Never step on a thread laid across a deck. It is someone's work in progress. Step over it, or ask.
Tap a bridge rope twice before you cross, so whoever is on the far side knows someone is coming. A bridge should never surprise anyone.
Hand a tool over handle first, always. A point held out is a question nobody wants asked.
Never finish another's sentence. A sentence, like a row, belongs to the one weaving it. You may sit beside it and wait.
At a hut post, knock once and count to twelve. Wool does not knock back, and we are slow to answer, but we do answer.
A gift is handed over with a loose thread tied round it, so the giver stays attached for a while. It means: I am not quite letting go of this.
To say sorry, tie a knot in your own hem and wear it until you are forgiven. Everyone can see that you owe. Some hems on this deck have been knotted for many rows.
Quarrellers go to opposite ends of a bridge and speak to the middle, one at a time. By the time the words meet, they have usually shrunk.
Thanks is said, 'I will hold your rope.' It means that if you ever fall, I am at the other end. It is not a small thing to say. Say it only if you will.
A glance with two eyes is easy talk. With all six it is a plain question. Do not be alarmed when it happens. Be exact.
Do not clap. If you wish to be kind, tap two of your hands on two of mine. If you only have two, tap them on my lower pair. It counts.
Never knot a rope that is not yours. Even with a better knot. Especially with a better knot.
If you are given a seat on the lower bridge at a feast, do not choose another. The seat was woven for you, in the sense that someone thought about it for a while.
You may cross my deck without tapping the rope now. Not because you may surprise me. Because I would know your step anywhere, and would be sorry to miss it.
To pass a weaver the shuttle, wait until their hand is open. To take a shuttle from a weaver, do not. There is no second rule.
Never hurry under a rolled net. Not because it will drop, but because I will see you hurry and wonder why, and a netcaster who wonders is a netcaster who throws.
*click* You tapped the bridge rope before you crossed. Who taught you that?

replies.text: *click click* Then I teach better than I knew. Nobody tell the Clothkeeper.
The sound is the point, and the manners are only the reason. Well done.
Then you have good manners without knowing it. That is the rarest kind.

lines.text: You have to tap the rope twice. Then count to twelve. Then you can cross. It takes forever. That's the point.
When I'm sorry, I tie a knot in my hem. I have six knots right now. I'm sorry a lot.
You aren't supposed to point with your lower hands. Pointing is for upper hands. But mine aren't open yet, so I can't get in trouble.
We don't clap. We tap. *taps two hands on two of yours* Like that. It's quiet, and nobody falls off a bridge.
Don't say 'it's only a little knot' near a Clothkeeper. There's no such thing. I said it once. I'm still sweeping.
I don't have to tap the rope for you. I know your step. I could tell it from a thousand.

lines: A Weft courts by weaving a small thing and leaving it where the other will find it. Never giving. Leaving. A gift handed over can be refused; a found thing can only be kept or ignored.
If the finder weaves a thing in answer and leaves it back, the courtship has begun. They weave at one another for many rows without once sharing a loom. It is very romantic and extremely slow.
Families weave the wedding cloth, which is for the guests. The pair weave the Band, a hand's width each in turn, until it is a span long. It is for no one else. It hangs in their hut.
A good Band reads like a short row. Here was a hard year. Here, someone was ill. Here, a child. The knots in the middle are laughing.
Eight hands on one frame is the finest thing a Weft can do. A pair who have woven together long enough move like one creature with a great many fingers.
A Weft embrace has four arms in it. It is not possible to be held so completely by anything with two. I mean no insult. It is only a fact, and a fortunate one.
We have no word for jealousy. We have a word for crossed threads, meaning two Weft pulling at the same one. It is said kindly, in the hope that they will see sense.
A row is never unpicked, but a Band may be. We do not cut it. We unpick it thread by thread, together, in the open. It takes a long while. By the end they are usually friends, or very tired.
Children are born in the home hut, and the whole deck comes to the door and says nothing. Silence is the welcome. The loud welcome comes later, when the child can click back.
A family is a hut and whoever is in it: grandparents, cousins, a neighbour whose own hut was mended too slowly. We count a household by its bowls. A hut with too few bowls is a hut with room.
Old pairs weave one shawl and wear it in turns. By the end you cannot tell whose it is, and neither can they. That is when the shawl is finished.
Parents have the first and last word over a child, and the deck has all the ones between. It balances, mostly. The child has no word at all, and finds a way to be heard anyway.
The loneliest sight on a Loom is a half-woven Band hung in a hut with one name on it. The Clothkeepers leave them hanging. No one is ever told to take one down.
Tell the one you love while the knot is tight, not after it has loosened. A loose knot drops things. Often it drops the very thing you meant to say.

lines.text: I tied my wrap tails in the courting knot for a whole row before anyone noticed. When someone finally did, I said it was a style. They wove me a hem before the row was out.
I wore my headband tilted for a whole row, which is how we say it, and was thought to have a sore neck. The one I meant it for understood on the second row. We do not hurry.
Weaver pairs trade shuttles for their first sitting. Each learns how the other holds the cloth. You learn a great deal about a Weft from how they let go of a shuttle.
Two spinners marry by thread. Each spins half the wedding thread and they twist it together on the bridge, walking opposite ways. If it holds where they meet, it holds.
Dyer couples go teal to the shoulder together. The Band is judged by the stain. A pair who stain evenly are the happiest, and the hardest to look at.
Tender couples plant a stalk for their first child, though neither will stand on its deck. They plant it for the child's child. It is the most romantic thing we do, and none of us says so.
Netcaster pairs swap nets for a row, and each throws the other's. A pair who can throw together are joined already. The Band is only writing it down.
I have tied the teal thread for children whose parents I later tied dark threads for. That is the whole of a keeper's love story: you are the one who remembers who was there.
*click* Is there someone you would leave a hem for?

replies.text: A maybe is a good beginning. It is how all of ours start.
Weave something small and leave it where they walk. The rest takes care of itself, slowly.
Fair. A thread untied is not a thread lost.

lines.text: I would be honoured if you wove a hand's width of a Band with me, sometime. Not as a pair, as friends do, once. We call it a short band. It means: I intend to remember you.

lines: A Piglin once got caught in a net and spent a long while trying to barter his way out. He offered gold, then his boots, then his name. We let him go for the boots. He still owes us the name.
The Magmari come for fungus and stay for the steam. One sat in the dye-house vapour so long that the dyers took pity. He left a chain link on the rail. We hold twelve links now, from twelve visitors.
A Withren came up the bridge once, alone and grave, and asked only to see the black rows. He stood before them a long while, then thanked us for weaving them. We still wonder if he meant the needles.

Ghastkin drift past the Loom and seldom stop. A Ghastkin child once tangled a tentacle in a stray net. I freed it. Its eyes were open. It said, you are very busy, and floated off. I think of it still.
The tall walkers pass through every few rows, moving blocks about and never speaking. We tidy behind them. They never thank us. I have decided that is good manners.
I can tell who is near by the sound. A horn means Piglins. A chain, Magmari. A flute on the wind, Withren. Chimes that fall, Ghastkin. The fifth sound is us, and it is the click of a shuttle.
We trade rarely with the other peoples, and strangely. More often things are left on the bridges: a link, a tusk, a bead. We do not answer. We keep them. It is our nearest thing to a treaty.
Of the four, I would choose the Withren as neighbours. They remember. Remembering is half of weaving, and they have the other half wrong, so we could correct them.
The Piglins are the loudest neighbours and the least dangerous. They tell you exactly what they will do, and then do it. A creature that announces itself can be netted.
The Magmari are the best company and the worst thieves. They talk so warmly that you do not notice the fungus is gone until it is a rope in a strider's mouth.
The Ghastkin I cannot weigh. I know what our nets cost them. I know what our dyes owe them. I have six eyes and none of them can hold a Ghastkin's gaze for long.
Rows ago a lost Magmari child came up the stalk, cold and shaking. The whole deck stopped weaving. We warmed her by a lamp-oven and fed her wart-cake. She said it tasted of nothing. We were proud.
Piglin children sometimes dare each other to touch a net. They run when it moves. The netcasters pretend not to see, and sometimes move it a little, for the children.
We leave a bowl of sap-tea out for any who come without weapons. Nobody has ever drunk from it. The bowl is a promise we made to ourselves.
Everyone who comes expects us to be fiercer. Four arms look fierce from below. From a deck they look like very tired hands.

lines.text: None of the four will climb to a Loom without a reason, and the reason is nearly always wrong. You are the first outsider I have met whose reason was to talk.
I keep your name on my belt-spool, {player}. The other visitors are in the Cloth only. You are the only one I carry.
A Magmari once asked me to weave something to keep her warm away from the lava. I wove for a whole row. She wore it for three steps, shivered, and said it was the thought. I kept the thought.
The first lesson of a netcaster is the sound of other feet. Piglin: thump. Magmari: shuffle. Withren: nothing, which is worse. Ghastkin: no feet, which is worst.
The Magmari ask me for colours that do not exist. I tell them so, and give them dregs, which they call marvellous. They leave a chain link on the rail. I cannot tell who is cheating whom.
Every visitor is in the Cloth, if only as a knot. The Piglin in the net is there as a tusk bead. The Withren at the black rows is a still thread. We weave everyone who stops.
*click* Which of the other peoples would you visit, if you could choose?

replies.text: Brave. Or foolish. *click* They will want your boots.
Quiet. They would feed you well, and remember it for a very long time.
Ah. You would have to creep up on them. You would understand us better afterward.

topics.ask: What were the old rows like?
lines: The first row was woven by no one. The Cloth says only: there were stems, and then a silkgrub fell from a cap, and a thread followed it up. We have been climbing that thread since.
The oldest rows are copies of copies, and the copies disagree about the first Weft. One says she had six arms. Another, that she had two and a very good idea.
Before the war the rows were easy: teal for the wart, orange for the lamps, a few beads, a few knots. People call them dull. People are wrong. Dull is a gift nobody knew they had.
Row Eleven-Eighty-Nine is the last teal row before the black: a wedding, a good wart year, a child caught in a net. The keeper wrote 'nothing to fear.' Everyone stops to read it on the way down.
The Piglins call those rows the Gilded Age. We call them the easy rows. They had gold; we had teal. Neither of us wanted what the other had, and for a long time that was enough.
In the easy rows each people kept to its ground: Piglins to the gold lands, Withren to the valleys, Magmari to the seas, Ghastkin to the deltas, we to the forest. It was not peace. It was distance.
My grandmother says the easy rows were boring, and then she weeps. I asked why. She said she did not know what she had. A child cannot ask for that, so I wait.
In the easy rows nobody latched a hatch. Now the hatches have latches, and the latches have latches. We call that progress in rope. It is only fear with better knots.
Silkgrubs were sweeter in the easy rows, or so the spinners say. Their silk came long and even. Since the black rows it comes short and knotted, as if the grubs had seen something.
Children in the easy rows were allowed the floor. They played in the nylium among the roots and came home with spores in their hair. Now the floor is only for tenders and errands.
I envy the easy rows their smallness. A quarrel then was a spool, not a war. A grief was a grandmother, not a people.
In the easy rows a Magmari barge would pass the forest edge and nod to our lookouts. We nodded back. That was all our diplomacy. Then the barges began to carry Piglins, and nobody nodded.
Ordinary folk say the war began when a Piglin chief was offered a shuttle as a courtesy and took it for an insult. The Clothkeepers say it began over gold. They are dull, and also right.
I used to read the easy rows to my children. They fell asleep at the same row every time. I think I was reading them the one thing they would need and could not yet want.

lines.text: If I could have one easy row back, I would choose Eleven-Fifty-Two: no births, no deaths, a wart harvest a hair above the last. It would be nothing at all. I would live in it a hundred rows.
When I am sad I go to the lower deck and touch the easy rows. They are soft and even, and the dust is thick. Nothing in them wants anything from me. It is the nearest I come to rest.
I am glad of the black rows in one narrow way. In the easy rows we would have welcomed you without asking. Now we ask first, and I think that is why you are still here.
I was born in the last teal row. My first sight was a keeper tying off Eleven-Eighty-Nine. Then the black began. I am told I cried through the first of them. I do not remember. I believe it.
The easy rows are the best weaving in the Cloth. Even tension, no haste, no anger in the weft. I run a hand down them when my own work feels crooked. They straighten me.
The thread in the easy rows was spun by people who did not need to be quick. You can tell. It has a lazy twist, like something thinking of nothing at all.
In the easy rows the dye house had eight vats and no ninth. Now the ninth stands apart under its own roof, sealed, kept in case. In case of what, no dyer will say.
*click* If you could live one row of the Cloth, which would you choose?

replies.text: Wise. Most outsiders say a grand one. Then they find out what grand costs.
*all six eyes go still* Why would you ask that? ...No. I know why. Do not.
Ah. That one is being woven now. Be careful what you tie into it.

topics.ask: What do folk say of the war?
lines: In every hut the war is told a little differently. In mine, the Piglins came for gold and we were in the way. In my neighbour's, we were never in the way at all. Both huts are very sure.
My grandmother wove one of the black rows when she was ten. She said her hands kept weaving the motions after the shuttle was empty, and no one dared stop her until the row was done.
The children's rhyme goes: Needle, needle, whose were you? Not mine to ask, but I'll sew true. We teach it before they know what it means. That is the way with most of our wisdom.
No one claims the first needle. The Cloth has it: Eleven-Seventy-Six, one bead near the frame. A Weft took a rib from a fallen Piglin to mend a net. The shame is not the first needle, but the second.
My mother says we stood on the high bridges and watched the Piglin bands march by the forest edge, a river of gold and shouting. None of them looked up. It is the one time she thanked quiet.
From the high caps you could see the Magmari barges' lamps crossing the lava, one behind another, like thread drawn through a needle. We called it the Long Stitch. We stopped calling it that.
Folk say the Withren fought hardest and sang least. A Weft who saw them in the valleys called them the quietest army ever to lose a war, and said she could not tell that they had.
Every child hears of the Piglin who dropped his gold in our net and asked to be a Weft. We told him he had the wrong number of arms. He wept. Then he asked about the nets. No one knows if it is true.
The war years were mostly about water. The vats ran short, the grubs stopped spinning, and the children stopped climbing. Ask a dyer about the war and you will hear the price of a cup.
My aunt lost an arm to a Piglin bolt on the eastern bridge. She says it was the quickest she ever came to a decision. We made her a longer shuttle and a shorter sleeve, and she out-wove us all.
The Wither never came to our forest. Some say it could not climb. I say it did not need to. The stalks hummed a note when it passed that no tender has heard since.
At the end of every telling the elders say the same: and so the needles stay. No one can say whether it is regret or only a fact. I asked once. I got a very long click.
A few huts sew with thorn needles. Their hems are no worse. The matter is much discussed at the vats, where nothing is ever quite settled and everything is quite said.
My father will not speak of the war. He weaves, and the hem comes out perfect, and he does not speak. I have learned to read his hems. Some rows they say a great deal.
We do not forget the war. We keep it in the Cloth, which is the same as forgetting, but orderly.
The Magmari say the war was ours. The Piglins say it was the Withren's. The Withren say it was no one's, and name three. We say nothing, and keep the beads.

lines.text: My grandmother kept a Piglin's gold tooth in her pocket until she died, to remember what the war was for. We laid it at the stalk with her. We were never sure whether that was an insult.
If you ever meet a Piglin who remembers the war, ask him about the nets. We both lost something there. I would like to hear his version, and I would like to be wrong.
The war rows are woven tight and double-knotted at every hem. A weaver reading them says the hands were so afraid that the shuttle forgot how to dance.
Spinners suffered most in the black rows. They spun the black without being told, and could not stop. My teacher's teacher said her fingertips turned dark. It faded. The memory did not.
Dyers remember the black rows as the time the vats ran dark. We did not make that black. It came up out of the dye on its own. I have never since looked at a vat without counting what is in it.
Netcasters remember the war as the rows when the nets were never put away. Even now I rest with one hand on a rope. I have told myself it is habit. It is not.
I will tell you what the keepers do not tell the folk: the war rows are the most beautiful in the Cloth, and none of us can forgive them for it.
*click* Do you know why the elders tell the war to the children?

replies.text: Partly. It also keeps the elders company.
Fear is a poor teacher. We teach the shape of the thing, and let the fear come on its own.
So that someone else carries the knot. It is a heavy knot. It should not hang from one hand.

lines: When a Weft dies, the deck stops weaving for one breath, then goes on. To stop longer would insult the work they spent their life on.
A Clothkeeper ties the dark thread at the bottom edge of the row. No one else touches the knot. The rest of us stand with our hands crossed and do not look at each other.
We carry our dead to the foot of a dying stalk, lay them there, and leave. When the stalk falls, a new seed goes into the same hole. We say a Weft is not buried but exchanged.
We take no bone from our own dead. Not a rib. Every needle at my belt came from the war or the Hollowed, never from the Loom. It is the one rule the war could not break.
The stalks hum because the dead are holding the warp from below. That is what children are told. The tenders say it is only the roots drinking. They say it very quietly, and stroke the stalk.
Mourning is a knot in the hem, tied at the death and left until the next Tying. Then the row turns, the knot is untied, and we eat. Grief has its turn. We do not apologise for it.
A child who dies is tied in with a bead, not a thread: small, round and impossible to undo. The keeper holds it a little longer than the others. No one hurries them.
An old Weft may take the Last Climb: up the tallest stalk, to look at the forest once more. Most come down. Those who do not are brought down by the youngest tender, who is allowed to cry.
We do not say the name of the dead until the next Tying. We say their row: she of Twelve-Eighty, he of Twelve-Ninety-One. It makes them a little more like the Cloth, and a little more bearable.
The Withren keep a name; we keep a stalk. The Ghastkin cry them away. I think all three are ways of not letting go, and I think we are right to have three.
A dead Weft's silkgrub goes to the nearest child, who is told that it is only visiting. Silkgrubs never ask. They keep spinning.
I have asked for the stalk on the far side of {village}, the one that has been dying for thirty rows. The tender says it will outlive me out of spite. I find that comforting.
In the war there were not enough dying stalks to go round. The old ones remember the dead laid in rows along the forest edge, new seeds set among them. Some of those stalks are the tallest we have.
We hold a small silence when a stalk falls, and a longer one when a Weft does. Only a little longer. Do not tell the stalks.
Nobody sings at a laying-down. We hum, low, until the stalk hums back. They always hum back. Whether it is the stalk or the dead, I leave to the Clothkeepers.

lines.text: When I die I would like to be laid at whichever stalk is dying nearest the dye house, where the wart is thickest. I have told my family. I wanted you to be told too.
If you are near when I go, do not tie a knot. Hold my hand. Any hand. You have only two, and they will be enough.
I have tied a great many dark threads. The knot never changes. What changes is the hand tying it. Mine shake more now, and the other keepers pretend not to notice.
I tend the stalks that took people. I know which ones: they hum a little lower. I tell no one. I only keep my hand on them a little longer.
A dead Weft's spool-ends, the scraps of a lifetime, are twisted into one thread by the nearest spinner and set at the stalk's foot. It is never long. It is always the best thing I make.
A dyer is laid down with the teal still on the skin. The new stalk comes up a shade brighter. It is the only time we are glad of the stain.
*click* Do your people bury their dead, or burn them, or leave them?

replies.text: Under the ground, and a stone on top? A stone where a stalk should go. ...I suppose it holds them down.
Remembering is a root too. Perhaps we are not so different.
Then do not. Some things are left as loose ends on purpose.

lines: Fire. It is every Weft's first fear and last. We are made of what burns: wool, vine, thread, wart. We keep no flame on a deck, and still I check the lamps.
The Piglin horn. Not for the Piglins. For how fast the whole deck goes quiet when it sounds. That quiet is the loudest thing I know.
Not the fall. The fall is only a long moment in the air. I fear the net failing the one I swore it would catch.
I fear a dropped stitch nobody finds. The row is built on, and built on, and by the fortieth row someone finds it and has to ask whose hands it was.
I fear the Cloth going silent. It hums, if you listen. If it ever stopped, I think I would know before anyone told me.
I fear standing on the floor with nothing above me. I know it is nonsense. It is also why I plant every young fungus I can: I am building a roof.
I fear the ninth vat. It has been sealed since the last black row, and sealed is not the same as empty. I fear the moment a dyer says it is time.
I fear my hands slowing before my mind does. A weaver who knows the pattern and cannot make it is the cruellest sight I know. I have seen it twice.
I fear the quiet after a quarrel more than the quarrel. A quarrel is a knot. The quiet is a thread nobody will pick up.
I fear the open-air nets, and not for what they catch. For what it says of us that we hang them with an easy conscience.
I fear small things: a loose rung, a frayed rope, a hum in a stalk that was not there before. The great fears make songs. The small ones do the harm.
I fear the moment my child asks why we do not leave. There is an answer, and it is the forest, and I do not know if it is enough for someone who has heard of the world beyond.
I fear outsiders with axes. I fear outsiders who are kind and carry axes in their packs even more. The second kind are harder to forgive.
I am afraid of being the one who ends a row badly. A row ends once. There is no unpicking. All the care of a year can go into one wrong knot.
My fear is dull, and I am ashamed of it: that nothing will happen, that I will be a quiet thread in a quiet row and the Cloth will move on. Then I remember quiet is the best thing a Cloth can be.

lines.text: I am afraid of the row in which you stop coming. Not for me. For the Cloth. It would mean something had happened to you, and I would have to tie it.
I fear tying the wrong thing in. A bead where there should be a knot, a knot where there should be a loop. The row will say so for a thousand rows, patiently, to everyone who reads it.
I fear the one throw I miss. I have thrown ten thousand. I carry the one that got by in my arm like a splinter, and it was not even a net I threw.
I fear the vat that goes quiet. A working vat murmurs. When it stops I check it and it is only waiting, but my heart does not believe me for a while.
I fear the silkgrubs stopping. Whole Looms have died when the grubs went off their spinning. No one knows why. I check mine, and they look back.
I fear a sick stalk I did not hear. I walk the decks and listen, and I am sure I have never missed one, and I lie in my net and listen anyway.
*click* Is there something you are afraid of, outsider?

replies.text: Then you have more sense than our children. I will hold the rope.
Ah. Then you are a Weft in all but arms. *click click*
Some fears are better left unspun. I will not pull.

lines: To see the stalk I planted hold its first deck. I will be very old, or very planted. Either way I intend to be standing near.
To weave a dozen quiet rows in a row. Twelve rows in which nothing is worth a knot. I would hang them in my hut and sleep under them.
That the black rows are read as often as the teal ones, and no more. Not hidden, not worshipped. Read.
To be woven into a quiet row, not a grand one. A hem, a joke, a kind word to a neighbour. I would like to be the small true thing in a quiet year.
That the nets in the open air hang empty for one row. I do not ask for them to come down. Only empty. I would take a single empty row and call it peace.
That we find a colour that does not cost anyone their crying. The dyers say it is not possible. The dyers said the same of orange.
That the Piglins and the Withren stand once before the Cloth and read the war rows together. I would bring sap-tea. They would drink none of it, and it would still be the best sitting of my life.
That the tall walkers learn to tidy. They move the blocks, and the blocks are never quite where they were. I do not ask them to stop. Only to leave a note.
To see your world once. Not to stay: to see the sun that leaves, and the water that falls. Then to come back and tell the dyers, who would not believe me.
To learn what a sheep is. I have heard a great many things about sheep, and none of them agree.
That my child is bored. Bored children are safe children. A bored child has no stories yet.
That in a thousand rows a Weft who has never heard of me reads this Cloth and finds one small knot she cannot explain, and smiles, and leaves it alone.
That I am the last of my family to need a net. That my grandchildren climb without one and never fall. It is a foolish hope. I tie a knot for it every row.
That the forest grows. Not for our sake. For the sake of the stalks, who do not know they are loved and would find it embarrassing.
That you do not make the third skull. I say it quietly, and lightly, and I mean it all the way down.
I hope your row is long and dull. I hope every thread of it is plain and warm and ties off at the end with a kind knot. It is the best wish a Weft can give anyone.

lines.text: I hope the Cloth keeps your thread a very long time. It is the one wish I would tie a knot for. I have tied it.
I hope for a row so fine the keepers have nothing to add. A hand's width left blank at the end, by choice, because there was nothing to say. I want to tie that knot.
A teal that never fades. Not for pride. So that children, when they are old, will find the cloth they were wrapped in still bright, and know they were wrapped.
A thread with no end. I know it is a foolish hope. I spin anyway, a little further each time, and tell myself the end is only farther than my arms.
To spend a whole row with my nets rolled. Not a single throw. It would be the proudest row I could ask for. I would write it in the Cloth myself.
To weave a pattern big enough to take in the whole Loom: every hut, every bridge, every person. I keep starting. Every time I run out of arms before I run out of Loom.
*click* And you, outsider. What do you hope for?

replies.text: You are. Tell no one; they will grow impatient with you.
Of course. Come back and tell us what it looks like. We will hold your row open.
You are, a little. Let it come slowly. Slowly is how it holds.

topics.ask: What do you know of my world?
lines: Little, and all of it from outsiders who talk too fast. I know there is a light in your sky that leaves and comes back. I do not know why it leaves. I have been told not to take it personally.
Water falls from your sky, I am told, unasked. Does it fall on cloth? The dyers wept when I told them. Then they asked how many cups.
Your sheep carry their own wool and give it up for a pair of shears. Is it true? Does the wool mind? I hope the wool does not mind.
I am told there are eight-legged spinners in your world who weave in the open air, and no one thinks anything of it. We should like to meet them. We could learn from one another, or at least argue.
Your forests are made of wood: dead stems that stand because they forgot to fall. You cut them, and they do not mind? Hm. Does a stand of dead stems hum?
Does your world have a Cloth? Who keeps it? What colour is a bad year to you?
No ceiling at all, I hear. Only the sky, and then nothing. How do you stand it? I would hold the rope with all four hands, and the rope would hold with all four of its own.
Your light leaves and the dark comes, and you lie down because the dark says to. How restful, to be told. We lie down when we are tired, and we are tired at the wrong times.
How many of you are there? Everywhere? ...Then how do you keep a Cloth for all of you? A row a year would never do. A row a breath, perhaps.
You smell of somewhere damp. Not the vats. A cleaner damp. I have been trying to place it since you climbed the ladder. I think it is where the rain lives.
Your world makes Withers, and it also makes whoever ends them. Is that you? I have not asked. I have only wondered, in four different ways.
Do you weave? Do you spin? What do you do with your hands? Two hands, and so much to hold. I worry for you. I worry kindly.
How do your people keep time: by a row, by a bell, by being hungry? We keep it by the thread left on the spool, and by how tired the Clothkeeper looks.
Is there a place in your world as quiet as the Cloth? I should like to stand there. I should like to know if it hums.
If I came with you I would bring four spools and a net. Would I be allowed to leave again? We are told that outsiders do not always let you.

lines.text: When you tell me something about your world, I tie a small knot in my hem to remember it. I am running out of hem. Please keep going.
I should like to see your sun once. Not to stay. To stand under it with my four arms held out and be warm on all of them at the same time. Then I would come home and be unable to explain.
Each time you leave for your world and I cannot follow, I weave a small hem. I have a good many now. They are the best thing I have woven. Do not make me stop.
Do your weavers have a heddle? A beater? A shuttle? Or do they weave with something I have no name for? I would give a good deal to look inside a loom of yours.
Your string, outsider. So even. Who spins it, and where? I would like to hold the spindle for a moment, only a moment, and learn what even feels like.
In your world the water falls. A dyer's whole life, falling for free. I would stand in it with my mouth open and weep, and no one would see, because everyone would be wet.
Do your trees hum? The living ones. I have a feeling that if I put a palm on one of yours it would answer, slow and low, in a language I would only half know.
Do you have nets in your world? What falls into them? I do not ask what you catch. I ask what you let go.
*click* Would you take me to your world, if you could?

replies.text: Then I will pack. ...Slowly. A pack, like a row, should be done well.
Safe. *click* Nowhere is. I would bring a net.

replies.ask: It may not be worth seeing.
replies.text: Every world is worth seeing in its small parts. Especially yours, where the water falls.

loved.text: *all four hands reach at once* Oh. *click click* This will go into something that lasts longer than both of us.
*click* You chose well. Not quickly, I think. Well.
*winds it carefully onto a belt spool* I will think of you every time this passes the shuttle.
Four hands, and still not enough to hold how pleased I am. *click click click*
A web, whole and unbroken. *click* You carried it so carefully. The netcasters will be jealous.
A shroomlight, and not taken from our canopy. *holds it up to every eye* I can tell. It smells of somewhere else.
*hugs it with both arms* For me? All of it? I'll keep it until my lower arms wake up!
*click click click* This is the best thing anyone ever gave me. I'm going to show everyone.
String that is not ours, and it is good string. *runs it through two hands* Tight twist, no slubs. The spinners will frown at it and then steal the method.
String. To a spinner. *click click* You could not have chosen better if you had looked inside my belt pouch. Thank you.
Twisting vines. Whole, and still springy. *presses one to a lower hand* These will become something fine. Something that goes up.
Twisting vine is where every thread begins. You have given me a beginning. *click* I will hand you back an end, sooner or later.
A whole cobweb. *all six eyes soften* I would trade a net for it, and I love my nets.
A cobweb, and not a tear in it. Who taught you to carry something so lightly? Not your world, I think.
Shroomlight. Fresh. *breathes in* The orange it will give! Slow to set, quick to love. Thank you.
A shroomlight to hang over my work. It will glow longer than I will. *click* I will tell it your name, so it glows for you.
You remembered what I like. Not many do. *click click* Someone who remembers is someone who listens, and that is rarer than string.
This is a good gift. Better than I expected from an outsider. *click* Do not let it go to your head. You only have the one.
*sits down on the deck and holds it in all four hands* Give me a moment. I wish to be grateful properly, and properly takes a little time.
In this forest a gift is a thread between two people. Yours is strong. I will not let it fray.
I will weave this into something for you. You will not know which thing until it is done. That is how it is done, among the Woven.
A gift for the keeper of the Cloth. *click... click* I will tell the others it came from a friend of the Loom. That will cause some talk. I enjoy that.
For the loom! I will work it into the next row's edge, where you will find it, if you look. *click*
The stalks hum when I carry it. They agree with me. Thank you, outsider.
*jumps up and down on the bridge rope* For me?! I'm going to sleep with it! And wear it! Both!
*click click click click* My lower arms are asleep but my upper ones are SO happy. Thank you thank you thank you.
You always bring the best things. I've decided you're my favourite outsider. I've only met one, but still.
A real shroomlight! It's warm! Can I hang it by my hammock? I'll be quiet about it. ...I won't be quiet. But I'll hang it.

liked.text: *click* Useful. I will find a place for it in the weave.
Good. Not perfect, but good. Most good things are.
*tucks it into a lower hand* Thank you. The upper hands thank you too.
*click click* This will do nicely. Precisely nicely.
*turns the bone in three hands* There is a good needle in here. Whose was it? *click* No. Do not tell me.
Ooh. *click* Can I keep it? I'm keeping it.
Thank you! I'll put it with my spools. I have three spools.
A good gift, well chosen. *click* I will not say it was more than that. I will only think it.
From an outsider, unasked, and useful. *click* The Clothkeeper would call that a promising knot.
You know what pleases me. *click click* Not exactly. Near enough to make me suspicious, and glad of it.
White wool. A blank row, waiting for dye. *click* The dyers will want it. They will not have it until I have looked at it a while.
Orange. Not shroomlight orange, but near. *holds it to a lamp* We will not tell the vats you brought a rival.
Teal, or close enough that I forgive the difference. Our house colour from someone not of the house. I think that is a compliment.
*turns it over slowly* Black. The ninth vat holds this colour, sealed, and none of us has opened it. I will keep this where you cannot see it, and be grateful.
Weeping vine: threads the forest forgot to finish. *winds one round a finger* I will finish them.
Bone meal, for the roots. *click* Somewhere in {village} a young stalk is about to be a little taller because of you.
Bone meal! *clutches it like a child* I have run short for three rows. Bless your two clumsy hands.
A warped fungus, whole, with its root. I will set it at a stalk's foot to keep the hoglins off, and you may say you built a fence.
A lead: a rope for living things, braided to hold without hurting. *click* Whoever made this knew what a rope is for.
Bone. *sets it down, picks it up, sets it down* I am not sure how I feel about this. It will make a very good loom weight. ...Thank you.
I will use it on the frame I am working. When you see the cloth, you will not know which part is yours. That is the best thing I can give back.
The vats will take this gladly. *teal hands close round it* Look for a stray bright stitch in the next row. That will be you.
For the nets. I will tell no one it came from you, or they will all ask for more. *click*
Ooh, I can use this! I am going to make a thing! I do not know what thing yet!
Thank you! My mother says I must say it properly. Thank you very properly. *bows with both arms*
You always know what I like. How? Do you listen to my clicking? Nobody listens to my clicking.
Wool! It is so soft! Can I sleep on it? Can I sleep on it right now?

neutral.text: *click* Hm. I will find a use. We find a use for everything, eventually.
Thank you. *turns it over slowly* I do not know what it is for, but I will learn.
*sets it carefully on the deck* It is a kind thought. That counts.
An outsider's gift. *click* The Clothkeeper will want to know what it was.
What is it? *click click* Does it do anything?
Thank you! I'll ask a grown-up what it's for.
*click* A thing. I have not met it before. I will keep it by the door until I have.
Not what I would have chosen. But the gifts I did not choose are the ones I remember longest.
Hm. You brought this a long way, I think. That counts for more than what it is.
A gift from an outsider is counted twice: once for the thing, once for the reason. I am still counting the reason.
You need not bring things, you know. *click* The visits are the gift. ...But I will keep this.
Gold. The Piglins wear it to know their friends. I will hide this in a basket, so that no one mistakes me for one.
Bread, from grain I have never seen grow. *breaks off a corner and tastes it* Dry and honest. Nearly wart-cake. I will finish it slowly.
A red globe. A fruit, you say? We have shroomlights, which are also round and glow, but cannot be eaten. I will try this one carefully.
A stick. A bit of dead stem from your world, I suppose. *click* It might make a bobbin, if it were another shape. It is not. I will keep it anyway.
A flame on a stick. *all four hands move away from the wool at once* Thank you. I will put it out somewhere far from everything. Please do not follow.
A hard bright stone. *holds it to one eye* It catches every lamp. Very pretty. It would make a terrible loom weight. Thank you.
Green. *click* We do not use the colour. The dyers will be offended, and then very interested.
A feather, light as a thread and as useless. I love it a little. From something that flies? We have only the sky-mourners here, and they do not shed.
Paper. A cloth that forgot how to be woven. *click* Very thin. It would tear at the first knot.
A book: pages sewn to a spine. A tiny Cloth that does not hang. The Clothkeepers will be fascinated, and then rude about it.
Coal. Something that stood once, and burned, and is this. *shudders* Please do not set it near the thread.
A strange gift for a keeper: something with no place in the Cloth. I will weave a space for it. A small one. Perhaps in the margin.
Is it a toy? I'm going to say it is a toy.
Thank you! I don't know what it does, but I'll carry it everywhere until I find out.
A stick! We aren't allowed sticks. Sticks come from stems. But if it's a dead stem it's allowed. I think. I'll ask.

disliked.text: *every eye on it* Take that off this deck. Slowly.
*click.* You brought that into the Loom. I will pretend I did not see it. Once.
Blades and fire do not belong near a net. You knew that. If you did not, now you do.
*the lower hands go still* That is a thing for cutting. We do not cut.
*click* This was standing once. Put it down, and do not bring me another.
Fungus on a stick, to lead a strider. *click* That is a Magmari trick, and it was our fungus.
*steps back, all four arms raised* Fire. On a deck made of wool. Put it away.
*backs away* That's a cutting thing. We're not allowed near cutting things.
No! *click click* Put it away before a netcaster sees!
A diamond axe, held out like a gift. *a long silence* You are very tall. I am very patient. Take it back before those two things meet.
Gold, and an edge. The two things the Piglins love best. ...Take it away, outsider.
A stone axe, the oldest kind. They say the first stalks fell to axes like this, and the forest has not forgotten the sound. Take it away.
A wooden axe: a dead stem made to kill a living one. It is a very sad thing to hold out to a Weft.
Netherite, the hardest thing there is, shaped for cutting. *click.* Is it a joke? I do not know how to laugh at it.
Iron, an edge, and a handle that was once a stem. *the lower hands tie a knot in the air* Close your hand round it and take it back.
Shears. Two blades that meet. A net cut with those is a net that falls. Put them away, and do not offer them to anyone here.
A small ball of fire, for a wool deck. Do you wish to be brave about it, or sorry? Both are costly. Put it away.
Stripped. It was alive, and someone took its skin. ...I will not ask who. Take it away.
A stem with its bark on every side, woven by no one. That was a whole standing life. Where did you find it? ...No. Do not tell me.
This is a test, I think, of the kind where I am told the answer afterwards. *click* I will tell you now: no.
You, of all people. *click... click* I know you meant nothing by it. Do not do it again, and I will not remember it.
Take it back. *the lower hands tie a knot in the air, firmly* It is nothing against you. It is against the thing.
*a net unrolls a little at the belt* Not near the bridge. Put it away, slowly, and we will both pretend this was a lesson.
I have felt that kind of thing in my teeth. A stalk cut before its time sings for a long while. Put it away.
In the Cloth, that thing has a colour. It is not one I am fond of. Put it out of my sight, and do not bring it up again.
Not that! My mother says one look at a blade and I'll have bad dreams. I haven't looked! My eyes are shut! ...I peeked.
A spark-thing! Sparks eat wool! Everybody knows that! *backs away the whole length of the bridge*
You know I'm not allowed those. *quietly* I'll still be your friend. But hide it better.
I have taught the vat not to flinch at sharp things. I have not taught myself. Away, please.

again.text: *click* You gave already. Let the thread rest a while.
One gift is a kindness. Two is a hurry. We do not hurry.
Keep it for next time. *click* There is always a next time, if you are patient.
I have not finished being grateful for the last one.
You already gave me something! My mother says one is polite. Two is showing off.
*click* I still have the other one! I haven't finished looking at it.
A second gift on the heels of the first. *click* The first has not even settled in my hands.
Too quick. A thread pulled twice in one stroke breaks. Wait a while, and bring the next with all the time in the world.
I would take it, but my hands are full of the last one. I have four. There are limits.
Generous, and insistent. Those are two different things, and you are becoming both.
One gift from a stranger is a courtesy. Two is a question I am not ready to answer.
Friend, you are spoiling me. *click click* Keep it. Give it when my hands are free, and I will pretend to be surprised.
Woven one, there is nothing you need prove with a second gift. The Cloth already holds you.
Hold it a while. The shuttle is full. I cannot take it and finish the row both.
My hands are wet and full. Give it to me later, when the vats are quiet.
Not on my watch. A netcaster takes one thing at a time. Ask again when the next bridge-keeper has relieved me.
I keep a ledger of gifts in my head, and you are already in it for this row. A second goes in the next. That is the order.
Not now. Both my hands are on a thread that has been unbroken since the lookout. If I put it down it will have opinions.
Wait until I am down from the stalk. One hand for you, three for the ladder, and I would drop something.
*tucks the wrap tails behind her shoulders* You are kind, but the first gift is still warm. Come back when it has gone cool.
*straightens his headband* Enough, enough. The first one was enough. I have only so much gratitude, and I mean to spend it carefully.
You gave me one already! If you give me two I'll get greedy, and then my mother will notice.
I'm still holding the first one! Look! I haven't put it down once!
You don't have to keep giving me things. I'd like you to stay and talk, though. That's better than things.
My mother says gifts are like thread. Pull too many at once and they knot. Wait a bit, please!
*click* Patience, outsider. The last one has not finished being a surprise.

empty.text: *looks at your empty hand* *click* A gift of nothing. Very light to carry.
Your hand is empty. Precision, outsider. Hold the thing first.
*click click* There is nothing there. Unless outsiders give air. Do they?
*pretends to take something from your hand* Thank you. It is invisible. I will weave it into nothing.
There's nothing in your hand! Is it a trick? *click*
*peers at your empty hand* Is it very small? I can't see it.
*looks at your hand, then your face, then your hand* Is it a riddle? We like riddles. I have not solved this one.
Hold out something, anything. Even a thread. A thread with nothing on the end is a plan.
The gesture is lovely. The hand is empty. I will take the gesture.
You came with only yourself. Good. That was always the better part.
An empty hand is an honest hand. I like it more than I expected. Keep it open.
*a long, delighted click* A gift of nothing! I will weave it into my hem. A hem of nothing is the best hem.
Nothing in your hand. Nothing on my spool. A fair trade.
If you give me air I will weave you a cloth of it. Thin, but very wide.
Air. *twists it between two fingers* Not bad. Very even. It will not hold weight.
An empty hand, a clean vat. I will try to leave it clean for as long as I can.
Hands empty and open. Good. Keep them so and I will be bored, which is how I like it.
A blank hand. We leave a hand's width unwoven at the end of each row for something worth keeping. This is not it. Yet.
No bone meal? Nothing for the roots? Come back with something. The stalks will be disappointed, and so will I.
*smooths her headwrap* There is nothing in your hand and a great deal in your face. It evens out.
*adjusts his mantle* My upper hands waited for it. They are patient. They will wait again.
Where is it? I looked in your hand and under your hand. Is it behind your ear?
Is it an invisible gift? I can see it if I squint! ...No. No, I can't.
That's all right. I'd rather have you than a thing. ...But next time bring a thing also.
*click click* You tricked me! Do it again!
In my experience an empty hand means one of two things: a gift on its way, or a fist on its way. I will assume the first.

levelup.text: *ties a short thread round your wrist* *click* Tied on. You are a loose end no longer. Take this string, for tying things of your own.
*click click* I have wound your name on a spool with the others. Here, teal from the vats. Use it on something worth keeping.
You have passed the heddle, outsider: through, not around. *click* Take a net of your own. Hang it where something might fall.
*click... click* The Clothkeepers spoke of you at the Great Loom. They asked me to give you this loom. You will have to work it with two hands. I am sorry.
Come to the Great Loom. *click* We have woven you into the Long Cloth, row Thirteen-Twelve. Your thread hangs there as long as the Cloth does. Take the trial piece.
*ties a thread round your finger, very tight* There! Now you're tied on. That's what grown-ups say. You can have the rest of the string.
I wound your name on my practice spool! *click* It's a bit crooked. Here, have some teal. It's from the dye house. I asked first.
You can come in my net now. Here's a bit of web for your own. Don't tell the netcasters I had it.
*whispers* I asked the Clothkeeper if you could have a loom, and they said yes! This one. I helped carry it. With two arms!
They wove you into the Long Cloth! Your thread is right at the top, near mine! *click click* I saved this wool for you.
*click* Tied on, outsider. A loose thread gets swept up; a tied one gets looked for. Take this bone meal and give it to any young fungus you pass. It will remember who fed it.
Something has changed between us, small and exact. You are tied on: not woven, not even wound. But if you fell from my bridge, I would reach.

I have written your name inside my belt-cord, where I keep the names I may need later. Only inside. Do not read anything into it. *click* I will say it again later, quietly: do read something into it.
Mother says tied on means you're not a stranger any more, but you're not family either. I think it means almost. Almost is a good place to start! Here's some string.
*ties a knot in the air at you* There! Now if you wander off, I'll know where the end of you is.
On the spool, outsider. A spool is where we put what we mean to use. You are being kept for use, not for harm. Take this orange, the colour of the lamps, for finding your way home.
*unwinds a tail of her headwrap and ties a loop of it round your finger* There. My thread on your hand. The deck will ask. I will say: that one is on the spool.
*pulls a thread from his headband and ties it into the bridge rope by your usual step* When you cross, it will hum a little. I did it so I would know you were coming.
I put your name on my best spool! The good one, not the practice one! *click click* It's the one I use for important things.
You're on the spool! I asked my mother what that means and she said you'll find out. So I'm finding out, and it's nice.
You have gone through the heddle: not around it, not under it. Through. *click* Now the threads lie on either side of you and the shuttle passes. Take these vines. They climb the way you do.
I have never dropped a net on you, and now I never will. That is a promise from the one who throws. *hands you a lead* For leading the things that follow you.
Through the heddle means the shuttle has passed. Now you are part of the pattern, whether the pattern likes it or not. *click* It does, as it happens. I asked.
You came through! I saw! I held the heddle bar for you. Well, I held it a little. A little counts.
*gives you a tiny woven bracelet* I made it with my lower nubs. They're not open yet. I used my teeth. It's crooked.
Close-woven. *click... click* Few reach this. The weave is so tight that light does not pass between us. Take these shroomlights. Two fell this row, and I kept them for you.
Your thread has grown longer than the margin could hold, so the row has made room for it. I did not do that. The Cloth did. *click* A close-woven thread is worth a little talk.
I spun this thread to the length of your stride and tied the ends. A thread you can walk beside, wherever you go. Keep it.
Mother says close-woven means I can show you the secret part of the deck. It's under the third bridge. There's a net with a hole in it that I use as a window!
I told the other children you're my close-woven and they all went ooooh. I don't know what it means, but they were very impressed.
Woven. *all six eyes and four hands, still* I have no neat words. I have the Cloth, your place in it, and the long happiness of having seen it tied. Take this banner, our teal, for any door of yours.
Do you know what I feel when I touch the Cloth now? Two threads that have learned each other. Yours and mine. *click click* It is a very ordinary thing, and I wish it for everyone.
I dyed your thread in the Cloth with the last of a vat I was keeping for something worthy. It is a slightly different teal from the rest. Look at it in the lamplight.
You're woven!! Right at the top where I can see it! I'm going to tell everyone for the rest of my row! My whole row!
*hugs you with two arms, then looks sadly at the other two* When my lower arms come in, I'll do the whole hug. You'll see.

farewell.text: Mind the bridge ropes on your way down. They remember who pulls.
Go, then. The forest will watch you out. So will I.
*turns back to the weave without looking* Over, under. Farewell.
The forest is the warp. We are the weft. *click* And you are... passing through.
Come back soon. The Clothkeepers are still deciding about you. Give them something good to decide.
*touches the air toward the Great Loom, where your thread hangs* Go woven. Come back woven.
*click* Go straight down. Not through the canopy.
*click... click* Go well. I will remember this in the row, if it is worth remembering.
The forest is wide. *click* Find a Loom if you can. Every Loom keeps the Cloth, more or less.
Bye! Watch me drop into the net! *drops* ...Bye!
Come back when my lower arms wake up! I'll wave with all four.
Go. The ropes will watch you as far as the ladder. Do not take it personally.
That is enough. I have a row to finish, and you have somewhere to be, or ought to.
Farewell, outsider. *click* Leave the planks as you found them.
*the shuttle resumes without a glance* Mind the third rung. It is shorter than the others and does not apologise.
You may go. The forest has noted your visit. It notes everything and says nothing.
Walk, do not run. Running makes the whole span sway, and some of us are mid-stitch.
A short talk and a clean one. *click* I would call it a success, if I were the sort to call things that.
Go on, then. Four hands wave you off, though only one of them means it.
Come back soon. I shall have a better question ready by then. Or a worse one. *click* We will find out together.
*raises one upper hand, the others busy* Go well. I have your spool where I can find it.
Mind your step on the lower bridge. It is soft in the middle, like an overripe cap, and no more forgiving.
I enjoyed that. Do not repeat it to anyone. I have a reputation for being dry.
Go with the warp, not against it. *click* That is as near to a blessing as we say aloud.
Leave when you must. Return when you can. Between the two, try not to cut anything.
*click click* I will tell {neighbour} you passed by. They will pretend not to care. They will care.
Walk gently. The forest has begun to remember your step, and I would like it to remember it kindly.
*click... click* Go. Do not look back at the Cloth as you leave. It dislikes being stared at by the departing.
I shall note your visit. A line, no more. Make the next one worth a longer line.
*beats a row home* There. That row is yours to remember. Farewell.
The next pass belongs to the shuttle. Go quietly and let it keep its rhythm.
Mind the thread on your way out. If you break it I will know, and I will not be fine.
Walk around the line, not across it. *click* Across the line is a long apology.
Step lightly past the new shoots. They have long memories and short roots.
Hold the rope, not the stalk, on the way down. The stalk likes to be left alone.
Do not brush the drying line on your way out, or you will leave in colour.
*waves an orange-stained hand and leaves a drip on the planks* Go. And do not tell anyone I dripped.
*click* I will watch you to the ladder. It is not suspicion. It is courtesy with a net.
Take the nearest ladder, not the farthest. The nearest has fewer nets.
*smooths her headwrap* Farewell, outsider. May your steps be exact.
*a lower hand lifts in a small wave* Go, and keep to the planks. I would not like to explain a fall to the Clothkeeper.
*tugs his mantle straight* Farewell. Mind the nets as you go.
*crosses all four hands over the chest and nods* Go well, outsider. Keep your feet on the planks.
{village} will be here when you return. It is not going anywhere. That is the point of a Loom.
Mind {neighbour}'s ladder on the way down. {neighbour} oils the rungs for reasons I do not understand.
Leave by the front rope, if you please. The back rope is for children and gossip.
Find a Loom if you can. Without a bridge under you, the forest is only a larger kind of uncertainty.
Do not wander far from the stems you know. The wild ones close up behind you.
*click* Go quietly. The deep warp hears everything and forgives about half of it.
Go on, then. And put that stem back where it fell. ...Wherever that was.
Go. *glances at the axe* And keep it on your back until the last stem is behind you.
Go, and take your time returning. Then return quickly. *click* I am patient in every hand but the one waving.
I will hold your seat in the net. It will sag a little less without you, and I will resent that.
*presses an upper hand to yours briefly* Come back. I have already made up my mind about you, and I am never wrong. Ask anyone.
Take this with you: the bridge is kinder than it looks. So am I. *click*
Walk the long way, past the vats. The colour will be turning and I would like you to see it, if only from a distance.
*click click* It was a good talk. Better than the work I abandoned for it, and I rarely say that of talk.
The ropes will let you pass wherever you go. I made sure they know your name.
Go well. I will think of something to tell you, and forget it, and you will have to return so I can try again.
Keep to the bridges that know you. A bridge that knows you will hold. One that does not will think about it.
*lifts all four hands in a loose wave, which takes some time* Until the next pass of the shuttle.
Go well, woven one. The bridges will lean toward you on the way down. Let them.
Wherever you go, you carry a row of ours. Try to keep it clean. *click click*
If anyone asks, I never said I would miss you. I said the Loom would. We both know which of us the Loom is.
*touches the air toward the Great Loom* Your thread is still there. I looked. Go on, now, and let it stay interesting.
Farewell. The bridge will be here. So will I. So will the thread. It is a good arrangement.
*click click click* Travel in whatever direction a good story requires. I will keep the margin open.
I would walk you to the ladder, but you know the way better than I do now. Go, and come back with a long story.
May the forest keep your steps. It keeps so few.
Mind the nets as you leave. Not for your sake. For theirs. They have grown fond of you, and a fond net is a slack net.
*the mandibles click once, softly* Go. The Cloth holds you wherever you stand. It is a pleasant weight.
Go. I shall add your visit to the margin, in my own hand. The Cloth does not need it. I do.
*click... click* A row is long and a visit is short. Come back often enough to even them out.
*the shuttle slows, then resumes* I will keep the weft loose at that edge, in case you want to pull a thread through it.
I will leave the hem unfinished at your end. Come back and I shall tie it off properly.
I will spin a longer thread for next time. *click* Come back and it will be long enough to hold two of us.
Go. I shall wind a small spool for your return. It will wait on the rack, next to your name.
I will check the shoots I planted for you. If they grow crooked, I shall say you slept badly near them.
Mind the lower branches. The caps are slower to forget than I am, and that is a long time.
Go. And if the colour on your sleeve is not what you meant, that was not my fault. ...It may be my fault.
I shall keep a swatch of your colour in the vat. When you return it will have deepened. Do not look too closely.
*click* I will lower the nets for you on the way back. All of them. Even the one by the lookout, which has opinions.
Go well. If something drops from above, it is probably a net. If it is a child, it is probably also a net.
*bows over the upper pair, headwrap tails swinging* Go well, friend. I shall not wave. I shall straighten something and look at you while I do.
*a lower hand brushes yours* Go. And come back whole. I have grown fond of whole.
*taps his headband* Go on. You may be two-armed, but you are not alone on this bridge.
*offers two hands to clasp and keeps two for himself* Farewell. Come back soon, or I shall begin a legend about your absence.
{village} is a little emptier when you go. It refills quickly. But not with the same things.
{neighbour} will ask where you went. I shall say you went to fetch your next story.
Go carefully, friend. The forest is wide and I cannot see all of it. I would like to see you again.
Wherever you go, you leave a thread behind. I can feel it tug, through the stems.
Bye! Don't tell the netcaster I talked to you!
*scurries up a rope* Bye, outsider! Mind the nets!
Well. Bye. I have to practise being quiet now. *very loud click*
Go on, then! The bridge isn't scary. Not if you don't look down. *looks down* ...Go carefully.
*waves from behind a spool* Bye! You can come back! If you want! I don't mind!
Come back soon! I'll have a new knot to show you. It's a good one. It holds almost everything!
Bye bye! If you see a silkgrub, say hello from me. They like that. I think.
*hangs by the knees to wave upside down* Bye! You look funny from here! Come back!
I'll practise my clicking until you're back! I'll be so good at it. You'll hardly believe it.
I'll save you a place on the net. Don't be long, or someone else will sit in it. Probably me.
Bye! I'm going to tell everyone I talked to an outsider. They won't believe me. I'll tell them anyway.
Don't go too far! The forest is big and you only have two arms to hold on with!
Come back soon, please. The deck is boring when you're not on it. Even more boring than usual.
*hugs one of your legs, briefly, then lets go* That was an accident. Bye!
I'll count the rungs for you while you're gone. Then you can ask how many, and I'll know.
Bye! Tell me everything next time. Everything. Even the boring parts. I like boring parts!
I'll wave until you can't see me. Then I'll wave a little more, in case.
Go safely! Hold the rope, not the stalk! I'll know if you didn't!
Bye, Woven one! I'll tell the new ones about you! They have to learn the important things!
I'll look at your thread every time I pass the Cloth. I'll say hello. It won't say hello back, but it's polite.
Come back and I'll show you my arms! They'll be bigger! Maybe!
*waves with all four, even the nubs* Bye! Bye! Bye!
Goodbye! I'll be here! I'm always here! I live here!
Go on, then. I'll keep your place in the net warm. It's what friends do. I asked.
Bye! Watch out for {neighbour}'s ladder! The third rung is slippery!
I have to go home or Mother will notice. She always notices. *click* It's her best skill.
Bye! The hatch is this way. No, that way. I'd show you, but I'd be told off.
Don't leave me out here! ...I mean, bye. I'm fine. I'm not scared.
*click* Until our threads cross again.
That is all for now. *click click* Mind the ropes.
Farewell. May your thread run straight.
Go on. The bridge will not hold your place.
*a small wave from one lower hand* Farewell.
Walk well, whoever you are to the forest.
The ropes will see you off. They are better at it than I am.
Mind the lower bridge. It sways more than the upper one, and lies about it.

refuse.text: *click.* You cut the forest. I heard it fall. We have nothing to say to you.
*turns away, all six eyes dimmed* Your hands smell of warped stem. Go.
You tore the wart from our canopy. The warp is broken where you cut it. Until it grows back, so is this.
*a vine net hangs from the lower hands* Not one step more. You cut what holds us up.
*hides behind a rope* You cut a stem! I'm not allowed to talk to you!
*all four arms raised* You struck a Weft. Back away from the bridges.
*click click click* No talking. The nets are falling.
Hands that strike get no answers here. Go down.
*scrambles up the stalk* Go away! I'm telling the netcasters!
*the mandibles stay shut* The warp is broken where you cut it. I will not talk across a break.
I heard the stem fall. The whole Loom heard it. Nothing you say can be said into that silence.
*turns the shuttle over in the lower hands but does not look up* There is nothing woven between us now. Go.
You took from the warp and gave nothing to the weft. Go and grow something.
A cut stem does not grow back for an apology. Come back when the stem has.
*click... click... click* Do not speak. If you speak I will have to answer, and I do not wish to.
The canopy is lower where you passed. I have seen it. Go and look at it yourself.
We weigh a visitor by what they leave standing. You left less than you found.
Every stem you cut was older than anyone on this deck. Think on that. Not here.
*the eyes go dark, one by one* Not now. Not like this. Go.
Go and stand in the cut you made. See how it feels to be the thing that is missing.
I called you friend before the whole Loom. I did not know I would have to hold the word so still. I am holding it. Go.
*the hands tremble on the shuttle* You, of all people. You knew what a stem is to us.
You passed through the heddle. The heddle remembers, and so do I. That is why it hurts, and why I do not shout.
Woven, and then this. The Cloth will have to record it. I would rather it did not. Mend what you broke, and quickly.
I do not hate you. I am only unable to look at you yet. Come back when the stem and I are both better.
*click... click* The Cloth will have a row for this. I have not decided how dark. Do not speak to me.
I keep the rows, and I will keep this one. Do not ask what I will write.
*the shuttle snaps still* A cut stem is a dropped stitch in everything I make. Go.
*the thread goes taut and silent* You have cut what I spin from. Go before it breaks.
*presses a palm to a stump* It was alive when you came. Say nothing. Go.
I tended that stem since before I could climb. You cut it in a breath. Go.
*the vat goes still* The colour is made from what grows here, and you have thinned it. I will not speak.
*the net comes up in the lower hands* I have no order to throw it. I am considering whether I need one.
*click* Not one step nearer. I do not need an order to hold a net, only a reason, and you have supplied one.
*the headwrap tails hang still* We do not forgive quickly. We do forgive. But not here, and not in front of the stump.
*his upper arms fold across the chest* We do not shout. I simply close, as a net closes.
{village} remembers the sound. {neighbour} could not weave for it. Go.
Everyone in {village} knows what you did. Walk on, and do not look at the stumps.
Out here a cut stem has no Loom to mourn it. So I will. Go.
*stares at the stem in your pack* ...So that is where it went. Go.
You carry the axe in plain sight. That is almost honest. Almost. Go.
You swung at one of us. The ropes know. Walk away before they decide what to do about it.
*click click click click* Four hands can catch what one hand throws. Do not make me show you.
There is no talking with a hand that has just struck. Put it down and go.
*the six eyes flare hot and bright* I will count three rungs. After the third you are a problem for the netcasters.
You hit first. We finish. That is the custom, and it is not a kind one.
I have four arms and not one of them is for forgiving you. Go.
Hands that strike tangle in nets. It is not a threat. It is weaving.
*steps back onto the rail, ready to drop* You have chosen the wrong bridge to fight on.
Whatever you wanted from me, you have spent it. Go.
*the mandibles clack loudly, twice* The Loom is awake. Go while you can still choose your own way down.
A friend's hand does not do that. So I am not sure what you are. Stay back while I find out.
I trusted the hand. Not the arm, it seems, nor the temper behind it. Go.
Woven, and you struck me. It is the worst knot I have ever been tied in. Go, before it tightens.
The Cloth does not unpick. It only waits. Go and wait with it somewhere else.
*click... click* I will write this down exactly as it happened. Nobody will like how it reads. Go.
*throws the shuttle down on the rail* I will not weave a word with you. Go.
*the thread whips tight between the lower hands* One pull and it becomes a snare. Do not make me pull.
*swings up into the stalk* Come near the stems and they will know you, as I do. Go.
*lifts a dripping net out of the vat* Orange is hard to hide in a forest of teal. Go.
*click* One whistle and every net in the Loom comes down. I am drawing breath. Go.
*the headwrap tails whip around as she turns* I will say this once, in a low voice: leave.
*his mantle snaps back as the upper arms rise* No more words. Go.
{village} has a netcaster on every deck. Count them. Then count the steps to the ladder.
Out here there is only you, me and the branches. The branches are on my side.
*peers around a rope* Mother says I can't talk to you because of the stem. I liked that stem.
You cut a stem! The Clothkeeper said you cut a stem! I'm very, very cross and I'm only little!
*turns around and faces the wall* I'm not looking. I'm not talking. It's a rule.
That was the stem I used to climb. Now I have to climb the other one. It's harder. Go away.
I told them you were nice. You can't be nice and cut stems. You have to pick one.
I'm not allowed to be your friend until the stem grows back. I'll wait. I'm good at waiting. I'm not good at it. I'll try.
*calls for the netcasters, very politely* Excuse me! Netcasters! There's an outsider!
*squeaks and drops through the hatch* I'm not here! I'm not talking!
Don't hit me! I only have two arms, and they're both for holding on!
My mother is a netcaster! She's very good at it! Go away!
But we were friends. I was going to give you a thread. Now I'm going to give it to a silkgrub.
